children.title: Curvature Detection Failures
children.top_down_role: Coverage of regimes where insufficient spectral accuracy weakens complexity conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Detection Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that restricted directional tests can completely miss a negative eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\) and \(\gamma>0\), set \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-\gamma,0,\ldots,0)\) and let the tested subspace be \(S=\operatorname{span}\{e_2,\ldots,e_n\}\). Every unit \(u\in S\) satisfies \(u^{\mathsf T}Hu=0\), so any detector inspecting only Rayleigh quotients in \(S\) may report no negative curvature. Nevertheless, \(\lambda_{\min}(H)=-\gamma\), attained at \(e_1\), and the signed boundary step \(s=\pm\Delta e_1\) guarantees curvature decrease \(\tfrac12\gamma\Delta^2\). Therefore curvature detection requires coverage of, or a quantitative approximation guarantee for, the leftmost eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search subspace orthogonal to the negative eigenspace observes zero curvature even though a full-space direction yields γΔ²/2 decrease.
assumptions_latex: The detector queries directions only in \(S=\operatorname{span}\{e_2,\ldots,e_n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^{\mathsf T}Hu=0\) for every \(u\in S\), although \(\lambda_{\min}(H)=-\gamma\).

children.title: Joint Gradient-Curvature Decrease Certificates
children.top_down_role: Joint certificates for approximate second-order criticality.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m_k(x_k+s)=m_k(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TH_ks\), where \(g_k\in\mathbb R^n\), \(H_k=H_k^T\), and the trust region is \(\{s:\|s\|_k\leq\Delta_k\}\). Let \(\beta_k\geq\|H_k\|_k\), and let \(\tau_k<0\) be an available negative-curvature estimate with a corresponding feasible eigenpoint direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, unconstrained quadratic trust-region models; the certificate concerns predicted model decrease, not actual objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible step \(s_k\) has a joint gradient-curvature decrease certificate with constants \(\kappa_{\mathrm{nmd}},\kappa_{\mathrm{snc}}\in(0,1]\) and scaling factors \(
u_k^{\mathrm c},
u_k^{\mathrm E}>0\) if \[\|s_k\|_k\leq\Delta_k\] and \[m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{nmd}}\max\left\{ rac12\|g_k\|_{k,*}\min\left( rac{\|g_k\|_{k,*}}{ eta_k},
u_k^{\mathrm c}\Delta_kight),- rac12\kappa_{\mathrm{snc}}	au_k(
u_k^{\mathrm E})^2\Delta_k^2ight\}.\] The curvature term is required only when \(	au_k<0\); otherwise it is taken as zero. The certificate therefore requires one step to attain a fixed fraction of the larger of a Cauchy-type gradient decrease and an eigenpoint-type negative-curvature decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a symmetric quadratic model on a trust region, a feasible step is jointly certified when its predicted reduction is at least a fixed positive fraction of the larger of two benchmarks: the Cauchy decrease generated by the model gradient and the eigenpoint decrease generated by detected negative curvature. The curvature benchmark is zero when no negative eigenvalue is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_k\) is jointly gradient- and curvature-certified exactly when it is trust-region feasible and satisfies the displayed maximum-of-two-decreases inequality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(C_k\) and \(E_k\) denoting the two nonnegative benchmark terms, the condition is equivalently \(m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{nmd}}C_k\) and \(m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{nmd}}E_k\).
special_cases_latex: If \(H_k\succeq0\), then the curvature benchmark vanishes and the certificate reduces to a Cauchy-decrease certificate.
If \(g_k=0\) and \(\tau_k<0\), the certificate requires decrease of order \((-\tau_k)\Delta_k^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Whenever either \(g_k\neq0\) or \(\tau_k<0\), the certified predicted reduction is strictly positive.
The certificate rules out termination at a point having either a nonzero model gradient or detected negative curvature.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that \(H_k\) accurately represents the objective Hessian.
Actual objective decrease additionally requires a model-accuracy and step-acceptance condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Decrease Component
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the first-order component of a joint trust-region decrease certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic model \(m(s)=m(0)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\), define \[D_g=\frac12\|g\|\min\!\left\{\Delta,\frac{\|g\|}{\|H\|}\right\},\] using \(\|g\|/\|H\|=+\infty\) when \(H=0\). The exact Cauchy step \(s_C\), obtained by minimizing the model on the feasible negative-gradient ray, satisfies \(m(0)-m(s_C)\ge D_g\). More generally, a step attaining a fraction \(\kappa_g\in(0,1]\) of Cauchy decrease satisfies \(m(0)-m(s)\ge\kappa_gD_g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient component is the standard Cauchy lower bound and remains valid up to the fraction of Cauchy decrease attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(s_C)\ge D_g\), and fractional Cauchy decrease gives \(m(0)-m(s)\ge\kappa_gD_g\).

children.title: Curvature-Decrease Component
children.top_down_role: Coverage of the second-order contribution to joint criticality progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Decrease Component
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the second-order component of a joint trust-region decrease certificate, including the zero component in the absence of negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic model \(m(s)=m(0)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\) with symmetric \(H\), define \[D_H=\frac12\Delta^2\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}.\] If \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\), let \(u\) be a unit leftmost eigenvector, choose its sign so that \(g^{\mathsf T}u\le0\), and set \(s_E=\Delta u\). If \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge0\), set \(s_E=0\). In both cases, \(m(0)-m(s_E)\ge D_H\). If a unit direction \(d\) instead satisfies \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd\le-\gamma\) for some \(\gamma>0\), signing \(d\) against \(g\) gives the computable decrease guarantee \(m(0)-m(\Delta d)\ge\tfrac12\gamma\Delta^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The curvature component is half the squared radius times the negative part of the smallest eigenvalue; a signed boundary eigenpoint achieves it when negative curvature exists, while the zero step covers the nonnegative-curvature case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(s_E)\ge D_H=\tfrac12\Delta^2\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\).

notation.meaning: Signed leftmost-eigenvector boundary step under negative curvature, and the zero step otherwise.

children.title: Joint Criticality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Coverage of decrease guarantees supporting simultaneous gradient plus curvature targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Criticality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines first- and second-order decrease components into one checkable model certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_g\) and \(D_H\) denote the gradient- and curvature-decrease components. A feasible trust-region step \(s\) has a joint decrease certificate with quality \(\kappa\in(0,1]\) when \[m(0)-m(s)\ge\kappa\max\{D_g,D_H\}.\] This inequality is verifiable from the model data, the computed step, and certified bounds used to form the two components. Moreover, if the same step satisfies \(m(0)-m(s)\le\kappa\tau\) for some \(\tau\ge0\), then necessarily \(D_g\le\tau\) and \(D_H\le\tau\), simultaneously certifying small first- and second-order model criticality measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step capturing a fixed fraction of the larger gradient and curvature bounds jointly certifies decrease; small certified decrease forces both components to be small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(s)\le\kappa\tau\) implies \(D_g\le\tau\) and \(D_H\le\tau\).

children.title: Imbalanced Component Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage of cases where one criticality component dominates iteration complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Imbalanced Component Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies loss from controlling only one component when gradient and curvature scales are highly unequal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative decrease components \(D_g\) and \(D_H\), \[\frac12(D_g+D_H)\le\max\{D_g,D_H\}\le D_g+D_H.\] Thus a certificate based on the maximum is uniformly equivalent, within factor two, to an additive joint certificate. In contrast, a gradient-only guarantee has relative strength \(D_g/\max\{D_g,D_H\}\), which tends to zero when \(D_H/D_g\to\infty\). Symmetrically, a curvature-only guarantee becomes arbitrarily weak when \(D_g/D_H\to\infty\). Hence neither component alone provides a uniform joint certificate over imbalanced regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum and sum of the two components differ by at most two, but either single-component certificate can become arbitrarily weak under imbalance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{D_g,D_H\}\) is uniformly joint, whereas either \(D_g\) or \(D_H\) alone has no positive uniform relative factor.

children.title: General Criticality-Measure Decrease

knowledge_statements.title: General Criticality-Measure Decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends Cauchy decrease to a convex feasible set and its first-order criticality measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, \(x\in C\), and \(0<\Delta\le1\). Define \(\chi(x)=\max\{-g^{\mathsf T}d:x+d\in C,\ \|d\|\le1\}\), and let \(d_*\) attain this maximum. For \(m_x(s)=m_x(0)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\) with \(\|H\|\le\beta\), where \(\beta>0\), set \(t=\min\{\Delta,\chi(x)/\beta\}\) and \(s=td_*\). Convexity makes \(x+s\in C\), and \[m_x(0)-m_x(s)\ge\frac12\chi(x)\min\!\left\{\Delta,\frac{\chi(x)}{\beta}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible first-order criticality measure replaces the gradient norm in a Cauchy-type decrease bound over closed convex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, with \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_x(0)-m_x(td_*)\ge\tfrac12\chi(x)\min\{\Delta,\chi(x)/\beta\}\).

notation.meaning: Upper bound on the model-Hessian norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decrease Certificate Relative to a General Criticality Measure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, \(\mathcal F\subseteq X\) a closed feasible set, \(m_k\) a local model at \(x_k\in\mathcal F\), and \(\chi_k\geq0\) a criticality measure satisfying \(\chi_k=0\) at the targeted model-critical points. Let \(\Delta_k>0\) and \(\mathcal S_k(\Delta_k)=\{s:x_k+s\in\mathcal F,\ \|s\|_k\leq\Delta_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-dimensional deterministic framework covering constrained or non-Euclidean criticality measures; no particular outer trust-region update is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nondecreasing forcing function \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) with \(\omega(0)=0\) and \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), a feasible step \(s_k\in\mathcal S_k(\Delta_k)\) has a general criticality-measure decrease certificate with constant \(\kappa_{\chi}\in(0,1]\) if \[m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k)\geq\kappa_{\chi}\,\omega(\chi_k,\Delta_k).\] In the common first-order scaling, \(\omega(\chi,\Delta)=\chi\min\{\chi/\beta_k,\Delta\}\) for some \(\beta_k>0\). For a differentiable objective over \(\mathcal F\), one admissible measure is \[\chi_k=\left|\min_{d}\{\langle\nabla m_k(x_k),d\rangle:x_k+d\in\mathcal F,\ \|d\|_k\leq1\}\right|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step is certified relative to a general criticality measure when it is feasible and its predicted model reduction dominates a fixed fraction of a positive forcing function of the measured noncriticality and trust-region radius. A standard constrained measure is the magnitude of the best feasible unit first-order descent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is the conjunction of \(s_k\in\mathcal S_k(\Delta_k)\) and \(m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k)\geq\kappa_{\chi}\omega(\chi_k,\Delta_k)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathcal F=X=\mathbb R^n\) with the Euclidean norm, the displayed feasible-direction measure equals \(\|\nabla m_k(x_k)\|_2\).
For a convex feasible set, \(\chi_k=0\) is the first-order variational inequality \(\langle\nabla m_k(x_k),y-x_k\rangle\geq0\) for all \(y\in\mathcal F\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\chi_k>0\), then every certified step gives strict predicted decrease.
The formulation separates the outer complexity argument from the particular geometry used to define criticality.
boundary_notes: The exact forcing function must be matched to the model class and smoothness assumptions.
No inspected source in the supplied hints stated this abstract formulation with all displayed quantifiers.

notation.meaning: Positive forcing function for predicted decrease.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For data \((g,H,\Delta)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb S^n\times(0,\infty)\), define \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) and \(\mathcal B(\Delta)=\{s:\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblems; the definition specifies the information returned to an outer method and allows exact or approximate inner solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region subproblem solver-certificate system is a mapping \[\mathcal A:(g,H,\Delta)\longmapsto(s,\mathcal C)\] such that \(s\in\mathcal B(\Delta)\) and the certificate \(\mathcal C\) makes an explicitly declared predicate \(P(g,H,\Delta;s,\mathcal C)\) checkable. An exact certificate consists of \(\lambda\geq0\) satisfying \[(H+\lambda I)s=-g,\qquad H+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad\lambda(\Delta-\|s\|_2)=0.\] An outer-complexity-compatible approximate certificate may instead assert a uniform model-decrease bound \[q(0)-q(s)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}\,[q(0)-q(s^{\mathrm C})],\qquad\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}\in(0,1],\] where \(s^{\mathrm C}\) is the Cauchy point. Thus the system couples an inner output with verifiable optimality or sufficient-decrease data rather than identifying a solver solely by its iteration mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver-certificate system maps each quadratic trust-region instance to a feasible step and checkable certificate. The certificate may establish exact global optimality through a multiplier and shifted positive-semidefinite Hessian, or establish approximate adequacy through a fixed fraction of Cauchy-point model reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every output is feasible and is accompanied by data satisfying either the stated exact optimality conditions or a declared approximate decrease predicate sufficient for the outer method.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For the Euclidean quadratic subproblem, the exact multiplier conditions are necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
The approximate decrease condition can be written \(-q(s)\geq-\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}q(s^{\mathrm C})\) because \(q(0)=0\).
special_cases_latex: A secular-equation method returns the exact form of \(\mathcal C\).
A truncated Krylov method commonly returns the approximate decrease form together with a boundary or negative-curvature termination flag.
immediate_consequences_latex: The outer method can reason about convergence using \(P\) without depending on the internal representation used by \(\mathcal A\).
An exact certificate automatically implies every fractional Cauchy-decrease certificate with \(\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}\leq1\).
boundary_notes: A small linear-system residual alone is not an exact global-optimality certificate when \(H\) is indefinite.
The definition does not prescribe arithmetic complexity for producing the certificate.

notation.meaning: Certificate data returned with the trial step.
Global minimizer of the quadratic model along the negative-gradient ray within the trust region.

children.title: Exact Secular Trust-Region Solver Family
children.top_down_role: Spectral and multiplier-based approaches to high-accuracy solutions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), with \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Write \(H=U^T\Lambda U\) and \(\lambda_1=\lambda_{\min}(H)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblems solved to global optimality by spectral or shifted-factorization methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact secular trust-region solver is a procedure that returns \((s_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfying \[(H+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\qquad H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad\lambda_*\geq0,\qquad\|s_*\|_2\leq\Delta,\qquad\lambda_*(\Delta-\|s_*\|_2)=0.\] In the nonsingular boundary case, \(\lambda_*>\max\{0,-\lambda_1\}\), \[s(\lambda)=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g,\] and \(\lambda_*\) is the root of the secular equation \[\|s(\lambda)\|_2^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}=0.\] In the singular hard case, \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_1\) and the solver augments a particular solution of \((H+\lambda_*I)s=-g\) by a vector in \(\ker(H+\lambda_*I)\) so that \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This solver family computes a globally minimizing step and its nonnegative multiplier. Away from singularity, it locates the multiplier by a one-dimensional secular equation. In the hard case, it uses the leftmost eigenspace to complete a particular solution to the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(s_*\) is a global minimizer of \(q\) over \(\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\), and \(\lambda_*\) certifies that fact through the displayed conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The shifted-Hessian conditions are equivalent to global optimality for the Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblem.
When \(H\succ0\) and \(\|H^{-1}g\|_2\leq\Delta\), one has \(\lambda_*=0\) and \(s_*=-H^{-1}g\).
special_cases_latex: If the unconstrained minimizer is infeasible, complementarity forces \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\).
If \(g\) is orthogonal to the eigenspace of \(\lambda_1<0\), the singular hard-case construction may be necessary.
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiplier is bounded below by \(\max\{0,-\lambda_1\}\).
Positive definiteness of \(H+\lambda_*I\) makes the minimizing step unique.
boundary_notes: The definition concerns mathematical exactness; practical implementations normally solve the secular equation to finite tolerance.
The simple secular root formula does not by itself cover the singular hard case.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the model Hessian.

children.title: Exact Trust-Region Characterization

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Trust-Region Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality characterization for the Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblem, including the hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|s\|\le\Delta}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\), where \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\Delta>0\). A vector \(s_*\) is a global minimizer if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\ge0\) such that \[(H+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\qquad H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad \|s_*\|\le\Delta,\qquad \lambda_*(\|s_*\|-\Delta)=0.\] The multiplier is unique, although the minimizing step need not be unique in the hard case. If \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\), then \(s_*=-(H+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\); singularity permits an additional component in its null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region step is globally optimal exactly when it satisfies shifted stationarity, positive semidefiniteness, feasibility, and complementary slackness for a nonnegative multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_*\) is globally optimal if and only if the displayed system holds for some \(\lambda_*\ge0\).

children.title: Secular-Equation Solvers
children.top_down_role: Coverage of scalar root-finding approaches for trust-region multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Secular-Equation Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact spectral secular solver with explicit interior, regular-boundary, and singular hard-case branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), symmetric \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\), compute \(H=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)Q^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n\), and set \(h=Q^{\mathsf T}g\). If \(H\succ0\) and \(\|H^{-1}g\|\le\Delta\), output \(s=-H^{-1}g\) and \(\lambda=0\). Otherwise set \(\lambda_L=\max\{0,-\lambda_1\}\). If the equation \[\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{h_i^2}{(\lambda_i+\lambda)^2}=\Delta^2\] has a root \(\lambda>\lambda_L\), output \(s=-Q\operatorname{diag}((\lambda_i+\lambda)^{-1})h\). If no such root exists and \(A=H+\lambda_LI\) satisfies \(A\succeq0\), \(g\in\operatorname{range}(A)\), and \(\|A^\dagger g\|\le\Delta\), set \(p=-A^\dagger g\), choose \(z\in\ker(A)\) so that \(\|p+z\|=\Delta\), and output \(s=p+z\) and \(\lambda=\lambda_L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order the Hessian eigenvalues, use the unconstrained positive-definite solution when feasible, otherwise solve the secular equation above its admissible endpoint or add a null-space component at a singular hard-case endpoint.
assumptions_latex: The eigenvalue decomposition and any secular root are computed exactly.
The singular branch is used only when \(g\in\operatorname{range}(H+\lambda_LI)\) and \(\|(H+\lambda_LI)^\dagger g\|\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \((s,\lambda)\) satisfies the exact trust-region optimality characterization.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal eigenvector matrix of the Hessian.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based accuracy for a multiplier–step pair in the quadratic trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) on \(\{s:\|s\|\leq\Delta\}\), a pair \((s,\lambda)\) has multiplier accuracy \((\eta_{\mathrm d},\eta_{\mathrm c})\) if \(\|s\|\leq\Delta\), \(\lambda\geq0\), \(B+\lambda I\succeq0\), and \[\|(B+\lambda I)s+g\|\leq\eta_{\mathrm d},\qquad \lambda\,|\Delta-\|s\||\leq\eta_{\mathrm c}.\] The exact regime is \(\eta_{\mathrm d}=\eta_{\mathrm c}=0\); an absolute inexact regime fixes positive tolerances, while a relative regime scales them by prescribed problem quantities such as \(\|g\|\) and \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier accuracy is measured by stationarity and complementarity residuals while retaining primal feasibility, nonnegative multiplier, and positive-semidefinite shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((s,\lambda)\) is an exact certificate when both tolerances vanish and an inexact certificate otherwise.

knowledge_statements.title: Secular Solver Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the ordinary secular root equation in the trust-region hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=U\operatorname{diag}(\theta_i)U^{\mathsf T}\), \(h=U^{\mathsf T}g\), and seek \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\theta_1\}\) from \[\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{h_i^2}{(\theta_i+\lambda)^2}=\Delta^2.\] If \(h_i=0\) for every \(i\) with \(\theta_i=\theta_1<0\) and \(\|(B-\theta_1I)^\dagger g\|<\Delta\), no root exists in that open interval. The minimizer instead has \(\lambda=-\theta_1\) and \(s=-(B-\theta_1I)^\dagger g+z\), where \(z\in\ker(B-\theta_1I)\) is chosen so that \(\|s\|=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual secular root disappears in the hard case; a minimum-eigenvector component must be added to a pseudoinverse solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solver restricted to nonsingular secular roots is incomplete under the displayed orthogonality and norm conditions.

children.title: Economical Trust-Region Solver Family

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) on \(\|s\|\leq\Delta\), let \(s^{\mathrm C}\) minimize \(q(-tg)\) over \(0\leq t\leq\Delta/\|g\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic quadratic subproblems where low inner cost is prioritized over nearly exact minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\{\mathcal A_n\}\) is an economical trust-region solver family with decrease constant \(\kappa_{\mathrm{eco}}\in(0,1]\) if, for every dimension and every instance \((g,H,\Delta)\), it returns a feasible step \(s\) using only a prescribed limited set of operations—typically matrix-vector products with \(H\), inner products, and vector updates—and certifies \[q(0)-q(s)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{eco}}\,[q(0)-q(s^{\mathrm C})].\] A curvature-aware member may additionally return a feasible \(u\) with \(u^THu<0\) and require \[q(0)-q(s)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{curv}}\max\{q(0)-q(s^{\mathrm C}),\,-\tfrac12u^THu\}.\] The defining feature is the explicit sufficient-decrease certificate, not a claim that \(s\) nearly minimizes the full subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An economical solver produces a feasible step using inexpensive operations and certifies at least a fixed fraction of Cauchy-point reduction. Curvature-aware versions also compare against a feasible negative-curvature benchmark. Exact or high-relative-accuracy solution of the full subproblem is not required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step is feasible and satisfies the declared uniform fractional-decrease inequality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(q(0)=0\), the basic certificate is \(q(s)\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{eco}}q(s^{\mathrm C})\).
special_cases_latex: Returning \(s=s^{\mathrm C}\) gives \(\kappa_{\mathrm{eco}}=1\) for the basic certificate.
Truncated conjugate gradients is economical when Hessian-vector products are available without forming \(H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(g\neq0\), the basic certificate gives strict predicted decrease.
Outer first-order convergence analyses based only on Cauchy decrease can accept every member of this family.
boundary_notes: Economical refers to the inner operation model and does not imply a universal wall-clock advantage.
A Cauchy-only certificate need not expose negative curvature.

children.title: Cauchy Subproblem Solvers
children.top_down_role: Coverage of economical solutions restricted to a steepest model direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Cauchy Subproblem Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization of the quadratic model along the negative-gradient ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) and radius \(\Delta\), return \(s_C=0\) if \(g=0\). Otherwise set \[\alpha_C=\begin{cases}\min\{\|g\|^2/(g^{\mathsf T}Bg),\,\Delta/\|g\|\},&g^{\mathsf T}Bg>0,\\ \Delta/\|g\|,&g^{\mathsf T}Bg\leq0,\end{cases}\qquad s_C=-\alpha_Cg.\] Then \(s_C\) minimizes \(q\) over the feasible negative-gradient ray \(\{-\alpha g:0\leq\alpha\leq\Delta/\|g\|\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cauchy solver exactly minimizes the model on the feasible negative-gradient ray, truncating at the trust-region boundary when necessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(g\neq0\), \(s_C\in\arg\min\{q(s):s=-\alpha g,\ 0\leq\alpha\leq\Delta/\|g\|\}\).

children.title: Dogleg Subproblem Solvers
children.top_down_role: Coverage of piecewise paths combining gradient-based plus Newton-like behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Dogleg Subproblem Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical dogleg construction for a positive-definite quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(B\succ0\) and \(g\neq0\). Define \(s_U=-\alpha_Ug\), where \(\alpha_U=\|g\|^2/(g^{\mathsf T}Bg)\), and define the Newton step \(s_N=-B^{-1}g\). Define the returned dogleg step \(s_D\) as follows. If \(\|s_N\|\leq\Delta\), set \(s_D=s_N\). If \(\|s_N\|>\Delta\) and \(\|s_U\|\geq\Delta\), set \(s_D=-\Delta g/\|g\|\). Otherwise choose the unique \(\tau\in(0,1)\) satisfying \(\|s_U+\tau(s_N-s_U)\|=\Delta\), and set \(s_D=s_U+\tau(s_N-s_U)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dogleg follows the steepest-descent segment and then the segment toward the Newton step, stopping where this path meets the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned dogleg step \(s_D\) satisfies \(\|s_D\|\leq\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Unconstrained minimizer along the negative-gradient ray.

children.title: Low-Dimensional Subspace Solvers
children.top_down_role: Coverage of reduced trust-region models over selected subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Dimensional Subspace Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region minimization restricted to a prescribed small-dimensional linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), and let \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) have orthonormal columns. Solve \[y_*\in\arg\min_{\|y\|\leq\Delta}\left\{(V^{\mathsf T}g)^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}(V^{\mathsf T}BV)y\right\}.\] Return \(s=Vy_*\). Then \(\|s\|=\|y_*\|\leq\Delta\), and \(s\) minimizes \(q\) over \(\operatorname{range}(V)\cap\{s:\|s\|\leq\Delta\}\). Common economical choices include subspaces containing \(g\), an approximate Newton direction, or a detected negative-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the trust-region model onto a small orthonormal basis, solve the reduced problem, and lift its minimizer to the full space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Vy_*\in\arg\min\{q(s):s\in\operatorname{range}(V),\ \|s\|\leq\Delta\}\).

children.title: Economical Solver Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Economical Solver Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cheap feasibility and model-decrease certificate for an approximate trust-region step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), let \(s_C\) be the Cauchy step. A computed step \(s\) has an economical decrease certificate with constant \(\kappa\in(0,1]\) when \[\|s\|\leq\Delta,\qquad q(0)-q(s)\geq\kappa\bigl(q(0)-q(s_C)\bigr).\] The certificate is verified using feasibility and two model values; it does not assert global optimality of the subproblem. If the outer trust-region analysis requires only a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease, any step satisfying this predicate meets that inner-solve requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step is certified economically when its predicted decrease is at least a fixed fraction of the Cauchy-step decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(s_C\) is the Cauchy step for the same model and radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities certify feasibility and fraction-of-Cauchy model decrease.

children.title: Krylov Trust-Region Solver Families
children.top_down_role: Matrix-free Krylov families for large-scale indefinite subproblems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), where \(H=H^T\), and define \(\mathcal K_j(H,g)=\operatorname{span}\{g,Hg,\ldots,H^{j-1}g\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-scale, finite-dimensional, matrix-free Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblems, including indefinite models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Krylov trust-region solver family generates, at inner iteration \(j\), a step \[s_j\in\arg\min\{q(s):s\in\mathcal K_j(H,g),\ \|s\|_2\leq\Delta\},\] or an approximation carrying the same declared decrease certificate, using products \(Hv\) rather than an explicit factorization of \(H\). A truncated conjugate-gradient member stops at the first boundary intersection or detected nonpositive curvature \(p_j^THp_j\leq0\); a Lanczos member forms an orthonormal basis \(V_j\) and solves the reduced problem \[\min_{\|y\|_2\leq\Delta}\ \|g\|_2e_1^Ty+\tfrac12y^TT_jy,\qquad T_j=V_j^THV_j,\qquad s_j=V_jy.\] The family is matrix-free because all dependence on \(H\) occurs through Hessian-vector products and the reduced tridiagonal representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov solver restricts the trust-region model to a growing space generated by the gradient and repeated Hessian actions. Truncated conjugate-gradient variants stop at the boundary or on nonpositive curvature, while Lanczos variants solve a small tridiagonal trust-region problem and lift its solution to the original space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each returned step lies in the trust region and in a generated Krylov subspace, and its computation requires no explicit dense factorization of \(H\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under exact arithmetic, the Lanczos relation \(HV_j=V_jT_j+\beta_je_{j+1}e_j^T\) yields the displayed reduced quadratic.
A full-dimensional Krylov space recovers the original Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
special_cases_latex: For \(H\succeq0\), truncated conjugate gradients either reaches an interior minimizer or intersects the boundary.
When negative curvature is encountered, minimizing along the current direction to the boundary supplies a curvature-exploiting step.
immediate_consequences_latex: Storage can be based on vectors and short recurrences rather than a dense Hessian factorization.
Increasing \(j\) cannot increase the exact restricted minimum value because the Krylov spaces are nested.
boundary_notes: Finite-precision loss of orthogonality can distinguish practical Lanczos implementations from the exact-space definition.
A Krylov method initiated only by \(g\) can require augmentation to handle a hard-case eigendirection orthogonal to \(g\).

notation.meaning: Order-\(j\) Krylov subspace generated by \(H\) and \(g\).
Symmetric tridiagonal projection of \(H\) onto the Lanczos basis.

children.title: Steihaug–Toint Solvers
children.top_down_role: Coverage of truncated conjugate-gradient trust-region subproblem solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Steihaug–Toint Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated conjugate gradients for an indefinite quadratic trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(s_0=0\), \(r_0=g\), and \(p_0=-r_0\). At iteration \(j\), stop and return \(s_j\) if \(\|r_j\|\leq\eta\). If \(p_j^{\mathsf T}Bp_j\leq0\), return \(s_j+\tau p_j\), where \(\tau\geq0\) is the unique nonnegative value satisfying \(\|s_j+\tau p_j\|=\Delta\). Otherwise set \(\alpha_j=(r_j^{\mathsf T}r_j)/(p_j^{\mathsf T}Bp_j)\). If \(\|s_j+\alpha_jp_j\|\geq\Delta\), return \(s_j+\tau p_j\), where \(\tau\in[0,\alpha_j]\) satisfies \(\|s_j+\tau p_j\|=\Delta\). Otherwise update \(s_{j+1}=s_j+\alpha_jp_j\), \(r_{j+1}=r_j+\alpha_jBp_j\), and \(p_{j+1}=-r_{j+1}+\beta_jp_j\), where \(\beta_j=\|r_{j+1}\|^2/\|r_j\|^2\), and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated conjugate gradients stops at the requested residual tolerance, the trust-region boundary, or detected nonpositive curvature, always returning a feasible step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step \(s\) satisfies \(\|s\|\leq\Delta\) and is produced using products of \(B\) with vectors.

children.title: Lanczos Reduced Models
children.top_down_role: Coverage of Krylov projection for large-scale indefinite quadratic models.

knowledge_statements.title: Lanczos Reduced Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal Lanczos reduction of a quadratic trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\). Starting with \(v_1=g/\|g\|\), \(m\) Lanczos steps produce \(V_m=[v_1,\ldots,v_m]\) with \(V_m^{\mathsf T}V_m=I_m\) and a symmetric tridiagonal matrix \(T_m=V_m^{\mathsf T}BV_m\). For every \(s=V_my\), \[q(s)=\|g\|e_1^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}T_my,\qquad \|s\|=\|y\|.\] Hence minimizing \(q\) over \(\mathcal K_m(B,g)\) and \(\|s\|\leq\Delta\) is equivalent to the tridiagonal reduced trust-region problem over \(\|y\|\leq\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lanczos turns the Krylov-restricted trust-region problem into a norm-preserving tridiagonal problem of dimension equal to the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: Lanczos does not break down before step \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in\mathcal K_m(B,g),\ \|s\|\leq\Delta}q(s)=\min_{\|y\|\leq\Delta}\{\|g\|e_1^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}T_my\}\).

notation.meaning: Span of g, Bg, through B raised to the power m minus one times g.

children.title: GLTR Solver Families
children.top_down_role: Coverage of trust-region solution within expanding Lanczos subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: GLTR Solver Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Lanczos trust-region solution through expanding tridiagonal reduced models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate Lanczos bases \(V_m\) for \(\mathcal K_m(B,g)\) and tridiagonal matrices \(T_m=V_m^{\mathsf T}BV_m\). At selected dimensions compute a global solution \((y_m,\lambda_m)\) of \[\min_{\|y\|\leq\Delta}\ \|g\|e_1^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}T_my,\] including the reduced hard case when \(T_m+\lambda_m I\) is singular, and set \(s_m=V_my_m\). Stop when \(\|(B+\lambda_m I)s_m+g\|\leq\eta\); otherwise expand the Lanczos space and repeat. The output is \((s_m,\lambda_m)\), with \(\|s_m\|\leq\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GLTR repeatedly solves Lanczos tridiagonal trust-region models, handles reduced hard cases, and expands the Krylov space until the requested full-space residual test passes.
assumptions_latex: The reduced trust-region solver returns a global reduced minimizer and multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On residual-test termination, the algorithm returns \((s_m,\lambda_m)\) with \(\|s_m\|\leq\Delta\) and \(\|(B+\lambda_m I)s_m+g\|\leq\eta\).

notation.meaning: Lanczos basis of the current Krylov space.

children.title: Krylov Certificate Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Certificate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected and full-space optimality certificates for Lanczos trust-region iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_m=V_my_m\), where \((y_m,\lambda_m)\) is a global solution and multiplier for the reduced trust-region problem. Reduced optimality is certified by \[T_m+\lambda_mI\succeq0,\qquad (T_m+\lambda_mI)y_m+\|g\|e_1=0,\qquad \lambda_m\geq0,\qquad \lambda_m(\Delta-\|y_m\|)=0.\] A full first-order certificate additionally requires \[\|(B+\lambda_mI)s_m+g\|\leq\eta.\] If the Lanczos recurrence is \(BV_m=V_mT_m+\beta_{m+1}v_{m+1}e_m^{\mathsf T}\), then \[(B+\lambda_mI)s_m+g=\beta_{m+1}(e_m^{\mathsf T}y_m)v_{m+1},\] so the full residual norm is \(|\beta_{m+1}e_m^{\mathsf T}y_m|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced KKT conditions certify Krylov-space optimality; the final Lanczos recurrence coefficient and reduced solution give a directly checkable full-space stationarity residual.
assumptions_latex: \((y_m,\lambda_m)\) is a global reduced trust-region solution and multiplier.
\(\eta\geq0\) is the requested full-space stationarity tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced conditions and \(|\beta_{m+1}e_m^{\mathsf T}y_m|\leq\eta\) certify feasibility, reduced global optimality, and \(\eta\)-accurate full-space stationarity.

notation.meaning: Coefficient of the unrepresented term in the Lanczos recurrence.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Subproblem-Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner termination predicates commonly sufficient for first-order outer trust-region complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the model \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), an approximate step \(s\) admits a first-order outer-complexity certificate if, for fixed \(\kappa\in(0,1]\) and tolerance \(\eta\geq0\), \[\|s\|\leq\Delta,\qquad q(0)-q(s)\geq\kappa\bigl(q(0)-q(s_C)\bigr),\qquad \|(B+\lambda I)s+g\|\leq\eta\] for some \(\lambda\geq0\), together with \(\lambda(\Delta-\|s\|)=0\). The decrease condition supports global progress, while the residual and complementarity conditions quantify inner termination accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility, fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease, and approximate KKT residuals form a checkable inner-solve certificate for outer complexity analyses.
assumptions_latex: \(s_C\) is the Cauchy step for the same model.

children.title: Trust-Region Degeneracy Classes
children.top_down_role: Degenerate spectral regimes requiring specialized safeguards.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Degeneracy Classes for the Euclidean Trust-Region Subproblem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|s\|_2\leq\Delta}g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), with \(H=H^T\), smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\), and eigenspace \(E_1=\ker(H-\lambda_1I)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblems; degeneracy is classified spectrally at the optimal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((s_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfy the global trust-region optimality conditions. The instance is regular if \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\). It is singular-degenerate if \(H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\) is singular. A singular-degenerate instance is in the hard class when \[\lambda_1<0,\qquad P_{E_1}g=0,\qquad\lambda_*=-\lambda_1,\] and the minimum-norm solution \(s_p\) of \((H-\lambda_1I)s=-g\) satisfies \(\|s_p\|_2<\Delta\). Its global solutions then have the form \[s_*=s_p+z,
\qquad z\in E_1,
\qquad\|s_p+z\|_2=\Delta.\] A boundary-degenerate instance has singular \(H+\lambda_*I\) but does not satisfy every hard-class condition; an interior-flat instance has \(\lambda_*=0\), \(H\succeq0\) singular, and an interior minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular class has a positive-definite shifted Hessian. Singular classes have a nontrivial nullspace at the optimal multiplier. The hard class occurs when the gradient is orthogonal to the leftmost eigenspace, the multiplier equals the negative smallest eigenvalue, and a nullspace component must be added to reach the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every instance is classified by definiteness of \(H+\lambda_*I\), with the hard class characterized by the displayed orthogonality, multiplier, and boundary-completion conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The hard-class orthogonality condition is \(u^Tg=0\) for every \(u\in E_1\).

In the hard class, the ordinary secular path for \(\lambda>-
\lambda_1\) remains strictly inside the boundary and has no root.
special_cases_latex: Multiplicity of \(\lambda_1\) is allowed; orthogonality is to its entire eigenspace.
If \(P_{E_1}g\neq0\), the usual secular path approaches the boundary singularity and the canonical hard condition fails.
immediate_consequences_latex: Hard-class solvers must recover or approximate a leftmost-eigenspace vector.
The global minimizer can be nonunique when the shifted Hessian is singular.
boundary_notes: Ill-conditioning near the hard class is distinct from exact hard-case membership.
The classification applies to the Euclidean ball; other trust-region norms have different optimality systems.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto the smallest-eigenvalue eigenspace.
Minimum-norm particular solution at the singular multiplier.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Hard Case
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral hard case for the Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{\|s\|\leq\Delta}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), let \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\) and let \(E_1=\ker(B-\theta_1I)\). The hard case occurs when \(g\perp E_1\) and \[\|(B-\theta_1I)^\dagger g\|\leq\Delta.\] With \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\), every global solution has the form \(s_*=-(B-\theta_1I)^\dagger g+z\), where \(z\in E_1\) is chosen so that \(\|s_*\|=\Delta\). If the displayed inequality is strict, a nonzero eigenspace correction is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard case occurs when the gradient misses the leftmost eigenspace and a boundary solution requires adding a minimum-eigenvector component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal multiplier is \(-\lambda_{\min}(B)\), and global minimizers are pseudoinverse solutions completed in the leftmost eigenspace to reach the boundary.

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the smallest eigenvalue.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Curvature Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies singularity through the shifted Hessian in the quadratic trust-region optimality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic trust-region problem with symmetric matrix \(B\), gradient \(g\), and radius \(\Delta>0\), a global solution \(s_*\) admits a multiplier \(\lambda_*\ge 0\) satisfying \[(B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda_*(\Delta-\|s_*\|)=0.\] The solution lies in a singular-curvature regime precisely when \(B+\lambda_*I\) is singular. Solvability then requires \(g\in\operatorname{Range}(B+\lambda_*I)\); every solution of the stationarity equation has the form \(s_p+z\), where \(z\in\operatorname{Null}(B+\lambda_*I)\), subject to the trust-region norm and complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular-curvature case occurs when the optimally shifted Hessian is positive semidefinite but singular; feasible solutions may then differ by null-space components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B+\lambda_*I\text{ singular}\Longrightarrow g\in\operatorname{Range}(B+\lambda_*I)\text{ and }s_*\in s_p+\operatorname{Null}(B+\lambda_*I)\).

children.title: Nonunique Subproblem Solutions
children.top_down_role: Coverage of multiplicity in globally minimizing trust-region steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Subproblem Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes nonuniqueness of global solutions to the Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_*\) solve the quadratic trust-region problem and let \(\lambda_*\) satisfy its global optimality system. The global solution is unique whenever \(B+\lambda_*I\succ0\). If \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\) is singular, choose a particular solution \(s_p\) of \((B+\lambda_*I)s=-g\). The complete solution set is \[\mathcal S_* =\{s_p+z:z\in\operatorname{Null}(B+\lambda_*I),\ \|s_p+z\|\le\Delta,\ \lambda_*(\Delta-\|s_p+z\|)=0\}.\] Hence nonuniqueness holds exactly when this set contains at least two distinct elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive definiteness of the shifted Hessian gives uniqueness; singularity permits multiple global solutions exactly when two admissible null-space corrections satisfy complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal S_*|>1\iff\exists z_1\ne z_2\text{ in }\operatorname{Null}(B+\lambda_*I)\text{ satisfying the displayed feasibility conditions}\).

children.title: Degeneracy Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Coverage of solver protections needed under degenerate spectral structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerically stable solver protocol for nearly singular shifted trust-region systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(g\), symmetric \(B\), radius \(\Delta>0\), and tolerances \(\tau_{\rm curv},\tau_{\rm res}>0\), seek \(\lambda\ge\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\). If \(B+\lambda I\) is safely positive definite, solve \((B+\lambda I)s=-g\). Otherwise compute a pseudoinverse solution \(s_p=-(B+\lambda I)^\dagger g\), verify \(\|(B+\lambda I)s_p+g\|\le\tau_{\rm res}\), and add a null-space vector \(z\) so that \(s=s_p+z\) satisfies \(\|s\|=\Delta\). Return only after checking primal feasibility, approximate stationarity, and \(B+\lambda I\succeq-\tau_{\rm curv}I\); otherwise increase the spectral shift and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The safeguard switches to a pseudoinverse and null-space correction near singularity, and returns only after residual, feasibility, and curvature checks pass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|s\|\le\Delta,\quad\|(B+\lambda I)s+g\|\le\tau_{\rm res},\quad B+\lambda I\succeq-\tau_{\rm curv}I\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is appropriately an algorithmic safeguard, but no source supports the pseudoinverse, spectral-shift, and null-space policy. The procedure also does not specify how the multiplier is selected to enforce the trust-region optimality or complementarity conditions, so its precise solver guarantee is unreliable without a specialized reference.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an algorithm generate iterates \(x_k\) and evaluate an objective and derivatives. Let \(\chi_j(x)\geq0\), \(j=1,\ldots,q\), be prescribed criticality measures, and let \(\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_q)\in(0,1]^q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic worst-case evaluation complexity; the definition distinguishes evaluation counts from inner linear-algebra operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region method has an order-\(q\) evaluation-complexity bound \(N(\epsilon)\) on a problem class \(\mathcal P\) if, for every \(P\in\mathcal P\) and permitted initial state, after at most \(N(\epsilon)\) counted oracle evaluations it produces an iterate \(x\) satisfying \[\chi_j(x)\leq\epsilon_j\qquad(j=1,\ldots,q),\] or returns a separately specified valid terminal certificate. A polynomial accuracy bound has the form \[N(\epsilon)\leq C_0+C_1\Psi(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_q),\] where the constants are independent of the requested accuracies but may depend on fixed algorithmic parameters, smoothness constants, the initial optimality gap, and the problem class. The oracle model must state whether one iteration counts joint or separate evaluations of \(f,\nabla f,\ldots,\nabla^qf\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region complexity bound is a uniform upper bound on the number of declared oracle evaluations needed to reach all requested criticality tolerances over a specified problem class. Its constants cannot depend on those tolerances, and the oracle-counting convention must be explicit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method belongs to the bound family exactly when the displayed uniform quantified evaluation guarantee holds for every problem in \(\mathcal P\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a common tolerance \(\epsilon_j=\epsilon\), one may write \(N(\epsilon)=O(\Psi(\epsilon,\ldots,\epsilon))\), provided the hidden constant is accuracy-independent.
special_cases_latex: For \(q=1\) and \(\chi_1(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|\), this is first-order evaluation complexity.
For \(q=2\), typical measures combine gradient size with the negative part of the smallest Hessian eigenvalue.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing the oracle model can change the numerical count without changing the iterate sequence.
A convergence statement without a uniform finite \(N(\epsilon)\) is not an evaluation-complexity bound.
boundary_notes: The supplied source hints do not include a directly inspected modern worst-case trust-region complexity statement.
Iteration complexity and Hessian-vector-product complexity are separate notions unless explicitly identified.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Trust-Region Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case evaluation bound for reaching first-order criticality with a standard trust-region method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below on the iterates and have Lipschitz-continuous gradient there. Consider a trust-region method whose models have uniformly bounded Hessians, whose computed steps achieve a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease, and whose acceptance and radius rules yield a uniformly bounded number of rejected trials per accepted step. Then, for every \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\), the method produces an iterate \(x_k\) with \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon\) after at most \[N_f(\epsilon),N_g(\epsilon)\le C\epsilon^{-2}\] function and gradient evaluations, where \(C\) is independent of \(\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard smoothness, decrease, and radius-control assumptions, first-order trust-region methods need at most order epsilon to the minus two evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz continuous on the relevant level set
model Hessians are uniformly bounded and steps provide uniform Cauchy decrease
rejected trials per accepted step are uniformly bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le k<N}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon\text{ for some }N\le C\epsilon^{-2}\).

notation.meaning: number of function evaluations to first-order tolerance
number of gradient evaluations to first-order tolerance

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and bounded below on the relevant level set, and let a trust-region method generate \(x_k\). Define \(\chi_1(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic smooth nonconvex optimization; the object defined is a family of accuracy-dependent worst-case guarantees, not a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A first-order trust-region bound is a function \(N_1:(0,1]\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every problem in the declared smoothness class and every \(\epsilon_1\in(0,1]\), the method produces an iterate \(x_k\) with \[\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\leq\epsilon_1\] after at most \(N_1(\epsilon_1)\) counted evaluations. The canonical quadratic-model scaling class is \[N_1(\epsilon_1)\leq C_0+C_1\epsilon_1^{-2},\] where \(C_0,C_1\) are independent of \(\epsilon_1\). Membership requires an explicit declaration of whether an evaluation consists of \(f\) alone, \((f,\nabla f)\), or a larger derivative tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order trust-region bound uniformly limits the evaluations needed to find a point whose gradient norm is at most the requested tolerance. The canonical quadratic-model family scales quadratically in the inverse tolerance, with accuracy-independent constants and an explicit oracle convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The bound certifies existence of some evaluated iterate \(x_k\) with \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\leq\epsilon_1\) by evaluation count \(N_1(
\epsilon_1)\).

The stopping condition is \(\chi_1(x_k)
\leq\epsilon_1\) for \(\chi_1=

If the initial point already satisfies the tolerance, one may take \(N_1(

children.title: Second-Order Trust-Region Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Trust-Region Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional decrease-based bound for simultaneous gradient and negative-curvature tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\). Suppose every successful nonterminal trust-region iteration satisfies \[f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge c\min\{\epsilon_g^2,\epsilon_H^3\},\] where nonterminal means \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|>\epsilon_g\) or \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))<-\epsilon_H\). If at most \(q\) evaluations occur per successful iteration, including rejected trials, then an iterate satisfying both tolerances is obtained within \[N_{\rm eval}\le q\left\lceil\frac{f(x_0)-f_{\inf}}{c}\max\{\epsilon_g^{-2},\epsilon_H^{-3}\}\right\rceil+q.\] The constant is independent of the tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform gradient-or-curvature decrease gives evaluation complexity of order the maximum of gradient tolerance minus two and curvature tolerance minus three.
assumptions_latex: each successful nonterminal iteration gives the displayed decrease
evaluation overhead per successful iteration is at most \(q\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\rm eval}=O\!\left(\max\{\epsilon_g^{-2},\epsilon_H^{-3}\}\right)\) to obtain \(\|\nabla f\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f)\ge-\epsilon_H\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting bound follows from the stipulated decrease and bounded evaluation overhead, and complexity_bound fits the container. A source is nevertheless required for the specialized second-order trust-region decrease interface and its interpretation as an evaluation-complexity result.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Define \(\chi_1(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\) and \(\chi_2(x)=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A second-order trust-region bound is a function \(N_2:(0,1]^2\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every problem in the declared class and tolerances \((\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\), the method produces an iterate \(x_k\) satisfying \[\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\leq\epsilon_g,
\qquad\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-
\epsilon_H\] within \(N_2(
\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\) counted evaluations. A rate specification must state a function such as \[N_2(
\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\leq C_0+C_1\max\{\epsilon_g^{-2},\epsilon_H^{-3}\},\] or another source-supported combination, and must specify whether exact Hessians, Hessian-vector products, or probabilistic eigenvalue certificates are counted.

The two tolerances are independent, and the cost model must say how Hessian and negative-curvature information are obtained and counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
By count \(N_2(
\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\), some returned iterate simultaneously satisfies the displayed first- and second-order inequalities.

The target is \(\chi_1(x_k)
\leq\epsilon_g\) and \(\chi_2(x_k)
\leq\epsilon_H\).

With the coupling \(\epsilon_H=
\sqrt{\epsilon_g}\), the displayed illustrative maximum scales as \(\epsilon_g^{-2}\).

When \(\nabla f(x_k)=0\) but negative curvature exceeds \(\epsilon_H\), the method has not met the second-order target.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Trust-Region Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic evaluation bound expressed through Taylor-decrement criticality measures of orders up to \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(j=1,\ldots,p\), define the order-\(j\) Taylor criticality measure at radius one by \[\phi_j(x)=\max_{\|d\|\le1}\left[-\sum_{\ell=1}^{j}\frac{1}{\ell!}\nabla^\ell f(x)[d]^\ell\right].\] Suppose a higher-order trust-region method terminates when \(\phi_j(x)\le\epsilon_j\) for every \(j\), and every successful nonterminal iteration decreases \(f\) by at least \(c\min_{1\le j\le p}\epsilon_j^{(p+1)/(p-j+1)}\). If evaluation overhead is uniformly bounded, then \[N_{\rm eval}=O\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le p}\epsilon_j^{-(p+1)/(p-j+1)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stipulated higher-order Taylor decrease yields a maximum-over-orders evaluation bound, with each criticality tolerance carrying its order-dependent exponent.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(p\)-times differentiable and bounded below along the iterates
successful nonterminal iterations satisfy the displayed decrease
evaluation overhead per successful iteration is uniformly bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\rm eval}=O\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le p}\epsilon_j^{-(p+1)/(p-j+1)}\right)\) before all \(\phi_j(x)\le\epsilon_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record combines a particular Taylor-decrement convention with order-dependent exponents that depend on the precise higher-order trust-region framework. No source establishes that this measure, radius convention, decrease exponent, and smoothness regime belong to one valid theorem.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) possess derivatives through order \(p\geq3\). For \(1\leq j\leq p\), define the Taylor polynomial \(T_{f,j}(x,s)=f(x)+\sum_{\ell=1}^j\nabla^\ell f(x)[s]^\ell/\ell!\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic smooth nonconvex optimization using derivative information beyond the Hessian; criticality is measured by maximal Taylor decrement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta>0\), define the order-\(j\) Taylor criticality measure \[\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x)=f(x)-\min_{\|d\|_2\leq\delta}T_{f,j}(x,d).\] A higher-order trust-region complexity bound is a function \(N_p(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_p)\) such that, for every problem in the declared smoothness class, the method returns within that many counted evaluations a point \(x\) and radius \(\delta\in(0,1]\) satisfying \[\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x)
\leq\epsilon_j\frac{\delta^j}{j!}
\qquad(j=1,
\ldots,p).\] The definition of the family is completed only after specifying the accuracy dependence of \(N_p\), the derivative oracle, the Lipschitz or Hölder regularity of \(\nabla^pf\), and how the nonconvex Taylor subproblems are certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order trust-region bound controls the evaluations required to make every Taylor decrement through order p small at a declared radius. The normalization by the corresponding power of the radius distinguishes derivative order, while the oracle and inner Taylor-subproblem certificates must be specified separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The returned point meets all order-\(j\) Taylor-criticality inequalities for \(j=1,
\ldots,p\) within the declared evaluation budget.
equivalent_formulations_latex:
For \(j=1\), \(\phi_{f,1}^{\delta}(x)=
\delta\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\), so the normalized condition is first-order stationarity.
For \(j=2\), the Taylor-decrement condition jointly controls gradient and exploitable negative curvature.
special_cases_latex:
Setting a common tolerance \(\epsilon_j=
\epsilon\) gives a uniform order-\(p\) target.
For \(p=2\), the object reduces to a second-order Taylor-criticality bound rather than a genuinely higher-order one.

The inner Taylor-polynomial minimization difficulty is logically separate from the outer evaluation count.

The supplied higher-differentials source hint does not establish trust-region evaluation complexity.

children.title: Criticality Bound Strength Levels
children.top_down_role: Guarantees with distinct requested accuracies across criticality orders.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(\chi_j:X\to[0,\infty)\), \(j=1,\ldots,q\), be fixed criticality measures, and let \(\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,
\ldots,\epsilon_q)\) be independently requested accuracies.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic classification of finite-tolerance guarantees; it compares logical strength before comparing numerical rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A criticality bound has order set \(J\subseteq\{1,
\ldots,q\}\), tolerance vector \(\epsilon_J\), and budget \(N_J(
\epsilon_J)\) when it guarantees an output \(x\) satisfying \(\chi_j(x)
\leq\epsilon_j\) for every \(j\in J\). Bound \(B\) is target-stronger than bound \(A\) if its admissible-output set is contained in that of \(A\) for every common tolerance vector. For identical targets and oracle models, \(B\) is rate-stronger than \(A\) if \[N_B(
\epsilon)
\leq C N_A(
\epsilon)\] uniformly for sufficiently small \(\epsilon\), with \(C\) accuracy-independent. A coupled bound imposes relations such as \(\epsilon_2=
\epsilon_1^{1/2}\); an independent-tolerance bound permits every \(\epsilon\in(0,1]^q\). Coupled and independent bounds are not identified unless their tolerance domains coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy first compares which criticality conditions a bound guarantees, then compares evaluation rates only for identical targets and oracle models. Independent-tolerance guarantees are distinguished from bounds that impose a fixed relationship among accuracies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strength comparisons are valid only after aligning the order set, tolerance domain, problem class, terminal certificate, and oracle-counting convention.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Target strength is set inclusion of admissible terminal points.
Rate strength is asymptotic domination of budget functions on the same tolerance domain.
special_cases_latex: A second-order target is logically stronger than its first-order projection when both use the same \(\epsilon_1\).

A common-tolerance bound \(\epsilon_1=
\cdots=
\epsilon_q\) is a restriction of an independent-tolerance bound.
immediate_consequences_latex: A smaller exponent does not establish a stronger theorem when the stopping targets differ.
Evaluation and matrix-vector bounds cannot be rate-compared without a conversion model.

No inspected supplied source states this complete taxonomy.

notation.meaning: Set of criticality orders controlled by the bound.

children.title: Strong Criticality Bounds
children.top_down_role: Coverage of guarantees requiring simultaneous control across requested criticality orders.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Criticality Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a complexity guarantee requiring one iterate to satisfy all requested criticality conditions simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an iterate space, let \(\chi_j:X\to[0,\infty)\) be criticality measures, and let \(\epsilon_j>0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,r\). A strong criticality bound is a function \(N_{\rm str}:(0,\infty)^r\to\mathbb N\) such that the algorithm guarantees an index \(k\le N_{\rm str}(\boldsymbol\epsilon)\) satisfying \[\max_{1\le j\le r}\frac{\chi_j(x_k)}{\epsilon_j}\le1.\] Equivalently, one returned iterate satisfies \(\chi_j(x_k)\le\epsilon_j\) for every \(j\). Separate componentwise attainment bounds imply such a strong bound only when an additional persistence or simultaneous-attainment argument is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong criticality bound controls the work needed to produce one iterate that satisfies every requested criticality tolerance simultaneously. Separate bounds attained at potentially different iterates are not sufficient without an additional coupling argument.
assumptions_latex: all complexity counts refer to the same algorithmic trajectory
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists k\le N_{\rm str}(\boldsymbol\epsilon):\ \chi_j(x_k)\le\epsilon_j\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,r\).

children.title: Componentwise Criticality Bounds
children.top_down_role: Coverage of guarantees stated for distinct order-specific accuracy targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Criticality Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines separate complexity guarantees for individual criticality measures, possibly attained at different iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an iterate space and let \(\chi_j:X\to[0,\infty)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,r\). A componentwise complexity family consists of functions \(N_j:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every \(\epsilon_j>0\), \[\min_{0\le k\le N_j(\epsilon_j)}\chi_j(x_k)\le\epsilon_j\qquad(j=1,\ldots,r).\] The minimizing indices may differ among components, so these bounds alone do not certify simultaneous satisfaction. If each attained condition is persistent, meaning that \(\chi_j(x_k)\le\epsilon_j\) implies \(\chi_j(x_\ell)\le\epsilon_j\) for every \(\ell\ge k\), then \(\max_{1\le j\le r}N_j(\epsilon_j)\) is a simultaneous bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A componentwise complexity family gives a separate attainment budget for each criticality measure. The measures may reach their tolerances at different iterates; persistence or another coupling condition is needed to obtain a simultaneous bound.
assumptions_latex: all componentwise bounds refer to one iterate sequence
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le k\le N_j(\epsilon_j)}\chi_j(x_k)\le\epsilon_j\) separately for every \(j\); simultaneous attainment requires persistence or another coupling condition.

notation.meaning: complexity bound for attainment of the j-th tolerance

children.title: Mixed-Tolerance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage of complexity behavior under unequal criticality tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Tolerance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces several tolerance scales to one asymptotic parameter for comparing complexity exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a complexity guarantee have the separable form \[N(\boldsymbol\epsilon)\le C\max_{1\le j\le r}\epsilon_j^{-\beta_j},\qquad \beta_j>0.\] In a mixed-tolerance regime parameterized by \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), set \(\epsilon_j=c_j\epsilon^{\alpha_j}\), where \(c_j>0\) and \(\alpha_j>0\). Then \[N(\boldsymbol\epsilon(\epsilon))\le C\max_j c_j^{-\beta_j}\epsilon^{-\alpha_j\beta_j}=O\!\left(\epsilon^{-\max_j\alpha_j\beta_j}\right).\] Thus the component with largest product \(\alpha_j\beta_j\) determines the asymptotic exponent, while ties contribute only through constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When tolerances shrink at different powers of one parameter, the largest product of scaling and complexity exponents controls the overall asymptotic rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\boldsymbol\epsilon(\epsilon))=O\!\left(\epsilon^{-\max_j\alpha_j\beta_j}\right)\).

notation.meaning: relative shrinking exponent of the j-th tolerance
complexity exponent associated with the j-th tolerance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The power-law substitution and resulting maximum exponent are algebraically correct, and representation fits the regime-reduction role. No evidence or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied for retaining this taxonomy representation as candidate knowledge.

children.title: Bound-Comparison Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage of conditions supporting comparison between strong plus componentwise guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares certified monomial multi-tolerance upper-bound exponents under a fixed tolerance-scaling regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two methods have certified upper bounds \[N_A(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=O\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le r}\epsilon_j^{-a_j}\right),\qquad N_B(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=O\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le r}\epsilon_j^{-b_j}\right),\] where \(a_j,b_j\ge0\). Under the scaling \(\epsilon_j=c_j\epsilon^{\alpha_j}\), with \(c_j>0\), \(\alpha_j>0\), and \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), define \(\rho_A=\max_j\alpha_ja_j\) and \(\rho_B=\max_j\alpha_jb_j\). The displayed certified upper bound for method \(A\) has a smaller induced exponent when \(\rho_A<\rho_B\), and the displayed exponents tie when \(\rho_A=\rho_B\). This comparison concerns the stated upper bounds and does not by itself establish tight complexity or compare their constants. If \(a_j\le b_j\) for every \(j\), then \(\rho_A\le\rho_B\) under every positive power-law scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing how the tolerances co-vary, the reported upper bounds can be compared through their induced maximum exponents. A smaller exponent is a better certified rate, but it does not prove that the actual complexities are tight or ordered.
assumptions_latex: both bounds count the same evaluation resource
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_A<\rho_B\Longrightarrow\text{the displayed certified upper bound for }N_A\text{ has a smaller induced exponent than that for }N_B\).

notation.meaning: induced single-parameter exponents of the two certified upper bounds
