knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Multiplier Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary regimes in the multiplier form of cubic global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a global minimizer \(s_*\) of \(m(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs+\tfrac{\sigma}{3}\lVert s\rVert^3\), define \(\lambda_*:=\sigma\lVert s_*\rVert\). The multiplier is regular when \(\lambda_*>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\), so \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\). It is spectrally degenerate when \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_{\min}(H)>0\), so the shifted matrix is singular. It is zero-degenerate when \(\lambda_*=0\), which forces \(s_*=0\), \(g=0\), and \(H\succeq0\). These cases exhaust the boundary values permitted by \(\lambda_*\ge0\) and \(H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cubic multipliers are regular in the positive-definite shifted regime and degenerate at either a singular spectral shift or the zero-step boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(s_*\) is a global minimizer of the cubic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of the regular, spectrally degenerate, or zero-degenerate regimes described in the statement holds.

notation.meaning: multiplier equal to the regularization coefficient times the step norm
smallest eigenvalue of the quadratic matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classification follows from the multiplier identity and shifted positive-semidefiniteness condition

knowledge_statements.title: Cubic Solution Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundaries for smooth local stationary branches and for single-valued global-minimizer selection in cubic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \(\theta=(g,H,\sigma)\), where \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, and \(\sigma>0\), define the stationarity mapping \[F(s;\theta)=g+Hs+\sigma\lVert s\rVert s.\] If \(F(s_*;\theta_*)=0\), then its derivative with respect to \(s\) is \[D_sF(s_*;\theta_*)=\begin{cases}H_*+\sigma_*\lVert s_*\rVert I+\dfrac{\sigma_*}{\lVert s_*\rVert}s_*s_*^{\mathsf T},&s_*\ne0,\\H_*,&s_*=0.\end{cases}\] If this derivative is nonsingular, the implicit-function theorem gives a neighborhood of \(\theta_*\) in which there is a unique continuously differentiable stationary branch \(s(\theta)\) through \(s_*\), with symmetric perturbations of \(H\). Singular values of \(D_sF\) are boundaries where this local differentiable-branch guarantee is unavailable. Separately, if the global-minimizer set is not a singleton, the data-to-global-minimizer correspondence is set-valued; consequently, a globally selected minimizer need not admit a unique continuous branch even when an individual stationary point has a nonsingular local Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular stationarity Jacobian yields a unique smooth local stationary branch. A singular Jacobian removes that local guarantee, while multiple global minimizers create a separate boundary for single-valued global solution selection.
assumptions_latex: Perturbations of \(H\) remain in the space of symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(D_sF(s_*;\theta_*)\) is nonsingular, a unique continuously differentiable local stationary branch passes through \(s_*\); singularity of this derivative and nonuniqueness of global minimizers describe distinct stability boundaries.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the stationarity mapping with respect to the step

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the local branch statement follows from the finite-dimensional implicit-function theorem applied to the cubic stationarity mapping

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Worst-case evaluation complexity of cubic regularization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of twice-differentiable functions bounded below and having Lipschitz-continuous Hessians. Let an algorithm generate \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\) using cubic-regularized second-order models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global worst-case evaluation analysis for deterministic smooth nonconvex unconstrained optimization; operation costs of solving the cubic subproblem are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a criticality predicate \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(x)\), define the evaluation count on \((f,x_0)\) by \[N_{\mathcal A}(f,x_0;\varepsilon)=\inf\{k\geq0:\mathcal C_\varepsilon(x_k)\text{ holds}\},\] with value \(+\infty\) if no such iterate exists. The worst-case evaluation complexity is \[\mathcal N_{\mathcal A,\mathcal F}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F,\,x_0}N_{\mathcal A}(f,x_0;\varepsilon),\] after fixing admissible bounds on the initial objective gap and smoothness constants. Cubic-regularization complexity theory consists of finite upper or lower bounds on \(\mathcal N\) for first- or second-order predicates, counting objective, gradient, and Hessian evaluations according to the stated oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cubic-regularization complexity theory studies the largest number of oracle evaluations needed by a cubic method to produce an iterate satisfying a chosen approximate criticality condition. The count is first defined for one function and starting point, then maximized over a function class with fixed smoothness and initial-gap bounds. The definition separates evaluation complexity from the arithmetic or Hessian-vector-product cost of solving each cubic subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The central object is the worst-case stopping count \(\mathcal N_{\mathcal A,\mathcal F}(\varepsilon)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A rate \(\min_{1\leq i\leq k}\mu(x_i)\leq Ck^{-1/3}\) is equivalent to the bound \(N(\varepsilon)\leq\lceil(C/\varepsilon)^3\rceil\) for the predicate \(\mu(x)\leq\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(x)\) as \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\) gives first-order evaluation complexity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Constants hidden in order notation may depend on the Hessian Lipschitz bound, parameter safeguards, and initial objective gap, but not on \(\varepsilon\).
boundary_notes: Wall-clock time and subproblem arithmetic are not evaluation complexity.
A complexity statement is incomplete unless its function class, criticality predicate, and oracle count are specified.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Cubic Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case evaluation complexity for reaching first-order criticality by adaptive cubic regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\), and have \(L_2\)-Lipschitz Hessian on the relevant level set. Consider an adaptive cubic-regularization method whose trial model uses the exact gradient and Hessian, whose regularization parameters remain uniformly bounded above after unsuccessful updates, and whose accepted steps satisfy uniform model-decrease and approximate-solution conditions sufficient for standard cubic decrease. Then, for every \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\), the method produces an iterate \(x_k\) with \(\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert\le\epsilon\) after at most
\[N_1(\epsilon)\le C_1\bigl(f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\bigr)\epsilon^{-3/2}+C_0\]
objective, gradient, and Hessian evaluations, where \(C_0,C_1\) are independent of \(\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Lipschitz-Hessian and standard acceptance assumptions, cubic regularization reaches gradient norm at most epsilon in order epsilon to the minus three-halves evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has Lipschitz-continuous Hessian on the relevant level set.
The algorithm uses exact derivatives and standard successful-step acceptance.
Cubic subproblems satisfy uniform decrease and approximate-solution conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_1(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^{-3/2})\) evaluations suffice to obtain \(\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert\le\epsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the epsilon-to-the-minus-three-halves bound is the standard worst-case rate for cubic regularization with Lipschitz Hessian

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is the correct content kind and the order \(O(\epsilon^{-3/2})\) is the standard first-order cubic-regularization rate. The candidate describes the algorithmic decrease and inner-solve hypotheses only generically, while its explicit evaluation bound and constants require a theorem-specific authoritative citation. None is supplied.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below with \(L\)-Lipschitz Hessian, and let \(x_k\) be generated by a cubic-regularized Newton method with safeguarded positive coefficients.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic evaluation bounds for reaching first-order criticality in smooth nonconvex unconstrained optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[N_g(\varepsilon)=\inf\{k\geq0:\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\}.\] A first-order cubic bound of order \(\varepsilon^{-3/2}\) means that constants \(C_0,C_1\geq0\), independent of \(\varepsilon\), exist such that \[N_g(\varepsilon)\leq C_0+C_1\varepsilon^{-3/2}\] for all requested accuracies in the stated range. Equivalently, a nonasymptotic sequence estimate has the form \[\min_{1\leq i\leq k}\|\nabla f(x_i)\|\leq Ck^{-2/3}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order cubic bound counts how many iterations or derivative-evaluation rounds are needed before some generated point has gradient norm at most \(\varepsilon\). The characteristic cubic-regularization order is \(\varepsilon^{-3/2}\), equivalently a best-iterate gradient decay of order \(k^{-2/3}\). Constants may depend on smoothness, the initial objective gap, and algorithmic safeguards, but not on the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining rate class is \(N_g(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\), equivalently \(\min_{i\leq k}\|\nabla f(x_i)\|=O(k^{-2/3})\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Solving \(Ck^{-2/3}\leq\varepsilon\) yields \(k\geq(C/\varepsilon)^{3/2}\).
special_cases_latex: When one iteration evaluates \(f\), \(\nabla f\), and \(\nabla^2f\) once, the iteration and derivative-evaluation orders coincide.
immediate_consequences_latex: The exponent improves on the \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) first-order worst-case order associated with basic gradient descent on smooth nonconvex objectives.
boundary_notes: The definition is an order statement, not a claim that every cubic implementation attains the bound.
Subproblem Hessian-vector products are not counted unless explicitly included in the oracle model.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cubic Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case evaluation complexity for simultaneous gradient and negative-curvature tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the smoothness, lower-boundedness, acceptance, parameter-control, and certified inner-solve assumptions of adaptive cubic regularization, let \(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H\in(0,1]\). Using exact gradients and Hessians, the method produces an iterate \(x_k\) satisfying
\[\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert\le\epsilon_g,
\qquad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\ge-\epsilon_H\]
after at most
\[N_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\le C_2\bigl(f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\bigr)\max\{\epsilon_g^{-3/2},\epsilon_H^{-3}\}+C_0\]
objective, gradient, and Hessian evaluations. The constants are independent of the requested tolerances. In particular, choosing \(\epsilon_H=\epsilon_g^{1/2}\) gives the joint bound \(N_2=O(\epsilon_g^{-3/2})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cubic regularization reaches gradient tolerance and curvature tolerance in order the maximum of epsilon-gradient to minus three-halves and epsilon-curvature to minus three evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has Lipschitz-continuous Hessian on the relevant level set.
The adaptive cubic method has standard acceptance and bounded-parameter guarantees.
Inner solves provide uniform decrease, stationarity, and curvature certificates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)=O\!\left(\max\{\epsilon_g^{-3/2},\epsilon_H^{-3}\}\right)\) evaluations suffice for the displayed second-order conditions.

notation.meaning: evaluation count to approximate second-order criticality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-to-local iteration bound for the source's specified second-order method on the class F_{2,3}. The extract gives no convention for cases in which the logarithmic factor is nonpositive or undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be bounded below, let \(f(x_0)-\inf f\leq\Delta\), and suppose \(
abla^2 f\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz. Exact cubic regularization can return \(x\) satisfying \(\|

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of twice continuously differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\), let \(\mathfrak A_2\) be a class of algorithms accessing a prescribed second-order oracle, and let one oracle call return specified elements of \((f(x),

abla f(x)\|\leq\epsilon_1\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2 f(x))\geq-\epsilon_2\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such point is produced.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic worst-case oracle complexity. The function class, initialization restrictions, oracle information, success criterion, and unit of cost must be identical in the upper and lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method \(A_\star\in\mathfrak A_2\) is optimal over \((\mathfrak A_2,\mathcal F)\) with complexity scale \(\Phi(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\) if constants \(c,C>0\), independent of the tolerances, exist such that \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_{A_\star}(f;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\leq C\Phi(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\] and \[\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A_2}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_A(f;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\geq c\Phi(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\] for all sufficiently small admissible \((\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\). Optimality up to logarithmic factors replaces the constants by factors polynomial in \(\log(1/\epsilon_1)\) and \(\log(1/\epsilon_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order method is complexity-optimal in a specified algorithm and function class when its worst-case cost is bounded above by a constant multiple of a scale Phi and every method in that same class has worst-case cost bounded below by a positive constant multiple of Phi. Both comparisons use the same oracle, initialization rules, stopping tolerances, and cost accounting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_\star\) is optimal exactly when its worst-case oracle complexity matches the minimax complexity \(\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A_2}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_A(f;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\) up to the declared constant or logarithmic factors.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\Phi(\epsilon)=\epsilon^{-\alpha}\) in a one-tolerance formulation, exponent optimality means that no method in \(\mathfrak A_2\) has a uniformly smaller worst-case exponent than \(\alpha\), while some method attains \(O(\epsilon^{-\alpha})\).
special_cases_latex: For first-order stationarity only, set the target to \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\epsilon\) and omit \(\epsilon_2\).
For the coupled second-order target, one common convention is \(\epsilon_1=\epsilon\) and \(\epsilon_2=\epsilon^{1/2}\), but this coupling is part of the problem specification.
immediate_consequences_latex: An upper bound for one oracle model and a lower bound for a strictly weaker oracle model do not establish optimality in this definition.
Changing whether Hessian-vector products, full Hessians, or subproblem solves are charged changes the minimax comparison.
boundary_notes: This definition does not itself assert a particular optimal rate for cubic regularization.
Dimension-dependent lower bounds must state how the dimension may vary with the tolerances.
Randomized methods require an expected-cost or high-probability minimax criterion not covered here.

notation.meaning: Charged oracle complexity of algorithm A on objective f for the stated approximate second-order target.
Fixed comparison class of second-order algorithms.

review_flags: No inspected source in the supplied evidence set supports this exact minimax definition and its quantifiers; an authoritative second-order oracle lower-bound locator is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax oracle optimality within a second-order method class

children.title: Local Fast-Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local performance near stable nondegenerate minimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Fast-Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic local convergence of exact cubic steps near a nondegenerate strict minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_*\) satisfy \(
abla f(x_*)=0\) and \(
abla^2f(x_*)\succeq\mu I\) for some \(\mu>0\). Suppose \(
abla^2f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x_*\), and let \(\sigma_k\) remain bounded. If \(s_k\) globally minimizes \(
abla f(x_k)^Ts+	frac12s^T
abla^2f(x_k)s+	frac{\sigma_k}{6}\|s\|^3\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), then every sufficiently close initial point generates well-defined iterates converging to \(x_*\). Moreover, for some constant \(C>0\) and all sufficiently large \(k\), \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\leq C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a strict minimizer with positive-definite Hessian, exact cubic-regularization steps converge quadratically when the Hessian is locally Lipschitz and regularization parameters stay bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\sigma_k\leq\bar\sigma<\infty\), and each cubic model is minimized globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to x_*\) and \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\leq C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\) eventually.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local cubic steps are Newton perturbations of quadratic order near a uniformly positive-definite Hessian
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the local fast-convergence leaf, and the claim is plausible, but an authoritative cubic-regularization source is required for the exact neighborhood, regularity, model-minimization, and parameter hypotheses. The statement only says sigma_k remains bounded, whereas the assumptions specify 0<sigma_k<=bar sigma.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x_\star\), where \(\nabla f(x_\star)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x_\star)\succ0\). Let an iterative regularization method generate \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), possibly together with parameters \(\sigma_k\), and write \(e_k=\|x_k-x_\star\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional local behavior near an isolated nondegenerate minimizer. The definition concerns an eventual neighborhood and is separate from the method's global worst-case complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The method has a stable local fast-convergence regime of order \(q>1\) at \(x_\star\) if a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_\star\), constants \(C>0\) and \(k_0\), and an admissible parameter set \(S\) exist such that every initialization \((x_0,\sigma_0)\in U\times S\) produces well-defined iterates remaining in \(U\), converging to \(x_\star\), and satisfying \[\|x_{k+1}-x_\star\|\leq C\|x_k-x_\star\|^q\qquad(k\geq k_0).\] The regime is locally quadratic when \(q=2\). It is locally superlinear when \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_\star\|}{\|x_k-x_\star\|}=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularization method is in a stable local fast-convergence regime at a nondegenerate minimizer when all sufficiently close admissible initial states remain close, converge to that minimizer, and eventually satisfy an error recursion of order greater than one. Order two is quadratic convergence; a vanishing ratio of successive errors is superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining local estimate is \(e_{k+1}\leq Ce_k^q\) for some \(q>1\), uniformly for all admissible initial states in a sufficiently small invariant neighborhood.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Provided \(e_k>0\) eventually, Q-superlinear convergence is equivalent to \(e_{k+1}=o(e_k)\).
Q-order at least \(q\) can be expressed as \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k^q<\infty\).
special_cases_latex: If the regularization term becomes asymptotically negligible and the accepted step equals the Newton step, Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla^2f\) is the standard setting for local quadratic convergence.
If derivative or subproblem errors merely vanish relative to \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\), the resulting regime may be superlinear without being quadratic.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(q>1\), the asymptotic contraction factor \(e_{k+1}/e_k\) tends to zero.
Positive definiteness of \(\nabla^2f(x_\star)\) makes \(x_\star\) an isolated strict local minimizer.
boundary_notes: Fast decrease of objective values alone is not the same as Q-fast convergence of iterates.
The definition excludes degenerate minimizers and manifolds of minimizers.
R-order convergence and stochastic local rates require separate formulations.

notation.meaning: Distance of the kth iterate from the local minimizer.
Admissible local set of algorithmic parameter values.

review_flags: The supplied local-convergence hints were not established as supporting this regularization-specific invariant-neighborhood definition; a precise inspected locator is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Stable local fast-convergence regime

children.title: Cubic-Regularization Variants
children.top_down_role: Variants retaining cubic structure while changing information accuracy or objective access.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have the form \(F=f+h\), where \(f\) is twice differentiable on an open set containing \(\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(h\) may be identically zero. At iteration \(k\), let \(\bar f_k\in\mathbb R\), \(g_k\in\mathbb R^n\), a symmetric operator \(B_k\), a regularization parameter \(\sigma_k>0\), and a model term \(r_k:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Umbrella definition for methods retaining a positive cubic stabilizer while changing derivative accuracy, sampling, objective access, or a tractable nonsmooth component. It does not impose one common convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method is a cubic-regularization variant if every trial step is selected from a model \[m_k(s)=\bar f_k+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_ks\rangle+r_k(s)+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3,\qquad \sigma_k>0,\] where the constant term may be omitted when it does not affect step computation, and if the step-selection and acceptance rules use only the information channel declared for the variant. The defining structural condition is the explicit positive cubic term; \(g_k\), \(B_k\), \(r_k\), and the acceptance statistic may be exact, inexact, sampled, derivative-only, or composite according to stated accuracy and measurability rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cubic-regularization variant is a method whose trial model always contains a positive cubic norm term, while other model ingredients or the acceptance mechanism may use approximate derivatives, samples, no objective values, or a retained nonsmooth component. Each variant must declare its information source and accuracy conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common defining model has the form \(m_k(s)=\bar f_k+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\frac12\langle s,B_ks\rangle+r_k(s)+\frac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3\) with \(\sigma_k>0\).
special_cases_latex: Exact smooth cubic regularization uses \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), and \(r_k\equiv0\).
Composite-proximal cubic regularization uses \(r_k(s)=h(x_k+s)-h(x_k)\).
Subsampled cubic regularization forms \(g_k\) or \(B_k\) from sampled component derivatives.
immediate_consequences_latex: The cubic term dominates every fixed quadratic model along rays as \(\|s\|\to\infty\), so a lower-semicontinuous model with a proper lower-bounded residual term is coercive.
Different information and acceptance rules define genuinely different subclasses even when their displayed cubic models coincide.
boundary_notes: A trust-region quadratic model without an explicit cubic term is not a member of this family.
Positivity of \(\sigma_k\) alone does not supply derivative accuracy, sufficient decrease, or evaluation-complexity guarantees.
A generic power \(\|s\|^r\) with \(r\neq3\) belongs to broader regularized Taylor methods.

notation.meaning: Variant-specific residual or composite model term.
Exact or approximate symmetric Hessian model.

review_flags: No inspected authoritative source was available for this umbrella taxonomy and its exact structural boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Cubic-regularization variant family

children.title: Inexact Cubic Regularization
children.top_down_role: Cubic methods with approximate functions, derivatives, or subproblem solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Cubic Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive cubic steps with derivative and model-solution errors scaled to the trial-step length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\), form approximations \(g_k\) and \(B_k=B_k^T\), choose \(\sigma_k>0\), and compute \(s_k\) for the model \(m_k(s)=g_k^Ts+	frac12s^TB_ks+	frac{\sigma_k}{6}\|s\|^3\). Require \(m_k(s_k)<m_k(0)\), \(\|
abla m_k(s_k)\|\leq\kappa_s\|s_k\|^2\), \(\|g_k-
abla f(x_k)\|\leq\kappa_g\|s_k\|^2\), and \(\|(B_k-
abla^2f(x_k))s_k\|\leq\kappa_H\|s_k\|^2\). Accept \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when the prescribed actual-to-predicted reduction test succeeds; otherwise retain \(x_k\), increase \(\sigma_k\), and recompute. Stop when the chosen approximate stationarity test meets its tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method permits approximate derivatives and subproblem solutions, provided their errors shrink at step-dependent rates compatible with cubic-model accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The Hessian is Lipschitz on the region containing accepted iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), with inexactness controlled at order \(\|s_k\|^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but the record combines particular derivative-error and subproblem-residual conditions with an unspecified actual-to-predicted reduction test. Because several inequivalent inexact cubic frameworks exist, a source is needed to validate this exact combination and its intended stopping rule.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. At \(x_k\), let \(\bar f_k\), \(g_k\), and symmetric \(B_k\) approximate \(f(x_k)\), \(\nabla f(x_k)\), and \(\nabla^2f(x_k)\), and define \(m_k(s)=\bar f_k+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\frac12\langle s,B_ks\rangle+\frac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3\) with \(\sigma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth finite-dimensional formulation with step-scaled derivative errors and an inexact cubic-subproblem certificate. Other absolute or probabilistic accuracy models are separate variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An iteration is dynamically accurate inexact cubic regularization if its nonzero trial step \(s_k\) satisfies \[m_k(s_k)<m_k(0),\qquad \|
abla m_k(s_k)\|\leq\kappa_s\|s_k\|^2,\] and the approximate information satisfies declared bounds \[| ar f_k-f(x_k)|\leq\kappa_f\|s_k\|^3,\quad \|g_k-
abla f(x_k)\|\leq\kappa_g\|s_k\|^2,\quad \|B_k-
abla^2f(x_k)\|\leq\kappa_H\|s_k\|\] for fixed nonnegative constants \(\kappa_f,\kappa_g,\kappa_H,\kappa_s\). A method is inexact cubic regularization when every accepted or tested trial is accompanied by stated information-error and subproblem-termination certificates of this kind.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact cubic regularization computes a decreasing approximate cubic-model step whose model-gradient residual is second order in the step, while function, gradient, and Hessian errors are controlled at cubic, quadratic, and linear step scales, respectively. The method must certify these errors for each tested trial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining inexactness consists of certified model decrease, \(\|\nabla m_k(s_k)\|=O(\|s_k\|^2)\), and information errors of orders \(O(\|s_k\|^3)\), \(O(\|s_k\|^2)\), and \(O(\|s_k\|)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Hessian condition implies \(\|(B_k-\nabla^2f(x_k))s_k\|\leq\kappa_H\|s_k\|^2\), although the converse need not hold as an operator bound.
special_cases_latex: Exact cubic regularization is recovered when \(\kappa_f=\kappa_g=\kappa_H=0\).
Exact global solution of the cubic subproblem satisfies the residual condition with \(\kappa_s=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: As \(\|s_k\|\to0\), the permitted derivative errors vanish at the scales required by the displayed dynamic-accuracy convention.
The residual condition is checkable without requiring the exact global minimum value of \(m_k\).
boundary_notes: The displayed conditions are one precise dynamic-accuracy convention, not a claim that all inexact cubic methods use these exponents.
A small model-gradient residual alone does not exclude convergence to a nonglobal stationary point of a nonconvex cubic model.
Stochastic estimators require probabilistic accuracy events and are not covered by these deterministic inequalities.

notation.meaning: Approximate function value, gradient, and symmetric Hessian information.

review_flags: The exact step-scaled error convention and residual certificate need a supporting inexact-regularization source locator.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamically accurate inexact cubic regularization

children.title: Subsampled Cubic Regularization
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum cubic models based on sampled derivative information.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsampled Cubic Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum cubic regularization using sampled gradient and Hessian estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x)\), choose index multisets \(S_k^g,S_k^H\), form \(g_k=|S_k^g|^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_k^g}\nabla f_i(x_k)\) and \(B_k=|S_k^H|^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_k^H}\nabla^2f_i(x_k)\), and approximately minimize \(m_k(s)=g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{6}\|s\|^3\). Set the trial point to \(x_k+s_k\), accept it according to a sampled or exact model-agreement test, and adapt \(\sigma_k\). Sampling sizes must be chosen so that the required gradient and Hessian approximation events hold with the prescribed probability; stop when the selected probabilistic stationarity test is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum cubic method replaces full derivatives by sampled averages and chooses sample sizes to control derivative errors with prescribed probability.
assumptions_latex: \(f=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i\), with each sampled derivative well defined.
Samples are uniform, or the displayed averages are replaced by unbiased importance-weighted estimators.
Sample sizes enforce the derivative-accuracy conditions used by the acceptance analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\{x_k,x_k+s_k\}\), where \(s_k\) is computed from sampled derivative information.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subsampled cubic models replace finite-sum derivatives by unbiased sample averages
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and finite-sum scope fit the leaf. A source is required to specify the sampling law, derivative-accuracy events, sample-size requirements, acceptance test, and probabilistic stationarity guarantee; the current statement intentionally leaves these framework-dependent elements open.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where every sampled component has the derivatives used by the method. At iteration \(k\), let \(I_k^g\) and \(I_k^H\) be random or deterministic multisets of indices, sampled according to a declared scheme and measurable with respect to the iteration history.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum smooth optimization using sampled gradients and/or Hessians. Sampling guarantees and complexity claims require separate probability and sample-size assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subsampled cubic-regularization iteration forms \[g_k=\frac1{|I_k^g|}\sum_{i\in I_k^g}\nabla f_i(x_k),\qquad B_k=\frac1{|I_k^H|}\sum_{i\in I_k^H}\nabla^2 f_i(x_k),\] with the appropriate importance weights when sampling is nonuniform, and selects a trial step from \[m_k(s)=f_k^{\mathrm{base}}+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_ks\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3,\qquad \sigma_k>0.\] At least one of \(I_k^g\) or \(I_k^H\) is a proper subsample on some iteration, and any acceptance test, resampling rule, or stopping certificate must specify which sampled or exact quantities it uses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subsampled cubic regularization applies a cubic model to a finite-sum objective, replacing at least one full derivative aggregate by a declared sample average, with importance weights for nonuniform sampling. Its model, acceptance test, and stopping rule must identify which quantities are sampled and which are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining model uses sample-based \(g_k\) or \(B_k\) and retains the positive stabilizer \(\frac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For uniform sampling with replacement, the displayed averages are conditionally unbiased: \(\mathbb E[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb E[B_k\mid x_k]=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), provided the samples are conditionally independent of component values.
special_cases_latex: Full-gradient and subsampled-Hessian cubic regularization takes \(I_k^g=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and \(|I_k^H|<N\).
When both samples contain all indices with uniform weights, the iteration reduces to the full finite-sum cubic model.
immediate_consequences_latex: The per-iteration component-derivative cost is governed separately by \(|I_k^g|\) and \(|I_k^H|\).
Sampling without replacement generally changes variance but not the displayed uniform sample-average form.
boundary_notes: A stochastic expectation objective without an explicit finite-sum representation is outside this definition.
Unbiasedness alone does not provide the concentration bounds needed for high-probability convergence.
The base value \(f_k^{\mathrm{base}}\) does not affect step computation but can affect an objective-based acceptance ratio.
review_flags: No inspected source supports the exact finite-sum model and sampling conventions stated here.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-sum subsampled cubic regularization

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Function-Free Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-only cubic acceptance based on agreement between trial derivatives and the local model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x_k\), evaluate \(g_k=
abla f(x_k)\) and \(H_k=
abla^2f(x_k)\), compute an approximate minimizer \(s_k\) of \(m_k(s)=g_k^Ts+	frac12s^TH_ks+	frac{\sigma_k}{6}\|s\|^3\), and evaluate derivatives at \(x_k+s_k\). Accept the trial point when a derivative-agreement condition such as \(\|
abla f(x_k+s_k)-g_k-H_ks_k\|\leq\kappa_a\sigma_k\|s_k\|^2\) holds together with the model-step certificate. On rejection, retain \(x_k\) and increase \(\sigma_k\). This rule uses no value of \(f\); termination is based on derivative stationarity measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-function-free regularization accepts cubic steps using derivative agreement and model certificates, without evaluating objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable and its Hessian satisfies the smoothness condition underlying the derivative-agreement test.
Derivatives are available at the current and trial points.
The computed step satisfies the stipulated cubic-model certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The acceptance decision and stopping test require derivatives but no evaluations of \(f(x_k)\) or \(f(x_k+s_k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the objective-function-free leaf, but the proposed derivative-agreement inequality is presented only as an example and may not constitute the acceptance mechanism of a recognized objective-function-free regularization framework. A source is needed for the exact test, step certificate, parameter update, and complexity setting.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be smooth, but suppose the algorithmic oracle exposes derivatives \(\nabla^j f(x)\) for prescribed orders \(j\geq1\) and does not expose \(f(x)\). Let \(\mathcal H_k\) denote the sigma-algebra generated by past iterates, derivative observations, internal randomization, trial steps, and regularization parameters.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-based definition for methods that globalize regularized Taylor models without objective-value evaluations. It does not prescribe one particular derivative-only acceptance statistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A regularization method is objective-function-free if, for every iteration \(k\), its trial model may omit its additive constant, its step \(s_k\), acceptance indicator \(a_k\in\{0,1\}\), next iterate \(x_{k+1}\), and parameter \(\sigma_{k+1}\) are measurable functions only of \(\mathcal H_k\) and derivative observations at declared points, and no decision queries or uses any value \(f(y)\). For a cubic instance, the step model is \[\widehat m_k(s)=\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_ks\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3,\] while acceptance is determined by a stated derivative-based progress or stationarity certificate rather than the usual actual-to-predicted objective-decrease ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective-function-free regularization method computes steps, accepts or rejects them, updates its regularization parameter, and terminates using derivative observations and internal history only. It never evaluates or uses an objective value, and an additive model constant is therefore unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective-function-free operation is the information restriction \((s_k,a_k,x_{k+1},\sigma_{k+1})\in\sigma(\mathcal H_k,\text{declared derivative observations})\) with no dependence on any \(f(y)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Two objectives differing by an arbitrary additive constant generate identical algorithmic decisions under this definition whenever their exposed derivatives coincide.
special_cases_latex: A derivative-only cubic method can test a certified reduction in gradient norm or a Taylor-gradient consistency statistic at \(x_k+s_k\).
An algorithm that evaluates \(f\) only for reporting, but never permits those values to affect any decision, remains objective-function-free in the decision-theoretic sense.
immediate_consequences_latex: The classical ratio \((f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k))/(m_k(0)-m_k(s_k))\) cannot be used.
The generated trajectory is invariant under replacing \(f\) by \(f+c\) for any constant \(c\).
boundary_notes: Derivative-free optimization is different: it uses objective values but no derivatives.
Merely omitting the constant term from the model does not make a method objective-function-free if its acceptance test evaluates \(f\).
A complexity guarantee requires a concrete derivative-only certificate and smoothness assumptions beyond this information definition.

notation.meaning: Algorithmic history generated without objective values.

review_flags: A source defining the exact derivative-only information model and an accepted progress certificate is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-only objective-function-free regularization

children.title: Composite-Proximal Cubic Regularization
children.top_down_role: Cubic models retaining a tractable nonsmooth component.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F=f+h\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(\operatorname{dom}h\), and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with a tractable proximal or model subproblem. Let \(x_k\in\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(\sigma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional composite optimization. The nonsmooth term is retained exactly in the trial model; convexity of that term is an additional subclass assumption, not part of the structural definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The composite-proximal cubic model at \(x_k\) is \[m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle\nabla f(x_k),s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,\nabla^2f(x_k)s\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3+h(x_k+s).\] A composite-proximal cubic-regularization step is any admissible \(s_k\) with \(x_k+s_k\in\operatorname{dom}h\) satisfying a declared exact or approximate model-decrease and stationarity certificate for this model. The defining feature is that \(h(x_k+s)\) is not replaced by a derivative expansion; it remains an exact extended-real term that encodes nonsmoothness and domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite-proximal cubic regularization minimizes or sufficiently decreases a model containing the quadratic Taylor expansion of the smooth part, a positive cubic norm term, and the nonsmooth component evaluated exactly at the trial point. Feasibility is represented by membership of the trial point in the domain of the nonsmooth term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining model is \(T_2^f(x_k,s)+\frac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3+h(x_k+s)\), with \(x_k+s\in\operatorname{dom}h\).

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Cubic Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point representation of nonzero stationary composite cubic steps through a Euclidean proximal map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the composite model \(M_x(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs+\tfrac{\sigma}{6}\|s\|^3+h(x+s)\), a nonzero step \(s\) is stationary exactly when \(0\in g+Hs+\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\|s\|s+\partial h(x+s)\). Setting \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\|s\|>0\), this inclusion is equivalent to the proximal fixed-point equation \(x+s=\operatorname{prox}_{h/\lambda}(x-\lambda^{-1}(g+Hs))\), where \(\operatorname{prox}_{h/\lambda}(v)=\arg\min_z\{h(z)/\lambda+\tfrac12\|z-v\|^2\}\). The relation is implicit because both \(Hs\) and \(\lambda\) depend on the unknown step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero stationary composite cubic step is an implicit proximal fixed point whose proximal parameter is proportional to the step norm.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in g+Hs+\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\|s\|s+\partial h(x+s)\iff x+s=\operatorname{prox}_{h/\lambda}(x-\lambda^{-1}(g+Hs))\), with \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\|s\|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Subproblem Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable residual and decrease conditions for approximate composite cubic subproblem solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a composite cubic model \(M_x\), a step \(s\) has an \((\eta_d,	au)\)-structured certificate if \(M_x(s)\leq M_x(0)-\eta_d\sigma\|s\|^3\) and there exists \(v\in\partial h(x+s)\) such that \(r=g+Hs+	frac{\sigma}{2}\|s\|s+v\) satisfies \(\|r\|\leq\tau\|s\|^2\). The certificate is checked using the model value, a supplied subgradient \(v\), and matrix-vector products with \(H\). It certifies cubic-scale model decrease and approximate first-order stationarity of the structured subproblem; without an additional global-curvature condition, it does not certify global minimality when \(H\) is indefinite.

children.title: Composite Tractability Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Tractability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex proximal structure is essential; unrestricted nonconvex composite terms can encode discrete feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tractability of composite cubic subproblems does not extend from proper closed convex \(h\) to arbitrary nonconvex \(h\). Given a Boolean formula \(\phi\), let \(C_\phi\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be its satisfying assignments and set \(h=\delta_{C_\phi}\). With \(g=0\), \(H=0\), and \(\sigma>0\), deciding whether the model \(M(s)=\tfrac{\sigma}{6}\|s\|^3+h(s)\) has a finite minimizer is exactly deciding whether \(C_\phi\neq\varnothing\). Thus, after convexity and an efficiently computable proximal interface are removed, even existence or global solution of the structured cubic subproblem can encode Boolean satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing an arbitrary nonconvex composite term destroys generic tractability: a cubic subproblem can directly encode Boolean satisfiability.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is a Boolean formula on \(n\) variables.
\(h=\delta_{C_\phi}\) is allowed to be nonconvex and extended-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_s M(s)<+\infty\iff C_\phi\neq\varnothing\); hence unrestricted nonconvex composite cubic subproblems are not generically tractable.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space with norm \(\|\cdot\|_G\), let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be \(p\)-times differentiable, and let \(R_G:E\to[0,+\infty)\) be a positive homogeneous gauge of degree one with \(R_G(s)=0\) only for \(s=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Power Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-\(p\) Taylor models regularized by the canonical power \(p+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\geq1\), let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(p\)-times differentiable at \(x\), and define its degree-\(p\) Taylor polynomial by \(T_p(x,s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\tfrac1{j!}\nabla^jf(x)[s]^j\). A canonical-power regularized Taylor model is \(m_{p,\sigma}(x,s)=T_p(x,s)+	frac{\sigma}{(p+1)!}\|s\|^{p+1}\), with \(\sigma>0\). The exponent is canonical because a Lipschitz \(p\)-th derivative yields a Taylor remainder of order \(\|s\|^{p+1}\), so a sufficiently large \(\sigma\) can dominate that remainder.

knowledge_statements.title: Over-Regularized Taylor Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taylor models whose regularizer has power strictly above the canonical exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a degree-\(p\) Taylor polynomial \(T_p(x,s)\), an over-power regularized model has the form \(m_{p,r}(x,s)=T_p(x,s)+\tfrac{\sigma}{r}\|s\|^r\), where \(r>p+1\) and \(\sigma>0\). The larger exponent imposes stronger growth for large \(\|s\|\), but it is smaller than a canonical \(\|s\|^{p+1}\) term as \(s\to0\). Consequently, under only a Lipschitz \(p\)-th derivative, increasing \(\sigma\) does not make this term uniformly dominate a nonzero order-\(p+1\) Taylor remainder on every sufficiently small punctured neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Euclidean Regularized Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-based arbitrary-order Taylor regularization on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space with norm \(\|\cdot\|_X\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be \(p\)-times differentiable at \(x\), and choose \(r>p\) and \(\sigma>0\). The non-Euclidean regularized Taylor model is
\[
m_{x,\sigma}(s)=T_p(x,s)+\frac{\sigma}{r}\|s\|_X^r,
\qquad
T_p(x,s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^j f(x)[s]^j.
\]
Derivative tensor norms are the operator norms induced by \(\|\cdot\|_X\); thus model-error and criticality estimates must use the same primal norm and its dual norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized Taylor models in a non-Euclidean norm
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space equipped with a norm \(\|\cdot\|_G\) and dual norm \(\|z\|_{G,*}=\sup_{\|s\|_G\leq1}\langle z,s\rangle\). Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) possess derivatives through order \(p\), interpreted as multilinear forms with operator norms induced by \(\|\cdot\|_G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-geometric higher-order regularization in finite dimensions. Bregman or manifold regularizers require additional structure and are not identified with this norm-power definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A non-Euclidean regularized Taylor model of degree \(p\) and power \(r>p\) is \[m_{p,r,G}(x;s)=T_p^f(x,s)+\frac{\sigma}{r}\|s\|_G^r,\qquad \sigma>0,\] where all derivative norms, Hölder or Lipschitz conditions, step certificates, and criticality measures are evaluated using \(\|\cdot\|_G\) and its dual. It is genuinely non-Euclidean relative to a fixed reference formulation when \(\|\cdot\|_G\) is not the designated Euclidean norm up to a scalar multiple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-Euclidean regularized model replaces the Euclidean step norm by a declared alternative norm and consistently uses that norm and its dual for derivative bounds, stationarity, and subproblem certificates. The regularization power remains greater than the Taylor degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining model is \(T_p^f(x,s)+\frac{\sigma}{r}\|s\|_G^r\), together with consistent primal-dual geometric conventions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\|s\|_G=(s^TGs)^{1/2}\) for \(G\succ0\), the change of variables \(y=G^{1/2}s\) converts the regularizer to a Euclidean norm power while transforming every derivative tensor.
special_cases_latex: Weighted Euclidean geometry uses \(\|s\|_G=(s^TGs)^{1/2}\) with \(G\succ0\).
Coordinate-adapted models may use \(\ell_1\), \(\ell_\infty\), or block norms, subject to an appropriate subproblem certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Stationarity residuals naturally use the dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_{G,*}\).
In finite dimensions, norm equivalence transfers qualitative coercivity but changes quantitative constants.

A Bregman divergence generally is not homogeneous and therefore is not a norm-power regularizer.
Complexity constants can depend on dimension through norm-equivalence factors.

children.title: Arbitrary-Order Method Framework
children.top_down_role: Adaptive regularization mechanisms common across derivative and target orders.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), choose Taylor degree \(p\geq1\), target order \(q\leq p\), regularization power \(r>p\), and parameters \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\), \(\sigma_k>0\). Define \(m_k(s)=T_p^f(x_k,s)+\frac{\sigma_k}{r}\|s\|^r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic unconstrained framework using objective-based acceptance. It specifies the common mechanism across derivative orders but leaves the exact subproblem solver and criticality measure as declared components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iteration of the arbitrary-order method framework computes \(s_k\) satisfying a declared model-decrease and order-\(q\) model-criticality certificate, forms the unregularized Taylor prediction \(\Delta T_k=T_p^f(x_k,0)-T_p^f(x_k,s_k)>0\), and evaluates \[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{\Delta T_k}.\] It sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) otherwise, then updates \(\sigma_k\) within prescribed intervals that permit a decrease after very successful iterations, bounded change after successful iterations, and an increase after unsuccessful iterations. Termination uses a declared order-\(q\) criticality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The framework computes a certified step from a regularized degree-p Taylor model, compares actual objective decrease with unregularized Taylor-predicted decrease, accepts sufficiently successful trials, and changes the regularization parameter according to the quality of agreement. It targets criticality of a selected order q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The framework is the state transition determined by \(m_k\), the certified \(s_k\), the ratio \(\rho_k\), threshold acceptance, and an outcome-dependent update of \(\sigma_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the regularized-model decrement in the denominator defines a related framework, but its thresholds and analysis must be stated consistently and are not identical by definition.
special_cases_latex: With \(p=2\), \(r=3\), and \(q=1\), the framework specializes to first-order-target adaptive cubic regularization.
With \(p=2\), \(r=3\), and \(q=2\), it targets approximate second-order criticality.
immediate_consequences_latex: Rejected trials leave the optimization iterate unchanged while allowing the model parameter to change.
The same outer framework can host exact, iterative, or tensor-free subproblem solvers if they provide the required certificate.
boundary_notes: The denominator must be positive for the displayed ratio to be defined.
Derivative-only acceptance is an objective-function-free variant, not this objective-ratio framework.
A full algorithm must specify numerical update intervals and its exact criticality measure.
review_flags: An inspected arbitrary-order adaptive-regularization source is required for the precise ratio and parameter-update framework.

children.title: Regularization-Parameter Adaptation

knowledge_statements.title: Regularization-Parameter Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance-ratio update for an adaptive order-\(p\) regularization method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\), \(\sigma_k\geq\sigma_{\min}>0\), thresholds \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\), and factors \(0<\gamma_1<1<\gamma_2\leq\gamma_3\), compute a model-reducing step \(s_k\) and
\[
\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{T_p(x_k,0)-T_p(x_k,s_k)}.
\]
Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) if \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), and otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). Choose
\[
\sigma_{k+1}\in
\begin{cases}
[\max\{\sigma_{\min},\gamma_1\sigma_k\},\sigma_k],&\rho_k\geq\eta_2,\\
[\sigma_k,\gamma_2\sigma_k],&\eta_1\leq\rho_k<\eta_2,\\
[\gamma_2\sigma_k,\gamma_3\sigma_k],&\rho_k<\eta_1.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a step when actual reduction sufficiently matches Taylor-predicted reduction; decrease regularization after very successful steps and increase it after unsuccessful ones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update preserves \(\sigma_{k+1}\geq\sigma_{\min}\) and adjusts regularization according to model agreement.

notation.meaning: Ratio of actual to Taylor-predicted objective reduction.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\sigma_k\geq\sigma_{\min}>0\) be the regularization parameter, let \(\rho_k\) be a declared trial-success statistic, and choose thresholds \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\) and factors \(0<\gamma_1<1<\gamma_2\leq\gamma_3\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic multiplicative update used by objective-based adaptive regularization. The precise success statistic is external to this definition but must be fixed consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A regularization-parameter adaptation rule is acceptance-controlled when \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) for \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) otherwise, and \[\sigma_{k+1}\in\begin{cases}[\max\{\sigma_{\min},\gamma_1\sigma_k\},\sigma_k],&\rho_k\geq\eta_2,\\[\sigma_k,\gamma_2\sigma_k],&\eta_1\leq\rho_k<\eta_2,\\[\gamma_2\sigma_k,\gamma_3\sigma_k],&\rho_k<\eta_1.\end{cases}\] Thus very successful trials permit weaker regularization, successful trials prevent an obligatory decrease, and unsuccessful trials enforce stronger regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acceptance-controlled update classifies a trial as very successful, successful, or unsuccessful using two thresholds. It may decrease the regularization parameter after very successful trials, keeps it within a bounded nondecreasing interval after ordinary success, and must multiply it upward after failure, while maintaining a positive lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining state update is the displayed three-case inclusion for \(\sigma_{k+1}\), coupled with acceptance exactly when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A deterministic update selecting one endpoint from each displayed interval is a special case of the set-valued rule.
special_cases_latex: The common endpoint rule chooses \(\sigma_{k+1}=\max\{\sigma_{\min},\gamma_1\sigma_k\}\), \(\sigma_k\), or \(\gamma_2\sigma_k\) in the three respective cases.
If \(\eta_1=\eta_2\), the ordinary-success middle region is empty.
immediate_consequences_latex: The lower bound \(\sigma_k\geq\sigma_{\min}\) is invariant.
Each unsuccessful iteration satisfies \(\sigma_{k+1}\geq\gamma_2\sigma_k\).
Rejected steps can change \(\sigma_k\) even though they do not change \(x_k\).
boundary_notes: Threshold equality conventions must remain fixed at the interval boundaries.
A rule based on derivative-only certificates is admissible only after redefining \(\rho_k\) accordingly.
The update rule alone does not guarantee that \(\sigma_k\) is bounded above.

children.title: Higher-Order Model-Decrease Certificates
children.top_down_role: Progress certificates for regularized Taylor models.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Model-Decrease Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model reduction plus approximate Taylor criticality of the computed step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(q\)-times differentiable near \(s_k\), and equip \(\mathbb R^n\) with a specified norm \(\|\cdot\|\). A step-radius pair \((s_k,\boldsymbol\delta_k)\), where \(\boldsymbol\delta_k=(\delta_{k,1},\ldots,\delta_{k,q})\in(0,1]^q\), is a strong order-\(q\) model-decrease certificate if
\[
m_k(s_k)<m_k(0),
\qquad
\phi_{m_k,j}^{\delta_{k,j}}(s_k)\leq\theta\epsilon_j\frac{\delta_{k,j}^j}{j!}
\quad (j=1,\ldots,q),
\]
where
\[
\phi_{m,j}^{\delta}(s)=m(s)-\min_{\|d\|\leq\delta}T_{m,j}(s,d).
\]
The first inequality certifies strict predicted progress, while the remaining inequalities certify that \(s_k\) approximately satisfies every requested model-criticality condition through order \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed step certifies progress when it strictly lowers the regularized model and is approximately critical at every requested order, using an explicitly stated radius for each order.
assumptions_latex: The norm \(\|\cdot\|\) defining the radius balls is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((s_k,\boldsymbol\delta_k)\) provides strict model decrease and strong approximate model criticality through order \(q\).

notation.meaning: Degree-j Taylor polynomial of m at s along d.
Order-j Taylor decrement over the radius-δ ball.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional model-decrease and higher-order criticality certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m:E\to\mathbb R\) be a regularized Taylor model on a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(s\) be a candidate step, let \(q\geq1\) be an available derivative order, and let \(\delta>0\). Define the order-\(q\) Taylor decrement at \(s\) by \[\phi_{m,q}^{\delta}(s)=m(s)-\inf_{\|d\|\leq\delta}T_q^m(s,d),\] whenever the degree-\(q\) Taylor polynomial of \(m\) at \(s\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic certificate for approximate solution of a smooth regularized Taylor subproblem. Nonsmooth models require generalized or proximal criticality measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constants \(\kappa_D\in(0,1]\), \(\kappa_C\geq0\), and a reference set \(\mathcal D\subseteq E\) containing \(0\), a step \(s_k\) has a higher-order model-decrease certificate if \[m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)\geq\kappa_D\left(m_k(0)-\inf_{d\in\mathcal D}m_k(d)\right)\geq0\] and \[\phi_{m_k,q}^{\delta_k}(s_k)\leq\kappa_C\,\chi_k,\] where \(\delta_k>0\) and the nonnegative tolerance scale \(\chi_k\) are explicitly declared by the method. The first inequality certifies a fraction of the best reference-set model decrease; the second certifies approximate order-\(q\) criticality of the attained model point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order model-decrease certificate combines two checkable requirements: the trial step realizes a fixed fraction of the best model decrease over a declared reference set, and a Taylor-based order-q criticality decrement at the trial point is no larger than a declared tolerance scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is the conjunction of fractional model decrease and the residual condition \(\phi_{m_k,q}^{\delta_k}(s_k)\leq\kappa_C\chi_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(q=1\) in an unconstrained smooth model, \(\phi_{m,1}^{\delta}(s)=\delta\|\nabla m(s)\|_*\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(\mathcal D=E\) compares the step with a global model minimizer when the infimum is finite.
Taking \(\kappa_D=1\) requires globally optimal model decrease over \(\mathcal D\).
For \(q=1\), the criticality component is a scaled gradient-residual condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: The decrease component implies \(m_k(s_k)\leq m_k(0)\).
If \(\chi_k\to0\) and \(\delta_k\) is bounded away from zero in the first-order case, then the certified model-gradient residual tends to zero.
boundary_notes: Computing the reference infimum may itself be intractable; practical methods often replace it with a solver-specific lower bound or comparison step.
The Taylor decrement is not defined at nonsmooth model points without a generalized construction.
The definition does not assert that a certificate can be obtained at a prescribed computational cost.

notation.meaning: Order-q Taylor criticality decrement within radius delta.
Required fraction of reference-set model decrease.
Declared scale for the model-criticality tolerance.

children.title: Model Degree-Criticality Order Coupling
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between available derivatives and requested termination order.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,\qquad p,q\in\mathbb N,\qquad 1\le q\le p,\qquad T_{f,p}(x,s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^j f(x)[s]^j.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, unconstrained smooth optimization using a degree-(p) Taylor model and a Taylor-decrement termination test of order (q).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The model degree and criticality order are coupled admissibly when \(1\le q\le p\): the method may use derivatives through order \(p\), while termination is measured by the greatest order-(q) Taylor decrease on a prescribed radius. For \(\delta>0\), define
\[\phi_{f,q}^{\delta}(x):=f(x)-\min_{\|d\|\le\delta}T_{f,q}(x,d)=\max_{\|d\|\le\delta}\left[-\sum_{j=1}^{q}\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^j f(x)[d]^j\right].\]
A pair \((p,q)\) is therefore a model-degree–criticality-order coupling when a degree-(p) regularized Taylor step is used to seek a point satisfying \(\phi_{f,q}^{\delta}(x)\le\epsilon\chi_q(\delta)\), where \(\chi_q(\delta)=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\delta^j/j!\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model-degree–criticality-order coupling is a pair of integers p and q with 1 ≤ q ≤ p. The algorithm constructs steps from derivatives through order p, but evaluates termination through the maximum decrease predicted by the Taylor polynomial of order q on a radius δ. An approximate qth-order critical point satisfies that this maximum decrease is at most ε times the normalization sum from j=1 to q of δ^j/j!.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(p,q)\text{ is admissibly coupled}\iff p,q\in\mathbb N\text{ and }1\le q\le p,\quad\text{with termination }\phi_{f,q}^{\delta}(x)\le\epsilon\chi_q(\delta).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\phi_{f,q}^{\delta}(x)=0\iff T_{f,q}(x,d)\ge f(x)\quad\forall d\text{ with }\|d\|\le\delta.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(q=1\), \(\phi_{f,1}^{\delta}(x)=\delta\|\nabla f(x)\|\).
For \(q=2\), the measure tests both gradient and negative-curvature information through a quadratic Taylor subproblem.
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition \(q\le p\) ensures that every derivative used by the termination measure is available to the degree-(p) model.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe a complexity exponent, step-acceptance rule, or regularization power.
Pairs with \(q>p\) require derivative information absent from the stated model and are excluded.

notation.meaning: degree-p Taylor polynomial of f at x evaluated at displacement s
maximum predicted Taylor decrease of order q within radius δ
normalizing sum of powers of δ through order q

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Model Degree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree of derivative information used by an adaptive regularization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb N\). An order-\(p\) regularization model at \(x\) is
\[
m_{x,\sigma}(s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^j f(x)[s]^j+\frac{\sigma}{r}\|s\|^r,
\qquad r>p.
\]
Its regularized model degree is \(p\): the greatest derivative order occurring in its Taylor component. The regularization power \(r\) is a separate parameter and need not be an integer; in the canonical Lipschitz case it is commonly chosen as \(r=p+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized model degree is the highest derivative order retained in its Taylor polynomial, not the exponent of the added regularization term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed model has regularized model degree \(p\).

knowledge_statements.title: Requested Criticality Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Taylor-decrement criticality through a prescribed order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), an integer \(q\geq1\), radii \(\delta_j\in(0,1]\), and tolerances \(\epsilon_j>0\), define
\[
\phi_{f,j}^{\delta_j}(x)=f(x)-\min_{\|d\|\leq\delta_j}T_j(x,d),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,q.
\]
The requested criticality order is \(q\). A point \(x\) is a strong \((\boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\delta)\)-approximate order-\(q\) minimizer when
\[
\phi_{f,j}^{\delta_j}(x)\leq\epsilon_j\frac{\delta_j^j}{j!}
\quad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,q.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Criticality order q requires the Taylor decrement to be small at every order from one through q, using stated tolerances and radii.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities define strong approximate criticality of requested order \(q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-to-Order Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-availability condition linking model degree and target criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\) be the Taylor-model degree and \(q\) the requested strong criticality order. The admissible degree-to-order coupling is
\[
1\leq q\leq p.
\]
Under this condition, every Taylor polynomial \(T_j(x,d)\) needed by the criticality measures \(\phi_{f,j}^{\delta_j}(x)\), \(j=1,\ldots,q\), is constructible from derivatives already included among \(\nabla f(x),\ldots,\nabla^p f(x)\). The same coupling is required when an order-\(p\) regularized model is used to seek an order-\(q\) approximate minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Taylor model must use derivatives through at least the requested criticality order: q cannot exceed the model degree p.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) denotes model degree and \(q\) denotes requested criticality order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compatible regime is exactly \(1\leq q\leq p\).

children.title: Insufficient-Degree Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient-Degree Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic obstruction when requested order exceeds model degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(q>p\), an order-\(p\) Taylor oracle cannot by itself certify order-\(q\) criticality. Indeed, at \(x=0\), the functions
\[
f_0(t)=0,
\qquad
f_1(t)=-t^{p+1}
\]
have identical derivatives through order \(p\), but their degree-\(p+1\) Taylor decrements differ: \(\phi_{f_0,p+1}^{\delta}(0)=0\), whereas \(\phi_{f_1,p+1}^{\delta}(0)=\delta^{p+1}\). Hence identical order-\(p\) data can correspond to different higher-order criticality status, so a guarantee for \(q>p\) requires additional derivative information or structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When q exceeds p, two functions can share the entire available p-jet yet have different higher-order criticality, so a pth-order model cannot certify the target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Order-\(p\) derivative information is insufficient in general to certify requested criticality of order \(q>p\).

notation.meaning: Order-j Taylor decrement over radius δ.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Smoothness Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order regularization complexity without using the Hölder exponent in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be bounded below and have a \(\beta_p\)-Hölder continuous \(p\)-th derivative, where \(\beta_p\in(0,1]\) is unknown. Apply adaptive order-\(p\) regularization with a fixed power \(r>p\), acceptance-ratio parameter updates, and termination at first-order criticality \(\|\nabla f(x)\|_*\leq\epsilon\). For \(r>p+\beta_p\), the method requires
\[
O\!\left(\epsilon^{-\frac{p+\beta_p}{p+\beta_p-1}}+|\log\epsilon|\right)
\]
evaluations; thus its dominant power automatically reflects the operative smoothness. For \(p<r\leq p+\beta_p\), the bound is \(O(\epsilon^{-r/(r-1)})\), subject to the standard bounded-derivative assumption when the inequality is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive regularization can attain a first-order complexity exponent determined by unknown Hölder smoothness, while using only acceptance feedback to control regularization.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and \(\nabla^p f\) is \(\beta_p\)-Hölder continuous.
\(r>p\), with bounded lower derivatives along iterates if \(r<p+\beta_p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dominant evaluation exponent adapts to \(p+\beta_p\) without requiring \(\beta_p\) as an algorithmic input.

notation.meaning: Hölder exponent of the pth derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Universal adaptation to unknown Hölder smoothness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,\quad p\in\mathbb N,\quad \beta\in(0,1],\quad \|\nabla^p f(x)-\nabla^p f(y)\|\le L_{p,\beta}\|x-y\|^{\beta}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic unconstrained regularization methods whose operative Hölder exponent and constant are not supplied to the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A degree-(p) regularization method is universally smoothness-adaptive over a class \(\mathcal H_p\) if its update rule is independent of the unknown pair \((\beta,L_{p,\beta})\), yet for every \(f\in\mathcal H_p\) possessing some \(\beta\in(0,1]\) and finite \(L_{p,\beta}\), its accepted models eventually use sufficient regularization to control the Taylor remainder and its evaluation bound has the same tolerance exponent as a method tuned to that operative \(\beta\), up to constants independent of \(\epsilon\). Formally, if \(N_{\mathrm{tuned}}(\epsilon;\beta,L_{p,\beta})\le C(\beta,L_{p,\beta})\epsilon^{-a(p,q,\beta)}\), universality requires
\[N_{\mathrm{univ}}(\epsilon;f)\le \widetilde C(f)\epsilon^{-a(p,q,\beta)}\]
without using \(\beta\) or \(L_{p,\beta}\) as algorithmic inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal smoothness adaptation means that the regularization rule does not know the Hölder exponent or Hölder constant of the highest derivative in advance. Nevertheless, for every objective having some such regularity, the method controls its models and attains the same power of the requested tolerance as an algorithm tuned to that regularity, although constants may depend on the objective’s actual smoothness parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{universality}\iff (\beta,L_{p,\beta})\notin\text{algorithm inputs and }N_{\mathrm{univ}}(\epsilon;f)=O\!\left(\epsilon^{-a(p,q,\beta)}\right)\text{ for every operative }\beta.\]
special_cases_latex: When \(\beta=1\), the definition recovers adaptation to an unknown Lipschitz constant for the degree-(p) derivative.
For \(p=1\), it specializes to universal first-order regularization over Hölder-continuous gradients.
immediate_consequences_latex: A backtracking or regularization-parameter mechanism may certify smoothness locally without identifying a global value of \(L_{p,\beta}\).
boundary_notes: This definition does not claim a particular exponent \(a(p,q,\beta)\); that exponent belongs to a separate complexity result.
Dependence of constants on actual smoothness parameters is allowed; advance algorithmic dependence on them is not.

notation.meaning: union of objective classes having a Hölder-continuous pth derivative for some exponent in (0,1]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[p,q\in\mathbb N,\quad 1\le q\le p,\quad \epsilon\in(0,1),\quad \mathcal F_{p,\beta}=\{f:\nabla^p f\text{ is }\beta\text{-Hölder continuous}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic evaluation complexity indexed jointly by model degree and requested Taylor-criticality order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an algorithm \(\mathcal A_{p,q}\), define its arbitrary-order evaluation complexity by
\[N_{p,q}(\epsilon;\mathcal F_{p,\beta})=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_{p,\beta}}\inf\{k\ge0:\phi_{f,q}^{\delta_k}(x_k)\le\epsilon\chi_q(\delta_k)\},\]
where \(k\) counts evaluations of the objective and its derivatives through order \(p\), according to a fixed oracle-counting convention. An arbitrary-order complexity bound is a family of estimates
\[N_{p,q}(\epsilon;\mathcal F_{p,\beta})\le C_{p,q,\beta}\epsilon^{-a_{p,q,\beta}}+C'_{p,q,\beta}\]
valid for every admissible \((p,q)\), every \(\epsilon\in(0,1)\), and every problem in the stated class, with constants independent of \(\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary-order complexity bound is a family of worst-case evaluation bounds indexed by the Taylor-model degree p and the requested criticality order q, with q no larger than p. The complexity is the largest, over the chosen smooth problem class, of the first evaluation count at which the normalized qth-order Taylor-decrease measure is at most ε. A power-law bound has constants that may depend on the class and the orders but not on ε.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_{p,q}(\epsilon;\mathcal F_{p,\beta})\le C_{p,q,\beta}\epsilon^{-a_{p,q,\beta}}+C'_{p,q,\beta}\quad\forall\,1\le q\le p,\ \epsilon\in(0,1).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If one evaluation supplies \(f,\nabla f,\ldots,\nabla^p f\) simultaneously, \(N_{p,q}\) may equivalently count calls to that joint order-(p) oracle.
special_cases_latex: Fixing \(q=1\) gives higher-derivative bounds for first-order targets.
Fixing \(q=2\) gives curvature-aware second-order target bounds.
immediate_consequences_latex: The notation separates the outer evaluation count from the arithmetic cost of solving each regularized polynomial subproblem.
boundary_notes: A numerical value for \(a_{p,q,\beta}\) is not part of this definition.
Iteration, evaluation, tensor-operation, and bit complexity need not coincide.

notation.meaning: worst-case evaluations required for an ε-approximate qth-order point
tolerance exponent of a stated complexity family

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Derivative Bounds for First-Order Targets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong first-order evaluation bound using a degree-\(p\) regularized model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\geq1\), let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below, and suppose that \(\nabla^p f\) is Lipschitz continuous on the relevant level set. A degree-\(p\) adaptive regularization method using exact evaluations reaches a point satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\epsilon_1\) after at most
\[
O\!\left(\epsilon_1^{-\frac{p+1}{p}}\right)
\]
evaluations of \(f\) and its derivatives through order \(p\). More generally, if \(\nabla^p f\) is only \(\beta\)-Hölder continuous, the exponent becomes \((p+\beta)/(p-1+\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using derivatives through order p, adaptive regularization reaches first-order accuracy in order epsilon to the negative (p+1)/p evaluations under Lipschitz pth derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and \(p\)-times continuously differentiable.
\(\nabla^p f\) is Lipschitz continuous, or \(\beta\)-Hölder for the stated extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The evaluation complexity is \(O(\epsilon_1^{-(p+1)/p})\) in the Lipschitz case.

notation.meaning: Highest derivative order used by the model.
