children.title: Penalty Reformulation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage of nonlinear constraints represented through penalized objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Reformulation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts smooth quadratic and nonsmooth exact penalties for equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), two standard unconstrained reformulations are
\[
Q_\mu(x):=f(x)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|c(x)\|_2^2,
\qquad
P_\rho(x):=f(x)+\rho\|c(x)\|_1.
\]
The quadratic penalty \(Q_\mu\) is smooth when \(f\) and \(c\) are smooth, but generally enforces feasibility only as \(\mu\to\infty\). Under a constraint qualification at a constrained local minimizer \(x_*\) with multiplier \(\lambda_*\), the nonsmooth penalty is locally exact whenever \(\rho>\|\lambda_*\|_\infty\): \(x_*\) is then a local minimizer of \(P_\rho\) without taking an infinite-parameter limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic penalties retain smoothness but generally require diverging parameters; an L1 penalty is locally exact once its parameter exceeds an appropriate multiplier threshold.
assumptions_latex: At \(x_*\), a constraint qualification yields a multiplier \(\lambda_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_\mu\) represents the smooth asymptotic regime, whereas \(P_\rho\) is locally exact for \(\rho>\|\lambda_*\|_\infty\).

notation.meaning: equality-constraint multiplier at the local solution

children.title: Criticality-Preservation Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Criticality-Preservation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible Clarke stationarity of the L1 penalty under equality-constraint LICQ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_\rho(x):=f(x)+\rho\|c(x)\|_1\), and suppose \(c(x)=0\) and \(Jc(x)\) has full row rank. Then
\[
0\in\partial_C P_\rho(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there exists }\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\text{ with }\|\lambda\|_\infty\leq\rho
\text{ and }\nabla f(x)+Jc(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0.
\]
Consequently, feasible Clarke-stationary points of the exact penalty are precisely KKT-stationary points admitting a multiplier within the penalty box. Thus first-order criticality is preserved whenever \(\rho\) dominates the norm of a relevant KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible LICQ point, L1-penalty stationarity is equivalent to KKT stationarity with a multiplier whose infinity norm does not exceed the penalty parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_C P_\rho(x)\iff\exists\lambda:\nabla f(x)+Jc(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) and \(\|\lambda\|_\infty\leq\rho\).

knowledge_statements.title: Criticality Transfer Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-penalty stationarity transfers dual residual but not feasibility at fixed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Q_\mu(x):=f(x)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|c(x)\|^2\), set \(\lambda_\mu:=\mu c(x)\). Then
\[
\nabla Q_\mu(x)=\nabla f(x)+Jc(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda_\mu,
\]
so small penalty gradient gives a small Lagrangian stationarity residual, but supplies no parameter-independent feasibility bound. Indeed, for \(f(x)=-x\) and \(c(x)=x\), the unique stationary point of \(Q_\mu\) is \(x_\mu=1/\mu\). Its penalty criticality is zero while \(|c(x_\mu)|=1/\mu>0\) for every finite \(\mu\). Criticality therefore transfers to constrained criticality only after separately controlling feasibility or increasing \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small quadratic-penalty gradient controls a Lagrangian residual but not feasibility. Even exact penalty stationarity can remain infeasible for every finite quadratic-penalty parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Penalty stationarity alone does not imply constrained stationarity at finite \(\mu\); feasibility must be bounded separately.

notation.meaning: multiplier estimate induced by the penalty residual

children.title: Penalty Parameter Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Parameter Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp multiplier threshold for local exactness of an L1 penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min -x\) subject to \(x=0\). Its KKT multiplier is \(\lambda_*=1\), and the L1 penalty is \(P_\rho(x)=-x+\rho|x|\). For \(x>0\), \(P_\rho(x)=(\rho-1)x\); for \(x<0\), \(P_\rho(x)=-(1+\rho)x\). Hence \(x=0\) is not a local minimizer when \(0\leq\rho<1\), is a non-strict local minimizer when \(\rho=1\), and is a strict local minimizer when \(\rho>1\). Thus the multiplier norm is the sharp boundary in this example, and strict domination avoids threshold degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar equality problem, the L1 penalty becomes exact exactly at the multiplier magnitude; equality yields non-strict exactness, while a larger parameter yields strict local exactness.
assumptions_latex: The constrained problem is \(\min -x\) subject to \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=0\) minimizes \(P_\rho\) locally iff \(\rho\geq\|\lambda_*\|=1\), and the minimum is strict iff \(\rho>1\).

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier of the equality constraint

children.title: Expensive-Constraint Evaluation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes requiring separate accounting for constraint evaluation and enforcement.

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive-Constraint Evaluation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-oracle complexity does not control separately charged constraint evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a separated oracle model, let \(N_f\), \(N_c\), and \(N_J\) count evaluations of \(f\), \(c\), and \(Jc\), respectively. A bound \(N_f\leq B(\varepsilon)\) alone implies no bound on \(N_c+N_J\): between two objective calls, an implementation may perform an arbitrary number \(M\) of constraint or Jacobian calls for restoration, feasibility checking, or subproblem enforcement. Consequently, total evaluation complexity must be reported as a vector such as
\[
\bigl(N_f,N_c,N_J\bigr)
\]
or under an explicit cost model \(W=w_fN_f+w_cN_c+w_JN_J\). Treating constraints as inexpensive is therefore a substantive oracle assumption, not a consequence of objective-evaluation complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When constraint and Jacobian calls are charged separately, an objective-evaluation bound gives no total-cost bound unless constraint calls are also bounded or assigned an explicit cost.
assumptions_latex: Objective, constraint, and constraint-Jacobian evaluations are distinct oracle operations.
Constraint enforcement may invoke its oracle independently of the objective oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound on \(N_f\) alone does not bound \(N_c+N_J\) or weighted work \(W\).

notation.meaning: numbers of objective, constraint, and constraint-Jacobian evaluations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion is valid under the explicitly separated oracle model and failure_boundary fits the terminal container, but no source establishes that model or the claimed complexity-accounting consequence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalable realization of an oracle bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(n\) be problem dimension, \(\epsilon\) a requested tolerance, and \(N_j(n,\epsilon)\) the number of calls to primitive \(j\), each having realized cost \(c_j(n)\). Let \(W_{\mathrm{aux}}(n,\epsilon)\) and \(M(n,\epsilon)\) denote auxiliary arithmetic and memory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of evaluation-complexity guarantees into dimension-dependent computational resource bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle-complexity guarantee has a scalable realization on a problem family if an implementation exists for which \(W(n,\epsilon)=\sum_jc_j(n)N_j(n,\epsilon)+W_{\mathrm{aux}}(n,\epsilon)\) and \(M(n,\epsilon)\) satisfy the declared resource bounds uniformly over that family. The realization boundary is crossed when a hidden primitive—such as dense factorization, explicit tensor storage, exact nonconvex model minimization, or expensive projection—causes either \(W\) or \(M\) to exceed those bounds despite a favorable evaluation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation bound is scalably realizable only when the costs of each oracle call, all auxiliary solves, and memory remain within stated dimension-dependent limits. A favorable iteration or evaluation count is not a scalable guarantee if hidden dense algebra, tensor storage, projection, or subproblem solution dominates resources.
assumptions_latex: The problem family and computational primitives are fixed.
All dominant arithmetic, storage, and communication terms are assigned to \(W\) or \(M\).
Resource bounds are uniform over instances in the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scalability is the joint bound on \((W(n,\epsilon),M(n,\epsilon))\), not merely a bound on \(\sum_jN_j(n,\epsilon)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A vector resource model may retain evaluation, arithmetic, memory, and communication as separate coordinates.
A scalar model results after assigning platform-dependent weights.
special_cases_latex: A matrix-free method may achieve \(M=O(n)\) when each derivative product also costs \(O(n)\).
A sparse direct method is scalable only relative to a family whose fill-in remains controlled.
immediate_consequences_latex: Complexity comparisons require a common primitive-cost convention.
Inner-solve accuracy schedules can change realized work without changing the outer evaluation exponent.
boundary_notes: Scalable does not mean dimension independent.
Asymptotic resource bounds do not by themselves predict constants or hardware utilization.

children.title: Hessian-Free Regularization

knowledge_statements.title: Hessian-Free Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cubic regularization implemented using Hessian-vector products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\), \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(\sigma_k>0\), and an operator returning \(H_kv\), form
\[
m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}H_ks+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3.
\]
Use a Krylov iteration requiring only products \(H_kv\) to compute \(s_k\) satisfying \(m_k(s_k)<m_k(0)\) and \(\|\nabla_sm_k(s_k)\|\leq\kappa\min\{1,\|s_k\|\}\|g_k\|\). Evaluate \(f(x_k+s_k)\), accept the trial point when the ratio of actual to predicted decrease exceeds a prescribed threshold, and decrease or increase \(\sigma_k\) according to successful or unsuccessful acceptance. Output the first accepted iterate meeting the chosen criticality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cubic regularization can be realized without forming a Hessian by solving each model approximately in a Krylov space using only Hessian-vector products and an acceptance ratio.
assumptions_latex: The implementation can evaluate \(f\), \(\nabla f\), and products \(H_kv\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each regularized step can be computed and assessed without explicitly assembling or factorizing \(H_k\).

notation.meaning: Hessian or symmetric model-Hessian product with a vector

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, but the particular Krylov subproblem condition, acceptance mechanism, parameter update, and termination rule define a specific cubic-regularization variant whose correctness and provenance cannot be verified without an authoritative algorithm or theorem locator.

Equivalently, inner linear algebra uses products \((H_k+\sigma_kI)v=H_kv+\sigma_kv\). The implementation is Hessian-free when it neither forms nor stores \(H_k\), and its curvature cost is counted by the number of product-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hessian-free regularization adds a positive quadratic term to the local second-order model and solves the resulting model using only Hessian-vector products. The Hessian is never explicitly formed or stored, and computational complexity records the number and cost of curvature products used by the inner iteration.

Using an automatic-differentiation product gives a matrix-free exact-product implementation up to arithmetic error.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\), \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), radius \(\Delta_k>0\), and an operator returning \(B_kv\), approximately minimize
\[
q_k(s)=g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}B_ks
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|s\|\leq\Delta_k
\]
by truncated conjugate gradients or Lanczos iteration. Stop at an adequate residual, at the first boundary intersection, or upon detecting \(p^{\mathsf T}B_kp\leq0\), in which case move along \(p\) to the trust-region boundary. Accept \(x_k+s_k\) according to the ratio of actual to predicted reduction, update \(\Delta_k\), and terminate when the prescribed criticality test holds. No matrix representation of \(B_k\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large-scale trust-region step is computed by truncated CG or Lanczos using matrix-vector products, stopping for convergence, boundary contact, or negative curvature before ratio-based acceptance.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, and function values and gradients are available.
\(B_k\) is symmetric and accessible through products \(B_kv\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trust-region subproblem and negative-curvature response can be realized using only \(B_kv\) products and vector operations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrix-free trust-region outline and negative-curvature response are standard and algorithm is the correct kind, but the combined truncated-CG/Lanczos procedure and its stopping and update rules require a specific authoritative source locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable at an iterate \(x_k\), let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), let \(B_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be a symmetric linear operator, and let \(\Delta_k>0\). Define \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, unconstrained trust-region models realized through operator products rather than an explicitly stored Hessian or model matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region realization is matrix-free if its step \(s_k\) is computed in a Krylov subspace \(\mathcal K_j(B_k,g_k)=\operatorname{span}\{g_k,B_kg_k,\ldots,B_k^{j-1}g_k\}\), subject to \(\|s_k\|\leq\Delta_k\), and every access to \(B_k\) occurs only through products \(v\mapsto B_kv\). Thus no entries or factorization of \(B_k\) are required. The returned step is an approximate solution of \(\min_{\|s\|\leq\Delta_k}m_k(s)\), normally terminating upon a residual test, encounter with the trust-region boundary, or detection of \(d^TB_kd\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free trust-region method approximately minimizes a quadratic model over a norm ball using a Krylov process. The model operator is accessed only by multiplying it by trial vectors; its entries and a matrix factorization are never required. The inner process may stop after attaining its residual tolerance, reaching the trust-region boundary, or finding nonpositive curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(B_k\) is symmetric as an operator on \(\mathbb R^n\).
The implementation can evaluate \(B_kv\) for every Krylov vector \(v\) requested by the inner method.
The trust-region norm and radius \(\Delta_k\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_k\in\mathcal K_j(B_k,g_k),\quad \|s_k\|\leq\Delta_k,\quad\text{and the computation uses only }g_k\text{ and products }B_kv.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), the oracle \(v\mapsto B_kv\) is a Hessian-vector-product oracle.
Lanczos or truncated conjugate gradients realizes the reduced problem \(\min\{m_k(Q_jy):\|Q_jy\|\leq\Delta_k\}\) without forming \(B_k\).
special_cases_latex: For positive-definite \(B_k\) and an inactive boundary, the inner problem reduces to approximately solving \(B_ks=-g_k\) by conjugate gradients.
If a Krylov direction \(d\) satisfies \(d^TB_kd\leq0\), a truncated method may move to the boundary along the current path.
immediate_consequences_latex: Storage can be limited to Krylov vectors and auxiliary vectors rather than \(n^2\) matrix entries.
The relevant inner-operation count is the number of products \(B_kv\), not merely the number of outer iterations.
boundary_notes: Matrix-free does not mean derivative-free: exact or approximate Hessian-vector products may still be used.
A matrix-free interface alone supplies no dimension-independent bound on the number of Krylov iterations.

notation.meaning: The order-j Krylov subspace generated by B and g.

children.title: Scaling-Preconditioning Coupling
children.top_down_role: Metric and linear-algebra transformations affecting inner complexity.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m_k(p)=f_k+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp\), where \(B_k\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(D_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular. Set \(\widehat p=D_kp\), \(\widehat g_k=D_k^{-T}g_k\), and \(\widehat B_k=D_k^{-T}B_kD_k^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quadratic trust-region subproblems in which the same nonsingular transformation defines both the trust-region metric and the preconditioned linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Scaling and preconditioning are coupled when the trust region is \(\|D_kp\|_2\leq\Delta_k\) and the inner iteration is applied to the transformed model \(f_k+\widehat g_k^T\widehat p+\tfrac12\widehat p^T\widehat B_k\widehat p\) over \(\|\widehat p\|_2\leq\Delta_k\). Equivalently, the metric matrix is \(M_k=D_k^TD_k\), so feasibility is \(p^TM_kp\leq\Delta_k^2\), while the preconditioned Hessian is the congruence transform \(D_k^{-T}B_kD_k^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling and preconditioning are coupled when one nonsingular change of variables simultaneously defines the trust-region norm and the operator seen by the inner solver. The original ellipsoidal constraint becomes a Euclidean ball in transformed coordinates, and the quadratic operator undergoes the corresponding congruence transformation.
assumptions_latex: The transformed and original steps satisfy \(\widehat p=D_kp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{p^TD_k^TD_kp\leq\Delta_k^2}m_k(p)=\min_{\|\widehat p\|_2\leq\Delta_k}\left(f_k+\widehat g_k^T\widehat p+\tfrac12\widehat p^T\widehat B_k\widehat p\right).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The scaling metric is \(M_k=D_k^TD_k\succ0\).
Writing \(C_k=M_k^{1/2}\), the transformed operator is \(C_k^{-T}B_kC_k^{-1}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(D_k=I\), the usual Euclidean trust-region problem is recovered.
Diagonal \(D_k\) gives coordinate scaling; incomplete-factor choices give sparse preconditioning.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing the preconditioner while leaving the trust-region norm fixed generally changes the correspondence between transformed Krylov iterates and feasible original steps.
The spectrum of \(\widehat B_k\) governs transformed inner convergence, while \(D_k^TD_k\) governs the geometry of accepted steps.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that a chosen scaling improves conditioning.
Uniform complexity statements may additionally require bounded norms or condition numbers for the scaling sequence.

notation.meaning: Positive-definite trust-region metric induced by the scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal change of variables and its derivative transformation laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, usually diagonal, and set \(x=Dz\). The scaled objective and constraint mappings are \(\widehat f(z):=f(Dz)\) and \(\widehat c(z):=c(Dz)\). Their derivatives satisfy
\[
\nabla\widehat f(z)=D^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(Dz),\qquad
\nabla^2\widehat f(z)=D^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(Dz)D,
\]
and
\[
J\widehat c(z)=Jc(Dz)D.
\]
Thus variable scaling changes gradient, curvature, trust-region, and regularization geometry. Any stopping tolerance or norm stated in scaled coordinates must be translated through \(D\) before it is interpreted as an unscaled criticality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular variable scaling transforms gradients, Hessians, and constraint Jacobians by explicit chain rules; tolerances and algorithmic norms must therefore be interpreted in the chosen coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable and \(c\) is differentiable at \(Dz\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Derivatives transform as \(D^{\mathsf T}\nabla f\), \(D^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2fD\), and \(JcD\), so criticality tolerances are coordinate-dependent unless rescaled.

notation.meaning: objective and constraints in scaled coordinates

children.title: Subproblem Preconditioning

knowledge_statements.title: Subproblem Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate preconditioning of a cubic regularization subproblem by an invertible linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given gradient and Hessian approximations \(g_k\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(H_k=H_k^\top\), a parameter \(\sigma_k>0\), and an invertible preconditioner \(P_k\), set \(s=P_kz\) and form
\[\widehat m_k(z)=g_k^\top P_kz+\tfrac12 z^\top P_k^\top H_kP_kz+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\lVert z\rVert^3.\]
Compute an approximate minimizer \(z_k\) satisfying \(\widehat m_k(z_k)<\widehat m_k(0)\) and \(\lVert\nabla\widehat m_k(z_k)\rVert\leq\eta_k\), then return \(s_k=P_kz_k\). Equivalently, this minimizes the original quadratic model regularized by \(\lVert P_k^{-1}s\rVert^3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform the regularized subproblem into well-scaled coordinates, solve it to prescribed stationarity and decrease tolerances, and map the computed step back to the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_k=P_kz_k\) is a decreasing approximate solution of the preconditioned cubic model.

children.title: Scale-Aware Preconditioners
children.top_down_role: Coverage of preconditioners designed for nonuniform model geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Aware Preconditioners
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance condition ensuring that diagonal rescaling does not change the physical trial step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x=Dy\), where \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is invertible. The transformed gradient and Hessian are \(g_y=D^\top g_x\) and \(H_y=D^\top H_xD\). A preconditioner rule \(\mathcal P\) is scale-aware if
\[\mathcal P(D^\top g_x,D^\top H_xD)=D^{-1}\mathcal P(g_x,H_x).\]
Consequently, if the same internal step \(z\) is used in both coordinate systems, then \(s_x=\mathcal P(g_x,H_x)z\) and \(s_y=\mathcal P(g_y,H_y)z\) satisfy \(Ds_y=s_x\). Thus the physical trial point is invariant under the chosen scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scale-aware preconditioner transforms contravariantly with a variable rescaling, so solving in scaled coordinates produces the same physical step.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and every value of \(\mathcal P\) are invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ds_y=s_x\), so the preconditioned physical step is invariant under \(x=Dy\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: coordinate covariance follows directly from the chain rule and the stated step transformation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covariance identity algebraically implies Ds_y=s_x and the condition role fits the leaf, but this particular definition of a scale-aware preconditioner is uncited. An authoritative source is needed to establish that this is the intended optimization notion rather than a locally introduced covariance convention.

children.title: Preconditioning Robustness Limits
children.top_down_role: Coverage of regimes where conditioning improvements fail to preserve outer guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioning Robustness Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertibility of a preconditioner alone does not uniformly control transformed condition numbers or condition-number-dependent inner-work bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(H_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\) for \(0<\delta\leq1\) and the identity preconditioner \(P_\delta=I\). Then
\[\kappa(P_\delta^\top H_\delta P_\delta)=\kappa(H_\delta)=\delta^{-1}.\]
Consequently, the family of transformed matrices is not uniformly well conditioned as \(\delta\downarrow0\). In particular, for any inner-solver estimate of the form \(N_\delta\leq C\sqrt{\kappa(P_\delta^\top H_\delta P_\delta)}\) whose asserted uniform constant depends on the displayed factor, that factor diverges like \(\delta^{-1/2}\). Thus nonsingularity of each preconditioner does not by itself provide a uniform conditioning guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible preconditioner need not keep transformed subproblems uniformly well conditioned; therefore any inner-work guarantee that explicitly deteriorates with the transformed condition number can lose uniformity.
assumptions_latex: Any stated inner-work implication is restricted to an estimate that explicitly depends on \(\sqrt{\kappa(P_\delta^\top H_\delta P_\delta)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(P_\delta^\top H_\delta P_\delta)=\delta^{-1}\to\infty\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\), despite every \(P_\delta\) being invertible.

notation.meaning: spectral condition number of a positive-definite matrix
an inner-solver iteration bound when such a bound is under discussion

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). For \(i=1,\ldots,q\), let \(U_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be linear with \(n_i\ll n\), and let \(\phi_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth objectives represented as sums of low-dimensional element functions; overlapping element-variable sets are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) has a partially separable element representation if \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^q\phi_i(U_ix)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), with each \(U_i\) having low-dimensional range. If every \(\phi_i\) is twice differentiable, then \(
abla f(x)=\sum_iU_i^T
abla\phi_i(U_ix)\) and \(
abla^2f(x)=\sum_iU_i^T
abla^2\phi_i(U_ix)U_i\). An element model \(m_{i,k}\) or element Hessian approximation \(B_{i,k}\) is assembled analogously by summing \(m_{i,k}(U_is)\) or \(U_i^TB_{i,k}U_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially separable objective is a sum of element functions, each depending only on a low-dimensional linear image of the full variable. Variables may occur in several elements, so partial separability is more general than ordinary separability. Gradients, Hessians, and auxiliary models are assembled from the corresponding element quantities.
assumptions_latex: \(U_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i\times n}\) and \(n_i\) is small relative to \(n\).
\(\phi_i\) has the differentiability required for each displayed derivative identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^q\phi_i(U_ix),\quad \nabla^2f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^qU_i^T\nabla^2\phi_i(U_ix)U_i.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: An element function is invariant along \(\ker U_i\): \(\phi_i(U_i(x+z))=\phi_i(U_ix)\) for every \(z\in\ker U_i\).
For coordinate-extraction matrices \(U_i\), each element depends on a specified subset of components of \(x\).
special_cases_latex: If the element-variable sets are pairwise disjoint, the representation is separable.
If \(q=1\) and \(U_1=I\), the representation imposes no separability.
immediate_consequences_latex: Element derivatives and element models can be evaluated and stored in dimensions \(n_i\).
Overlapping elements contribute additively to the same entries or operator actions of the full Hessian.
boundary_notes: Low-dimensional elements do not by themselves guarantee that the aggregate evaluation cost is small; the number and overlap of elements also matter.
A general affine change of variables need not preserve a coordinate-based partially separable structure.

children.title: Partially Separable Objectives

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Separable Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum partial separability through low-dimensional linear element maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is partially separable of element width \(\omega\) if there exist differentiable element functions \(f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R\) and linear maps \(U_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i\times n}\) such that
\[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(U_ix),\qquad \max_{1\leq i\leq m}n_i\leq\omega.\]
Usually each \(U_i\) is a coordinate-selection matrix, so element \(i\) depends only on a variable set \(S_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|S_i|=n_i\). Partial separability concerns element width, not disjointness: different sets \(S_i\) may overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially separable objective is a sum of element functions, each depending through a linear map on at most a bounded number of variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(U_ix)\) with \(\max_i n_i\leq\omega\).

notation.meaning: linear element map, often a coordinate selector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-sum definition of partial separability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite element-sum formulation is plausible and appropriate as a definition, but definitions of partial separability differ over whether element maps must select coordinates, may be arbitrary linear maps, and whether smoothness belongs to the definition. A source is needed to fix the intended variant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a separable function recursively through scalar intermediate quantities.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is separable exactly when it can be written as a sum of component functions of scalar quantities, each of which is either linear in the original variables or itself separable.
assumptions_latex: z_i\text{ is either a linear function of }\mathbf{x}\text{ or a separable function}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is separable}\iff f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_i f_i(z_i)\text{ with the stated conditions on each }z_i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partially separable objectives and element range subspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines partial separability using translation-invariant element functions and identifies their effective subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is partially separable when \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}f_i(x)\) and, for every \(i\), there is a nonzero subspace \(\mathcal N_i\) such that \(f_i(x+w)=f_i(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(w\in\mathcal N_i\). The \(f_i\) are element functions, with range subspaces \(\mathcal R_i:=\mathcal N_i^\perp\). In the coordinate-dependence case, if \(\mathcal N_i\) is the span of coordinate directions absent from \(f_i\), then \(\mathcal R_i\) is spanned by the corresponding elemental-variable basis vectors. Moreover, \(f\) is invariant under translations in \(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathcal R_i\right)^\perp\), so attention may be restricted to the effective space satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathcal R_i=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially separable objective is a sum of element functions, each invariant along a nonzero subspace. The orthogonal complement is the element's effective range space. Directions orthogonal to all element range spaces do not affect the objective and may be removed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is partially separable if there exist diagonal matrices \(U_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and component functions \(f_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,M\), such that \[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^M f_i(U_i x).\] The selectors may be taken to be binary diagonal matrices. The intended nontrivial regime has \(M>1\) and \(m_i:=|\{j:(U_i)_{jj}\ne0\}|\ll n\). If \(M=n\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(U_i)=e_i\), then \(f\) is separable. Every function has the degenerate representation \(M=1\), \(U_1=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is partially separable when it is a sum of component functions selected by diagonal variable masks, with each nontrivial component intended to depend on far fewer than all variables. Coordinate separability is a special case, while one identity selector gives a trivial representation for any function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Element-function representation of a differentiable partially separable objective and the resulting Jacobian-gradient identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} be small index sets and suppose f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} has the representation \[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}f_i(x_{S_i}),\] with differentiable element functions f_i. Define r(x)=(f_1(x_{S_1}),\ldots,f_{n_e}(x_{S_{n_e}}))^T and J(x)=Dr(x). Then \[\nabla f(x)=J(x)^T e,\qquad e=(1,\ldots,1)^T.\] Each row of J has nonzeros only in the variables on which its element function depends, so the Jacobian is structurally sparse and may admit compressed evaluation based on its sparsity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially separable objective is a sum of differentiable element functions that each depend on few variables. Stacking those elements into a vector r gives the identity gradient f equals the transpose of r's Jacobian times the all-ones vector. Each Jacobian row is supported only on the variables used by its element function, yielding structural sparsity.
assumptions_latex: S_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\text{ and each }S_i\text{ is small relative to the full variable set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla f(x)=J(x)^T e,\qquad \operatorname{supp}(J_{i,:})\subseteq S_i.

children.title: Element Model Representations
children.top_down_role: Coverage of derivative plus regularization models maintained at component level.

knowledge_statements.title: Element Model Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assembly of a regularized Taylor model from low-dimensional element derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(U_ix)\), let \(u_{i,k}=U_ix_k\), \(g_{i,k}=\nabla f_i(u_{i,k})\), and \(B_{i,k}=\nabla^2f_i(u_{i,k})\). The second-order regularized model has the element representation
\[m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(g_{i,k}^\top U_is+\tfrac12 (U_is)^\top B_{i,k}(U_is)\right)+\frac{\sigma_k}{p+1}\lVert s\rVert^{p+1}.\]
Its assembled derivatives are \(g_k=\sum_iU_i^\top g_{i,k}\) and \(B_k=\sum_iU_i^\top B_{i,k}U_i\). The regularizer may remain global even though the Taylor terms are elementwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local element gradients and Hessians lift through their element maps and sum to the global regularized Taylor model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_k=\sum_iU_i^\top g_{i,k}\) and \(B_k=\sum_iU_i^\top B_{i,k}U_i\).

notation.meaning: gradient of element i at the current element point
element Hessian at the current element point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identities follow from the chain rule for a finite element sum

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted gradient and Hessian identities are correct, but the record combines a second-order Taylor model with a general exponent p+1 without identifying the regularization framework that permits this convention. A source is needed to confirm the intended model class and notation.

children.title: Element Assembly Complexity
children.top_down_role: Coverage of computational costs for combining component contributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Element Assembly Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and storage costs for assembling dense local element derivatives into sparse global derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose each \(U_i\) selects \(n_i\) coordinates and dense local derivatives \(g_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\) and \(B_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i\times n_i}\) are already available. Scatter-add assembly of
\[g=\sum_{i=1}^{m}U_i^\top g_i,\qquad B=\sum_{i=1}^{m}U_i^\top B_iU_i\]
requires \(O(\sum_i n_i)\) gradient additions and \(O(\sum_i n_i^2)\) Hessian additions. Storing the unassembled dense element Hessians requires \(O(\sum_i n_i^2)\) words. If \(n_i\leq\omega\), these costs are respectively \(O(m\omega)\) and \(O(m\omega^2)\), excluding derivative evaluation and subproblem solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With dense local derivatives, elementwise gradient assembly is linear in total element width and Hessian assembly is linear in total squared element width.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_g=O(\sum_i n_i)\), \(T_B=O(\sum_i n_i^2)\), and \(M_B=O(\sum_i n_i^2)\).

notation.meaning: gradient and Hessian assembly operation counts

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct operation count for scatter-add assembly

children.title: Separability Exploitation Limits
children.top_down_role: Coverage of coupling patterns that restrict gains from element structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Separability Exploitation Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded element width alone does not guarantee linear explicit assembly or storage because element overlaps may create a dense interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\geq2\), define
\[f(x)=\frac12\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(x_i-x_j)^2.\]
This objective has \(m=n(n-1)/2\) elements, each involving two variables, so its element width is \(\omega=2\). Nevertheless, its interaction graph is complete and
\[\nabla^2f(x)=nI-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\]
has \(\Theta(n^2)\) nonzero entries when stored explicitly. Moreover, \(\sum_{i=1}^m n_i^2=4m=\Theta(n^2)\). Thus uniformly bounded element width does not by itself imply linear explicit Hessian assembly or storage; element count and overlap structure must also be controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-variable elements can form a complete interaction graph, so constant element width alone does not guarantee linear explicit Hessian assembly or storage.
assumptions_latex: Each unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\) defines one element with \(n_i=2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega=2\) while both the explicit Hessian nonzero count and \(\sum_{i=1}^m n_i^2\) are \(\Theta(n^2)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit complete-graph quadratic and direct counting establish the stated assembly and storage limitation

children.title: Cross-Iteration Memory Models
children.top_down_role: Reuse of expensive information across outer iterations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\) be outer iterates for differentiable \(f\). Define \(s_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\), \(y_i=\nabla f(x_{i+1})-\nabla f(x_i)\), and fix a memory length \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth optimization with a bounded state that reuses curvature information from preceding outer iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounded cross-iteration memory model at iteration \(k\) is an implicitly represented operator \(H_k=\mathcal U(H_k^0;\{(s_i,y_i):i=\max(0,k-m),\ldots,k-1\})\), where \(H_k^0\) is a base operator and \(\mathcal U\) is a prescribed update composition. In limited-memory BFGS, each retained pair satisfies \(y_i^Ts_i>0\), \(\rho_i=(y_i^Ts_i)^{-1}\), and the BFGS inverse update is applied only to the most recent pairs; the oldest pair is discarded when a new pair is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-iteration memory model forms the current model operator from a bounded state retained from earlier outer iterations. In the canonical limited-memory quasi-Newton case, the state consists of recent displacement and gradient-difference pairs, and the current inverse-Hessian action is reconstructed implicitly from those pairs and a base operator.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at all retained iterates.
The memory contains at most \(m\) accepted pairs.
For the positive-definite L-BFGS variant, \(y_i^Ts_i>0\) for every retained pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M_k=\{(s_i,y_i):\max(0,k-m)\leq i\leq k-1\},\qquad |\mathcal M_k|\leq m.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The memory is a state recursion \(\mathcal M_{k+1}=\operatorname{tail}_m(\mathcal M_k\cup\{(s_k,y_k)\})\).
The product \(H_kv\) can be evaluated by the L-BFGS two-loop recursion without storing a dense \(n\times n\) matrix.
special_cases_latex: For \(m=1\), only the latest curvature pair is retained.
If no pair is retained, \(H_k=H_k^0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Pair storage is \(O(mn)\) rather than \(O(n^2)\).
The current search direction may depend on evaluations made at several previous outer iterations.
boundary_notes: This definition covers bounded curvature-pair memory, not arbitrary warm starts, cached factorizations, or unbounded algorithmic histories.
Reusing information does not guarantee that it remains accurate after a large change in local geometry.

notation.meaning: Retained memory state at iteration k.

children.title: Derivative Information Reuse

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative Information Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selective refresh of cached element derivatives across regularization iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each element \(i\), maintain a cache \((y_{i,k},g_{i,k},B_{i,k})\), where derivatives were evaluated at \(y_{i,k}\). At iteration \(k\), choose a refresh set \(R_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). For \(i\in R_k\), set
\[y_{i,k}=U_ix_k,\quad g_{i,k}=
abla f_i(y_{i,k}),\quad B_{i,k}=
abla^2f_i(y_{i,k});\]
for \(i
otin R_k\), retain the previous cache. Assemble \(\widetilde g_k=\sum_iU_i^	op g_{i,k}\) and \(\widetilde B_k=\sum_iU_i^	op B_{i,k}U_i\), solve the resulting regularized surrogate subproblem, and refresh further elements whenever prescribed accuracy tests fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refresh derivatives for selected elements, reuse the remaining cached derivatives, assemble a surrogate model, and expand the refresh set when accuracy tests fail.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i\) is twice differentiable at every refreshed element point.
\(R_k\) is selected before assembling the iteration model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\widetilde g_k,\widetilde B_k)\) combines current derivatives on \(R_k\) with cached derivatives outside \(R_k\).

notation.meaning: set of elements refreshed at iteration k
cached evaluation point for element i

These details determine whether the method is a defined algorithm and whether derivative reuse is safe, so a method-level source is required.

children.title: Memory-Based Surrogate Models
children.top_down_role: Local models assembled from information retained across multiple iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Based Surrogate Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A surrogate assembled from elementwise Taylor expansions centered at stored, possibly different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_{i,k}\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be a stored point for element \(i\). A second-order memory surrogate for \(f(x)=\sum_i f_i(U_ix)\) is
\[\widetilde f_k(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[f_i(y_{i,k})+\nabla f_i(y_{i,k})^\top(U_ix-y_{i,k})+\tfrac12(U_ix-y_{i,k})^\top B_{i,k}(U_ix-y_{i,k})\right],\]
where \(B_{i,k}\) approximates \(\nabla^2f_i(y_{i,k})\). The iteration model is \(\widetilde m_k(s)=\widetilde f_k(x_k+s)+\sigma_k\lVert s\rVert^{p+1}/(p+1)\). The centers need not coincide, but their discrepancies must be controlled for derivative accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A memory surrogate sums element Taylor models centered at stored element points, then adds the current regularization term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde m_k(s)=\widetilde f_k(x_k+s)+\sigma_k\lVert s\rVert^{p+1}/(p+1)\) is the memory-based regularized surrogate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multi-center Taylor expression is internally consistent and fits a representation leaf, but the final requirement that center discrepancies be controlled is not quantified. A source is needed to establish the intended memory-surrogate construction and its admissible error conditions.

children.title: Cross-Iteration Information Transfer
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing the relevance of stored information at a new iterate.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Iteration Information Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic derivative-error bounds for transferring element Hessians from earlier expansion points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume each element Hessian is Lipschitz continuous with constant \(L_i\), and set \(d_{i,k}=\lVert U_ix_k-y_{i,k}Vert\). If cached derivatives are transferred by
\[\widehat g_{i,k}=
abla f_i(y_{i,k})+
abla^2f_i(y_{i,k})(U_ix_k-y_{i,k}),\qquad \widehat B_{i,k}=
abla^2f_i(y_{i,k}),\]
then
\[\lVert
abla f_i(U_ix_k)-\widehat g_{i,k}Vert\leq	frac{L_i}{2}d_{i,k}^2,\qquad \lVert
abla^2f_i(U_ix_k)-\widehat B_{i,k}Vert\leq L_id_{i,k}.\]
After lifting and summing, global errors are bounded by the corresponding sums weighted by \(\lVert U_iVert\) and \(\lVert U_iVert^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz element Hessians permit controlled transfer of cached derivatives: gradient error is quadratic and Hessian error linear in staleness distance.
assumptions_latex: The segment joining \(y_{i,k}\) and \(U_ix_k\) lies in the element domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert e^g_{i,k}\rVert\leq L_id_{i,k}^2/2\) and \(\lVert e^B_{i,k}\rVert\leq L_id_{i,k}\).

notation.meaning: distance between current and cached element points

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Taylor remainder and Lipschitz-Hessian inequalities give the displayed bounds

children.title: Stale-Information Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of model reliability when retained information becomes insufficiently representative.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Information Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncontrolled cache age can reverse a gradient direction even for a smooth convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\), take the current point \(x_k=1\), and reuse the stale gradient evaluated at \(y_k=-M\), where \(M>0\). Then
\[
abla f(x_k)=1,\qquad \widetilde g_k=
abla f(y_k)=-M.\]
The reused-gradient direction \(d_k=-\widetilde g_k=M\) is an ascent direction at the current point because \(
abla f(x_k)d_k=M>0\). Moreover, \(|\widetilde g_k-
abla f(x_k)|=M+1\) is unbounded with the staleness distance \(|x_k-y_k|\). Thus smoothness alone cannot justify unrestricted reuse; cache distance, delay, or model-error tests must be bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stale gradient of a smooth quadratic can point exactly the wrong way, with error growing without bound as the cached point recedes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x_k)(-\nabla f(y_k))=M>0\), so the reused negative gradient is an ascent direction.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit one-dimensional counterexample is directly verifiable

children.title: Critical Geometry Failure Classes
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex geometries that limit low-order detection or high-order certification.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-Geometry Failure Class Relative to an Order
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(p\)-times differentiable near a critical point \(x_*\), and let \(T_p(x_*,s)=f(x_*)+\sum_{j=1}^p\tfrac1{j!}\nabla^jf(x_*)[s]^j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal classification relative to a chosen derivative order; it is not a claim that every nonconvex critical point belongs to the same subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an order \(p\geq1\), the critical-geometry failure class \(\mathfrak G_p\) consists of pairs \((f,x_*)\) such that \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\), \(x_*\) is not a local minimizer of \(f\), and the derivative information through order \(p\) fails to provide a locally decisive descent certificate: for every \(\delta>0\), either \(\min_{\|s\|\leq\delta}(T_p(x_*,s)-f(x_*))=0\), or the set of critical points intersects every neighborhood of \(x_*\) in a way not isolated by the selected criticality measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a derivative order, a critical-geometry failure class contains nonminimizing critical points for which the selected finite-order Taylor information or critical-set measure does not decisively reveal local descent or isolate the point. The definition deliberately separates failure of a certificate from failure of local minimality itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f,x_*)\in\mathfrak G_p\iff x_*\notin\operatorname{argmin}_{\mathrm{loc}}f\ \text{and the selected order-}\!p\text{ local certificate is nondecisive}.\)
special_cases_latex: For \(p=1\), every stationary nonminimizer is invisible to the gradient value at the point.
For \(p=2\), a negative Hessian eigenvalue excludes failure of curvature detection, whereas a positive-semidefinite singular Hessian may remain nondecisive.
immediate_consequences_latex: Membership depends on the chosen order and criticality measure.
A complexity guarantee for reaching small criticality does not alone exclude this class.
boundary_notes: The phrase “critical-geometry failure class” is not supported by the supplied sources as a standard named definition.
The displayed class combines Taylor nondecisiveness and nonisolated critical-set behavior; a source is needed to validate this exact taxonomy.

children.title: Curvature-Detectable Saddle Geometry
children.top_down_role: Nonminimizing critical points visible to curvature-aware methods.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), with gradient \(g_*\) and Hessian \(H_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained, twice-differentiable nonconvex optimization; detectability is by second-order curvature at the point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x_*\) has curvature-detectable saddle geometry if \(
abla f(x_*)=0\) and there exist \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\gamma>0\) such that \(d^T
abla^2f(x_*)d\leq-\gamma\|d\|^2\). Equivalently, \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x_*))\leq-\gamma<0\). The point is therefore a nonminimizing stationary point whose failure of the second-order necessary condition is visible to a curvature-aware oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature-detectable saddle is stationary but has a direction of strictly negative Hessian curvature. Equivalently, the smallest Hessian eigenvalue is negative and bounded away from zero by the stated margin. A method able to detect such curvature can distinguish this point from a second-order critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\exists d
eq0:\ d^T
abla^2f(x_*)d<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x_*))<0.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: After normalizing \(d\), detectability is \(\min_{\|u\|=1}u^TH_*u<0\).
For a tolerance \(\epsilon_H>0\), quantitative detectability is \(\lambda_{\min}(H_*)\leq-\epsilon_H\).
special_cases_latex: In one dimension, the condition is \(f'(x_*)=0\) and \(f''(x_*)<0\).
A strict saddle with a negative Hessian eigenvalue satisfies this definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: The point violates the second-order necessary condition \(H_*\succeq0\).
A trust-region model containing the negative-curvature direction decreases toward its boundary along one of the two signs of that direction.
boundary_notes: A stationary nonminimum with \(H_*\succeq0\) is not curvature-detectable under this definition.
The definition does not require all Hessian eigenvalues to be nonzero.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian at the critical point.

children.title: Strict-Saddle Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local landscape structure around nonminimizing strict critical points.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Saddle Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative finite-dimensional strict-saddle condition separating large gradients, negative curvature, and strongly convex minimizer basins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A twice continuously differentiable function \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) has \((\varepsilon,\gamma,r,\mu)\)-strict-saddle geometry on \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) if, for every \(x\in\mathcal D\), at least one condition holds: \(\lVert
abla f(x)Vert\geq\varepsilon\); \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\leq-\gamma\); or there exists a local minimizer \(x_\star\) with \(\lVert x-x_\starVert\leq r\) such that \(
abla^2f(y)\succeq\mu I\) for every \(y\in\mathcal D\) satisfying \(\lVert y-x_\starVert\leq2r\). Here \(\varepsilon,\gamma,r,\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point either has a large gradient, exhibits detectable negative curvature, or lies near a uniformly strongly convex local-minimum basin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in\mathcal D\), a large-gradient, negative-curvature, or strongly-convex-basin alternative holds.

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix
local minimizer defining a strongly convex basin
domain on which strict-saddle geometry is asserted

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantitative alternative is mathematically coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf, but strict-saddle definitions vary materially in their basin condition, neighborhood radius, domain restrictions, and use of strongly convex neighborhoods. An authoritative source is required for this exact four-parameter version.

children.title: Negative-Curvature Detectability
children.top_down_role: Visibility of saddle structure through curvature-sensitive information.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Detectability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative second-order condition under which a Hessian-based procedure can exhibit a saddle direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\varepsilon_H>0\). Negative curvature is \(\varepsilon_H\)-detectable at \(x\) if a Hessian-based procedure can return a vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[\|v\|=1,\qquad v^{\mathsf T}
abla^2 f(x)v\le -\varepsilon_H.\] With exact access to \(
abla^2f(x)\) and an exact eigensolver, this condition holds if and only if \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\le-\varepsilon_H\); a unit eigenvector associated with the smallest eigenvalue is then a detecting direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative curvature is detectable at the prescribed threshold when a Hessian-based procedure can exhibit a unit direction whose curvature is at most minus that threshold. With exact eigensystem access, this is equivalent to the smallest Hessian eigenvalue being at most minus the threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|v\|=1\) and \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2 f(x)v\le-\varepsilon_H\).

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Based Escape Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A descent step that escapes points possessing quantitatively negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L_H\)-Lipschitz Hessian. At \(x\), obtain a unit vector \(v\) with \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)v\le-\varepsilon_H\), choose its sign so that \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}v\le0\), and set \[s=\frac{2\varepsilon_H}{L_H}v,\qquad x^+=x+s.\] If \(L_H>0\), the third-order Taylor bound gives \(f(x^+)\le f(x)-2\varepsilon_H^3/(3L_H^2)\). The regime terminates when no direction below \(-\varepsilon_H\) is detected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed step along detectable negative curvature decreases the objective by order cubed curvature threshold divided by squared Hessian-Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x^+)\le f(x)-2\varepsilon_H^3/(3L_H^2)\).

children.title: Detection Failure Near Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Limits of curvature-based saddle recognition as the negative-curvature signal weakens.

knowledge_statements.title: Detection Failure Near Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold failure when the most negative Hessian eigenvalue approaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon_H>0\) and consider \(f_\delta(t)=-\delta t^2/2+t^4/4\) at \(t=0\), where \(0<\delta<\varepsilon_H\). Then \(f_\delta'(0)=0\) and \(f_\delta''(0)=-\delta<0\), so the origin is not a local minimizer. Nevertheless, it satisfies the approximate second-order test \(f_\delta''(0)\ge-\varepsilon_H\). Thus any detector that declares failure solely when curvature is below \(-\varepsilon_H\) cannot distinguish this increasingly degenerate saddle from an \(\varepsilon_H\)-second-order stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed curvature threshold misses saddles whose negative eigenvalue is nonzero but smaller in magnitude than that threshold.
assumptions_latex: Detection uses only the threshold test \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))< -\varepsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\delta''(0)<0\) but \(f_\delta''(0)\ge-\varepsilon_H\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example is algebraically correct and fits a failure-boundary container, but it has no cited source. A source with a specific locator is required for the threshold-detection limitation or this degenerating-saddle example.

children.title: Low-Order Signal Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate regions invisible to lower-order measures.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable at \(x_*\), and define the low-order signal \(\mathcal S_2(x_*)=(\nabla f(x_*),\nabla^2f(x_*))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise degeneracy of gradient and Hessian information in smooth unconstrained optimization, relative to discrimination of local minima from nonminima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x_*\) is low-order signal-degenerate if \(
abla f(x_*)=0\), \(
abla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\) is singular, and these data are nondecisive for local minimality: there exists a twice-differentiable \(\widetilde f\) with \(\widetilde f(x_*)=f(x_*)\), \(
abla\widetilde f(x_*)=0\), and \(
abla^2\widetilde f(x_*)=
abla^2f(x_*)\), but exactly one of \(f\) and \(\widetilde f\) has a local minimum at \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-order signal degeneracy occurs when the gradient vanishes and the Hessian is positive semidefinite but singular, so the value, gradient, and Hessian at the point do not determine whether it is locally minimizing. Another smooth function can share all those pointwise data while having the opposite local-minimality classification.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and the comparison function are twice differentiable at \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S_2^f(x_*)=\mathcal S_2^{\widetilde f}(x_*)\ \text{does not imply equal local-minimality status}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The second-order necessary conditions hold, but the positive-definite sufficient condition fails.
Descent or minimality is governed by higher-order terms or non-Taylor local behavior along \(\ker\nabla^2f(x_*)\).
special_cases_latex: At zero, \(f(t)=t^4\) and \(\widetilde f(t)=t^3\) have equal value, zero first derivative, and zero second derivative, but only the former has a local minimum.
If \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succ0\), this degeneracy is absent.
immediate_consequences_latex: A termination test based only on small gradient and almost-nonnegative Hessian cannot certify local minimality in this class.
Higher-order information may be required on the Hessian nullspace.
boundary_notes: Negative curvature is excluded because it already provides a second-order signal.
This is pointwise indistinguishability, not a claim about oracle lower bounds over a neighborhood.

children.title: Flat-Saddle Geometry
children.top_down_role: Degenerate saddle regions with weak local variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Saddle Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stationary saddle whose ascent and descent geometry is invisible to Hessian sign at the point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. A point \(x_*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a flat saddle if \[\nabla f(x_*)=0,\qquad \nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0,\] and every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) contains points \(y,z\in U\) such that \[f(y)<f(x_*)<f(z).\] Thus \(x_*\) is neither a local minimizer nor a local maximizer, while the Hessian at \(x_*\) contains no negative-curvature direction. The local descent and ascent geometry must therefore occur beyond the pointwise quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat saddle is stationary and has a positive-semidefinite Hessian, yet arbitrarily nearby points have both lower and higher objective values. Its saddle geometry is therefore invisible to the pointwise Hessian sign test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\), \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\), and every neighborhood of \(x_*\) contains points with objective values both below and above \(f(x_*)\).

notation.meaning: the symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite

children.title: Vanishing Gradient Signals
children.top_down_role: Loss of first-order discrimination near flat nonminimizing regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Gradient Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of first-order directional information at a stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), the gradient signal vanishes at \(x_*\) precisely when \[\nabla f(x_*)=0.\] Consequently, every directional derivative satisfies \(Df(x_*)[v]=\nabla f(x_*)^{\mathsf T}v=0\) for \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A first-order oracle queried only at \(x_*\) therefore supplies no descent direction, irrespective of whether \(x_*\) is a minimum, maximum, or saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary point every first directional derivative is zero, so a pointwise first-order oracle cannot classify the critical geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Df(x_*)[v]=0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: directional derivative of the function at the point along the direction

children.title: Vanishing Curvature Signals
children.top_down_role: Loss of second-order discrimination near degenerate saddles.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Curvature Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of quadratic directional information along a nontrivial subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable at a stationary point \(x_*\). Curvature signals vanish on a nonzero subspace \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) when \[K\subseteq\ker\nabla^2f(x_*).\] Hence \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x_*)v=0\) for every \(v\in K\), and the second-order Taylor model is constant along \(K\). If \(K=\mathbb{R}^n\), the entire Hessian vanishes and no pointwise quadratic model distinguishes ascent from descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature vanishes on the Hessian kernel, where the quadratic Taylor model provides no directional classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x_*)v=0\) for every \(v\in K\).

children.title: Higher-Order Saddle Detectability
children.top_down_role: Visibility of flat saddle structure through information beyond curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Saddle Detectability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detection by the first nonzero Taylor coefficient along a direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(p\)-times differentiable near \(x_*\), with \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\), and let \(v\ne0\). A saddle descent signal is detectable at order \(p\ge3\) along \(v\) if all directional coefficients of orders \(1,\ldots,p-1\) vanish and \[D^pf(x_*)[v]^p<0.\] For sufficiently small \(t>0\), Taylor expansion then yields \(f(x_*+tv)<f(x_*)\). If \(p\) is odd and the coefficient is nonzero, one of \(v\) or \(-v\) satisfies the displayed inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When lower-order directional terms vanish, a negative first nonzero higher-order Taylor coefficient reveals local descent and hence nonminimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) admits a directional Taylor expansion through order \(p\) at \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^pf(x_*)[v]^p<0\) implies \(f(x_*+tv)<f(x_*)\) for all sufficiently small \(t>0\).

notation.meaning: the p-th derivative tensor applied p times to the direction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the explicitly assumed directional Taylor expansion, the higher-order descent implication is correct and fits a detectability condition. No source with an inspectable locator is supplied, so the higher-order formulation cannot yet be accepted.

children.title: Persistent Signal Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Regions where several derivative orders remain insufficient for reliable classification.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Signal Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-order derivative oracles can remain blind to genuine descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(0)=0\) and \[f(t)=-\exp(-1/t^2)\quad\text{for }t\ne0.\] Then \(f\) is infinitely differentiable, \(f^{(k)}(0)=0\) for every integer \(k\ge1\), and \(f(t)<f(0)\) whenever \(t\ne0\). Thus the origin is not a local minimizer, although every finite-order Taylor oracle at the origin returns exactly the same derivative data as the constant-zero function. No fixed finite derivative order can detect this descent geometry from pointwise data alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth function can have every derivative vanish at a nonminimum, making all finite-order pointwise Taylor tests permanently inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: The oracle observes only finitely many derivatives at the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{(k)}(0)=0\) for all \(k\ge1\), yet \(f(t)<f(0)\) for every \(t\ne0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical smooth flat-function example correctly demonstrates failure of every fixed finite-order pointwise derivative test and fits a failure-boundary container. It nevertheless lacks the required source and specific locator.

children.title: Critical-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Set-valued critical geometry affecting identification and local behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Geometry of a Smooth Critical Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable on an open set \(\Omega\), and define \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\{x\in\Omega:\nabla f(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued geometry of stationary points for smooth unconstrained objectives; the definition distinguishes isolation, accumulation, and manifold structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local critical-set germ at \(x_*\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\) is the family \([\operatorname{Crit}(f)]_{x_*}=\{\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap B(x_*,r):r>0\}\). The point is isolated if some \(r>0\) gives \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap B(x_*,r)=\{x_*\}\); it is an accumulation point if every such ball contains another critical point. The critical set is locally a \(d\)-dimensional \(C^1\) manifold at \(x_*\) if some neighborhood \(U\) makes \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap U\) an embedded \(C^1\) manifold of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Critical-set geometry is the local structure of the stationary-point set around a chosen critical point. Its basic attributes include whether the point is isolated, whether other critical points accumulate there, and whether the nearby critical set forms a smooth manifold of a specified dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\{x\in\Omega:\nabla f(x)=0\}\), with local geometry determined by \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap B(x_*,r)\) as \(r\downarrow0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Isolation is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dist}(x_*,\operatorname{Crit}(f)\setminus\{x_*\})>0\).
Accumulation is equivalent to the existence of distinct \(x_j\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\) with \(x_j\to x_*\).
special_cases_latex: A discrete critical set has only isolated points locally.
A flat valley may have a positive-dimensional critical manifold.
immediate_consequences_latex: Point identification is qualitatively different for an isolated point and a positive-dimensional critical set.
Convergence of a criticality measure to zero need not select a unique limit point when the critical set is nonisolated.
boundary_notes: This definition does not classify each critical point as minimizing, maximizing, or saddle-like.
No inspected source in the supplied hints supports this exact critical-set-germ formulation.

notation.meaning: Open Euclidean ball of radius r around the point.

review_flags: A precise authoritative source for the critical-set germ and its algorithmic interpretation is required.

children.title: Nonisolated Minimizer Sets
children.top_down_role: Families of minimizing points lacking local isolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Minimizer Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local minimizers forming a set without isolated members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), a set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonisolated local-minimizer set if every \(x\in M\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) and an accumulation point of \(M\). Explicitly, for every \(x\in M\) there exists \(r_x>0\) such that \[f(y)\ge f(x)\quad\text{whenever }y\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and }\|y-x\|<r_x,\] and for every \(r>0\) there exists \(z\in M\setminus\{x\}\) with \(\|z-x\|<r\). If \(f\) is continuous and \(M\) is path-connected, then \(f\) is constant on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonisolated minimizer set consists entirely of local minima, with another member of the set arbitrarily close to each one. A continuous objective is constant on such a set when the set is path-connected.
assumptions_latex: For the final constancy assertion, \(f\) is continuous and \(M\) is path-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in M\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) and an accumulation point of \(M\).

children.title: Critical-Manifold Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure of smooth or stratified sets of critical points.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Manifold Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morse–Bott-type geometry of a smooth set of critical points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. An embedded \(C^2\) submanifold \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nondegenerate critical manifold for \(f\) if \[\nabla f(x)=0,\qquad \ker\nabla^2f(x)=T_xM\quad\text{for every }x\in M.\] Thus the Hessian vanishes on tangent directions and is nonsingular on the normal space \(N_xM=(T_xM)^\perp\). If its normal restriction is positive definite, \(M\) is locally minimizing in normal directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondegenerate critical manifold has Hessian kernel exactly equal to its tangent space; all nonzero second-order behavior lies in normal directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker\nabla^2f(x)=T_xM\) for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: tangent space to the manifold at the point
Euclidean normal space to the manifold at the point

children.title: Tangential Neutrality

knowledge_statements.title: Tangential Neutrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- and second-order variation vanishes along a critical manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\), and let \(M\) be a \(C^2\) submanifold satisfying \(
abla f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in M\). For every \(x\in M\) and \(v\in T_xM\), \[
abla^2f(x)v=0.\] Consequently, \(v^{\mathsf T}
abla^2f(x)v=0\), and the value of \(f\) is constant on each connected component of \(M\). Tangent directions are therefore neutral for both the first-order and quadratic models at points of the critical manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a smooth manifold of critical points, tangent directions lie in the Hessian kernel and the objective is constant on connected components.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a \(C^2\) submanifold contained in the critical set of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_xM\subseteq\ker\nabla^2f(x)\) for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: tangent space to the critical manifold

children.title: Normal-Direction Identification
children.top_down_role: Local recognition of displacement away from a critical manifold.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Direction Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral separation identifies directions transverse to a critical manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a \(C^2\) critical manifold of \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\). Normal directions are uniformly identifiable on \(M\) if there exists \(\mu>0\) such that, for every \(x\in M\), \[\ker\nabla^2f(x)=T_xM,\qquad \|\nabla^2f(x)v\|\ge\mu\|v\|\quad\text{for all }v\in N_xM.\] The zero eigenspace then identifies the tangent space, while its orthogonal complement identifies the normal space; the gap \(\mu\) separates neutral tangential modes from normal curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform spectral gap away from zero on the normal space separates transverse curvature from neutral tangent directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_xM=\ker\nabla^2f(x)\) and \(N_xM=(\ker\nabla^2f(x))^\perp\), uniformly separated by \(\mu\).

notation.meaning: normal space to the critical manifold

children.title: Local Behavior Near Critical Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Local Behavior Near Critical Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morse–Bott quadratic growth near a nonisolated critical manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable and let \(C\) be a \(C^2\) manifold of critical points on which \(f\) is locally constant. Suppose \(\ker \nabla^2 f(z)=T_zC\) and \(v^\top\nabla^2f(z)v\geq \mu\|v\|^2\) for every \(z\in C\) near \(\bar x\in C\) and every \(v\in (T_zC)^\perp\), with \(\mu>0\). Then some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) satisfy \[c_1\operatorname{dist}(x,C)^2\leq f(x)-f(\bar x)\leq c_2\operatorname{dist}(x,C)^2\quad(x\in U).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform positive curvature normal to a critical manifold yields local quadratic growth in the distance to that manifold, while tangent directions remain neutral.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2\) near \(\bar x\) and \(C\) is a local \(C^2\) critical manifold.
The Hessian kernel equals the tangent space and is uniformly positive on normal spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f(\bar x)=\Theta(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)^2)\) locally.

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the critical manifold at z.
Euclidean distance from x to C.

children.title: Limitations of Higher-Order Criticality Measures
children.top_down_role: Boundaries of Taylor surrogates as local-minimality certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Limitations of Higher-Order Criticality Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Taylor data cannot alone certify local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an order \(p\geq 1\), and let \(m\) be the smallest odd integer strictly larger than \(p\). For \(f(x)=x^m\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), \[f^{(j)}(0)=0\qquad(1\leq j\leq p).\] Thus every criticality measure determined solely by derivatives through order \(p\) takes at \(0\) the same value as it does for the constant function. Nevertheless, \(0\) is not a local minimizer of \(f\), because \(f(x)<0\) for every negative \(x\). Consequently, vanishing finite-order Taylor data is not a sufficient local-minimality certificate without additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any finite derivative order, an odd monomial of higher degree has vanishing measured derivatives at zero although zero is not a local minimum.
assumptions_latex: The criticality measure depends only on derivatives of orders at most \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vanishing order-\(p\) Taylor criticality does not imply local minimality.

notation.meaning: Smallest odd integer greater than p.

u,x_

Thus vanishing model decrement is only an order-relative condition and need not certify local minimality.

children.title: Higher-Order Model Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validity Boundary for a Higher-Order Regularized Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(p\geq1\), and consider \(m_k(s)=\widetilde T_{p,k}(s)+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{r}\|s\|^r\), where \(r>p\), \(\sigma_k>0\), and \(\widetilde T_{p,k}\) is an exact or approximate Taylor model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal boundary of the assumptions needed to transfer outer evaluation-complexity claims to realizable higher-order regularization methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The higher-order model validity region \(\mathfrak V_{p,r}\) consists of instances for which, on the relevant level set, an order-\(p\) Taylor remainder bound holds, the regularization power \(r\) dominates the remainder order, model-value and derivative errors satisfy prescribed step-scaled bounds, and the cost of producing an admissible model step is controlled in the declared computational oracle. children.title: Insufficient Higher-Order Regularity
