knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient Higher-Order Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the Hölder remainder required by high-order Taylor models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\geq1\), \(0<\beta<\alpha\leq1\), and \(f(x)=|x|^{p+\beta}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f\in C^p\), but its \(p\)-th derivative is generally only \(\beta\)-Hölder near zero and is not \(\alpha\)-Hölder there. Since the order-\(p\) Taylor polynomial at zero is \(T_p(0,s)=0\), \[\frac{|f(s)-T_p(0,s)|}{|s|^{p+\alpha}}=|s|^{\beta-\alpha}\longrightarrow\infty\quad(s\to0).\] Hence no local constant \(L\) can provide the nominal remainder bound \(|f(s)-T_p(0,s)|\leq L|s|^{p+\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function with only beta-Hölder pth derivative violates every stronger alpha-Hölder Taylor remainder bound, invalidating complexity results that require that bound.
assumptions_latex: The nominal analysis requires an order-\(p+\alpha\) Taylor remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The required \(O(|s|^{p+\alpha})\) model-error bound fails at zero.

notation.meaning: Order-p Taylor polynomial of f at zero evaluated at displacement s.

children.title: Miscalibrated Regularization Power
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between model power and operative smoothness.

knowledge_statements.title: Miscalibrated Regularization Power
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularization power exceeds the order of the operative model error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an order-\(p\) Taylor model has an operative remainder of order \(p+\beta\), where \(0<\beta\leq1\), and consider \[m(s)=T_p(x,s)+\frac{\sigma}{r}\|s\|^r,\qquad \sigma>0.\] If \(r>p+\beta\), then \(\|s\|^r=o(\|s\|^{p+\beta})\) as \(s\to0\). Therefore no fixed \(\sigma\) makes the regularization term dominate every remainder satisfying \(|f(x+s)-T_p(x,s)|\leq L\|s\|^{p+\beta}\). The usual model-majorization or acceptance argument is consequently unavailable unless the power is recalibrated, the coefficient varies with scale, or stronger smoothness is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the regularizer decays faster than the actual Taylor error, no fixed coefficient can uniformly control that error near zero.
assumptions_latex: The Taylor remainder is controlled only at order \(p+\beta\).
The regularization coefficient \(\sigma\) is fixed and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regularization term cannot uniformly dominate the operative Taylor remainder for small steps.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: asymptotic comparison of model-error and regularization powers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularization-Power Mismatch with Taylor Remainder Order
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an order-\(p\) model have remainder scale \(|f(x+s)-T_p(x,s)|\leq L\|s\|^{p+\beta}\), where \(\beta\in(0,1]\), and let its regularized model be \(m(s)=T_p(x,s)+\tfrac\sigma r\|s\|^r\) with \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-law regularization for smooth or Hölder-smooth nonconvex Taylor models; calibration is relative to the operative remainder exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regularization power is calibrated to the remainder when \(r=p+\beta\). It is underpowered when \(r>p+\beta\), because \(\|s\|^r=o(\|s\|^{p+\beta})\) as \(s\to0\) and a bounded coefficient \(\sigma\) cannot uniformly dominate the permitted remainder at small steps. It is exponent-mismatched whenever \(r\neq p+\beta\); the case \(r<p+\beta\) overregularizes asymptotically and generally belongs to a different rate model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularization power is miscalibrated when its step exponent does not match the order of the Taylor remainder assumed in the analysis. If the regularization term has a larger exponent, it vanishes faster than the allowed error and cannot uniformly dominate that error with a bounded coefficient. A smaller exponent produces a stronger small-step penalty and changes the nominal scaling and rate regime.
assumptions_latex: The remainder exponent \(p+\beta\) is valid on the relevant domain.
The regularization coefficient is finite and does not diverge as an arbitrary function of each trial step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r=p+\beta\ \text{is matched};\qquad r>p+\beta\ \text{is asymptotically underpowered}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Underpowering is \(\lim_{\|s\|\downarrow0}\|s\|^r/\|s\|^{p+\beta}=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a Lipschitz \(p\)th derivative, \(\beta=1\) and the matched power is \(p+1\).
Cubic regularization of a quadratic model corresponds to \(p=2\), \(\beta=1\), and \(r=3\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Rates proved for the matched exponent cannot be transferred unchanged to a mismatched exponent.
An underpowered regularizer may require an unbounded adaptive coefficient to compensate for small-step scaling.
boundary_notes: The term “overregularized” describes exponent scaling, not necessarily worse practical performance.
No inspected supplied source supports this exact matched-power definition and its complexity interpretation.

children.title: Uncontrolled Model Error
children.top_down_role: Approximation failures incompatible with acceptance or termination certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Model Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance ratios fail without error relative to predicted decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_k\) be a local model at \(x_k\), let \(s_k\) be a trial step, and define \(\Delta m_k=m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)>0\) and \(e_k=f(x_k+s_k)-m_k(s_k)\), assuming \(m_k(0)=f(x_k)\). The actual-to-predicted ratio is \[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{\Delta m_k}=1-\frac{e_k}{\Delta m_k}.\] Thus a bound such as \(|e_k|\leq\kappa\Delta m_k\) is necessary for ratio control based solely on the model. If \(|e_k|/\Delta m_k\) is unbounded, \(\rho_k\) can be arbitrarily negative despite positive predicted decrease, so acceptance and decrease certificates do not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When model error is unbounded relative to predicted decrease, a step predicted to improve the objective can have an arbitrarily bad acceptance ratio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unbounded \(|e_k|/\Delta m_k\) precludes uniform control of \(\rho_k\).

notation.meaning: Model error at the trial point.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact algebraic identity for model acceptance ratios

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(m_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be an approximate local model at \(x_k\), and let \(s_k\) be a proposed step. Define \(e_k^f(s)=f(x_k+s)-m_k(s)\) and, when differentiable, \(e_k^g(s)=\nabla f(x_k+s)-\nabla m_k(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic inexact local models used in acceptance ratios or derivative-based termination tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Model error is controlled at orders \((a,b)\) if finite constants \(\kappa_f,\kappa_g\), independent of \(k\), satisfy \(|e_k^f(s_k)|\leq\kappa_f\|s_k\|^a\) and \(\|e_k^g(s_k)\|\leq\kappa_g\|s_k\|^b\) whenever the algorithm invokes the corresponding value or derivative certificate. It is uncontrolled if no such declared uniform constants and orders exist, or if the implemented error tests permit violations on an infinite subsequence relevant to acceptance or termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model error is controlled when function-value and derivative discrepancies obey uniform bounds scaled to the trial-step size at every iteration where those quantities support acceptance or termination. It is uncontrolled when no such bounds are declared or when the required bounds may fail repeatedly along relevant iterations.
assumptions_latex: The model and true function are evaluated at common base points and trial steps.
The orders \(a,b\) required by the surrounding algorithm are fixed before classifying the errors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{uncontrolled}\iff\neg\exists\kappa_f,\kappa_g<\infty\ \forall k:\ |e_k^f(s_k)|\leq\kappa_f\|s_k\|^a,\ \|e_k^g(s_k)\|\leq\kappa_g\|s_k\|^b.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an acceptance ratio based on actual and predicted decrease, control may instead be expressed by bounding the error relative to the predicted decrease.
special_cases_latex: Exact models have \(e_k^f=e_k^g=0\) at every queried point.
A uniformly bounded absolute error need not be controlled as \(s_k\to0\) when a vanishing step-scaled tolerance is required.
immediate_consequences_latex: Acceptance ratios may cease to reflect true reduction when value error is of the same or larger order than predicted reduction.
A model-based termination certificate need not transfer to the true derivatives without derivative-error control.
boundary_notes: Random error requires probabilistic rather than deterministic quantifiers.

children.title: Hidden Inner-Solve Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Inner-Solve Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer evaluation complexity does not bound total computational work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an algorithm performing at most \(N(\varepsilon)\) outer iterations to obtain an \(\varepsilon\)-critical point. If iteration \(k\) invokes an inner model solver for \(J_k\) oracle calls or arithmetic steps, then its total inner work is \[W(\varepsilon)=\sum_{k=0}^{N(\varepsilon)-1}J_k.\] An outer evaluation bound controls \(W(\varepsilon)\) only when a uniform or summable bound on the \(J_k\) is supplied. In particular, if the model-subproblem stopping rule permits arbitrarily large finite \(J_k\), no function of \(N(\varepsilon)\) alone bounds total work; the evaluation complexity is therefore not an end-to-end computational complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound on outer objective evaluations says nothing about total work when the number of inner model-solver operations is left unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: The method has an outer bound \(N(\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without bounds on \(J_k\), \(N(\varepsilon)\) does not bound \(W(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Inner-solve work at outer iteration k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hidden Inner Cost in an Outer Evaluation Bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an algorithm generate outer iterations \(k=0,1,\ldots,K(\epsilon)-1\). At iteration \(k\), let \(J_k\) be the number of auxiliary inner operations needed to produce an admissible step, and let \(C_{k,j}\geq0\) be their costs in a declared primitive-operation oracle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity accounting that distinguishes outer objective/derivative evaluations from iterative subproblem, linear-system, eigenvalue, or tensor-model work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An outer complexity guarantee has hidden inner-solve cost when it bounds \(K(\epsilon)\), or the number of outer evaluations, but supplies no uniform bound on \(J_k\) or on \(W(\epsilon)=\sum_{k=0}^{K(\epsilon)-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J_k}C_{k,j}\). Formally, hidden cost is present if instances with the same declared outer bound can have arbitrarily large \(W(\epsilon)\) in the primitive-operation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner cost is hidden when a result bounds outer iterations or function and derivative evaluations but does not control the work required to obtain each accepted model step. The omitted work may include Krylov products, linear solves, eigenvalue iterations, tensor contractions, or repeated approximate minimization of a regularized model.
assumptions_latex: Outer and inner operations are distinguished by an explicit cost model.
Each outer step must satisfy an admissibility condition whose production may require iterative work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(\epsilon)\leq\overline K(\epsilon)\ \text{with no bound on }W(\epsilon)=\sum_{k<K(\epsilon)}\sum_{j\leq J_k}C_{k,j}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: There is no function \(\Psi\) in the stated theorem such that \(W(\epsilon)\leq\Psi(\overline K(\epsilon),n,\epsilon,\text{problem constants})\).
special_cases_latex: If every inner solve uses at most \(J\) unit-cost operations, then \(W(\epsilon)\leq J\overline K(\epsilon)\) and this particular cost is not hidden.
Counting Hessian-vector products but not their implementation cost leaves a lower-level oracle cost hidden.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two methods with equal evaluation complexity can have incomparable total running costs.
An evaluation-complexity result must be labeled by its oracle rather than presented as an arithmetic bound.
boundary_notes: Hidden does not mean negligible or necessarily large; it means uncontrolled by the stated guarantee.
No inspected source supplies this exact formal definition.

notation.meaning: Number of inner operations at outer iteration k.
Total inner work before reaching tolerance epsilon.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) possess a symmetric order-\(p\) derivative tensor \(A=\nabla^pf(x)\), viewed as a multilinear form on \((\mathbb R^n)^p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional realization cost for dense higher-order derivative information; sparsity, partial separability, and automatic differentiation may change the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The explicit tensor realization stores all independent symmetric coefficients of \(A\), whose count is \(N_{n,p}=\binom{n+p-1}{p}\), and permits contractions from those coefficients. An operator realization exposes only queries such as \((v_1,\ldots,v_p)\mapsto A[v_1,\ldots,v_p]\) or \(v\mapsto A[v]^{p-1}\). The explicit-realization cost boundary is reached when the allowed memory, construction time, or arithmetic budget is \(o(N_{n,p})\), so a generic dense tensor cannot be materialized within that budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense symmetric derivative tensor of order greater than two has one independent coefficient for every degree-p monomial in n variables. Explicit realization crosses its cost boundary when available storage or construction work grows more slowly than that coefficient count. At that point, only structured, sparse, elementwise, or operator-based access is compatible with the declared budget.
assumptions_latex: The tensor is treated as generic and dense unless additional structure is stated.
Symmetry of the derivative tensor is used when counting independent coefficients.
The order \(p\) and dimension \(n\) are part of the cost model.

equivalent_formulations_latex: For fixed \(p\), \(N_{n,p}=\Theta(n^p)\) as \(n\to\infty\).
For fixed \(n\), the coefficient count grows polynomially in \(p\) with degree \(n-1\).

children.title: Explicit Tensor Storage

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Tensor Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage count for dense order-p derivative tensors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in(\mathbb{R}^n)^{\otimes p}\) be an order-\(p\) tensor. Storing all ordered entries requires exactly \(n^p\) scalars. If \(A\) is fully symmetric and the representation stores one scalar for each permutation orbit, the number of distinct entries is \[S(n,p)=\binom{n+p-1}{p}.\] Consequently dense explicit storage is \(\Theta(n^p)\) for fixed \(p\), whether ordered storage or symmetry-reduced storage is used, although symmetry reduces the leading constant by approximately \(p!\). At \(b\) bytes per scalar, the respective memory requirements are \(bn^p\) and \(bS(n,p)\) bytes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense order-p tensor needs n-to-the-p stored scalars, or a binomial number when full symmetry is exploited.
assumptions_latex: The tensor is dense; symmetry is used only in the symmetry-reduced count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit storage uses \(n^p\) scalars, or \(\binom{n+p-1}{p}\) distinct scalars under full symmetry.

notation.meaning: Number of distinct entries of a fully symmetric order-p tensor.
Bytes used by one stored scalar.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Tensor Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative tensors represented through contraction oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An implicit representation of an order-\(p\) tensor \(A\) is an oracle that, for requested vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), returns \[\mathcal{O}_A(v_1,\ldots,v_p)=A[v_1,\ldots,v_p]=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_p=1}^n A_{i_1\cdots i_p}(v_1)_{i_1}\cdots(v_p)_{i_p},\] or returns specified partial contractions, without materializing every entry of \(A\). Such a representation is storage-efficient only relative to explicit storage when its persistent state is \(o(n^p)\); it is computationally efficient only when the required contractions can also be evaluated below the corresponding dense cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit tensor stores a procedure for requested contractions instead of all entries; storage savings alone do not guarantee cheaper contractions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a multilinear order-\(p\) tensor on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
The algorithm accesses \(A\) only through declared contraction queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tensor may be represented without explicit \(n^p\)-entry materialization.

children.title: Tensor-Vector Contraction Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor-Vector Contraction Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost of unstructured dense tensor contractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a dense, explicitly stored order-\(p\) tensor on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with no exploitable structure. Direct evaluation of the scalar contraction \(A[v_1,\ldots,v_p]\) reads \(n^p\) coefficients and uses \(\Theta(pn^p)\) scalar multiplications and additions. For fixed \(p\), this is \(\Theta(n^p)\) arithmetic and memory traffic. Likewise, contracting \(p-1\) modes and leaving one free, producing a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), has \(\Theta(n^p)\) dense arithmetic cost. Lower costs require sparsity, factorization, repeated-vector structure, or an implicit derivative procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without exploitable structure, scalar or one-free-mode contractions of a dense order-p tensor cost order n-to-the-p arithmetic for fixed p.
assumptions_latex: No sparsity, factorization, or specialized contraction oracle is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense scalar and one-free-mode contractions require \(\Theta(n^p)\) work for fixed \(p\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Driven Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension dependence hidden by evaluation-complexity notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a high-order method performs \(N(\varepsilon)\) iterations and each iteration explicitly forms an order-\(p\) dense derivative tensor and performs at least one dense contraction. In the unit-cost arithmetic model, its implementation requires at least \[\Omega\!\left(N(\varepsilon)n^p\right)\] tensor-entry processing operations and \(\Omega(n^p)\) working storage, or \(\Omega\!\left(\binom{n+p-1}{p}\right)\) storage when full symmetry is exploited. Thus an evaluation bound expressed only through \(N(\varepsilon)\) suppresses polynomial dependence on dimension; scalability requires a structured or implicit realization whose per-iteration cost has better dependence on \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every iteration forms and contracts a dense order-p derivative tensor, total work scales at least as the iteration count times n-to-the-p.
assumptions_latex: Each of \(N(\varepsilon)\) iterations processes a dense order-\(p\) tensor.
Tensor entries or equivalent dense contraction terms have unit processing cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Tensor Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CP representation and its storage and contraction savings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An order-\(p\) tensor \(A\) has a rank-\(R\) CP representation when \[A=\sum_{r=1}^R a_r^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes a_r^{(p)},\qquad a_r^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] This representation stores \(Rpn\) scalars instead of \(n^p\). Given vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\), its full contraction is \[A[v_1,\ldots,v_p]=\sum_{r=1}^R\prod_{j=1}^p\langle a_r^{(j)},v_j\rangle,\] computable in \(O(Rpn)\) arithmetic. The savings are valid only when \(Rpn\ll n^p\) and the factors are available or can be constructed without comparable dense-tensor cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-R CP factorization reduces storage and full-contraction work to order Rpn, provided obtaining the factors does not require dense-tensor cost.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) admits the displayed rank-\(R\) CP representation.
All factor vectors are explicitly available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Storage and full-contraction work are \(O(Rpn)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Tensor Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory and work thresholds for explicit dense derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be the available tensor-storage budget in bytes and let each scalar require \(b>0\) bytes. A dense order-\(p\) tensor in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is infeasible to store explicitly whenever \[bn^p>B.\] Even with full symmetry and optimal storage of distinct entries, explicit storage is infeasible whenever \[b\binom{n+p-1}{p}>B.\] Independently, if the per-iteration arithmetic budget is \(F\) operations, an unstructured dense contraction is infeasible whenever its required \(cn^p\) operations exceed \(F\), for the implementation-dependent constant \(c>0\). These inequalities define hardware-relative, not evaluation-complexity, feasibility boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit tensors exceed feasibility when their dense or symmetry-reduced byte count, or their contraction work, surpasses the available hardware budget.
assumptions_latex: The tensor is dense of order \(p\) in dimension \(n\).
Available memory is \(B\) bytes and each scalar occupies \(b\) bytes.
Dense contraction cost is at least \(cn^p\) operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed memory or arithmetic inequalities rule out the corresponding explicit realization.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct comparison of exact storage counts with hardware budgets

children.title: Complexity-Interpretation Limits
children.top_down_role: Prevents comparisons across incompatible computational and asymptotic viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparability Domain of an Optimization Complexity Bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Represent a complexity statement by a tuple \(\mathcal C=(\mathfrak P,\mathfrak O,\mathfrak A,\mathfrak T,\mathbf z,N)\), where \(\mathfrak P\) is the problem class, \(\mathfrak O\) the oracle and charged operations, \(\mathfrak A\) the algorithm class, \(\mathfrak T\) the termination predicate, \(\mathbf z\) the asymptotic variables held free, and \(N\) the resulting bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretation and comparison of worst-case optimization complexity statements; it does not define a new convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two complexity statements \(\mathcal C_1\) and \(\mathcal C_2\) are directly comparable only after their problem classes, oracle charges, termination predicates, and asymptotic variables are aligned, or after explicit reductions with quantified overhead map each differing component into a common framework. A complexity-interpretation limit is any unmatched component for which no such reduction is supplied. In that case, the numerical exponents or big-O expressions alone do not define an ordering of the methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complexity bound is meaningful only relative to its problem class, oracle, algorithmic permissions, stopping condition, and asymptotic variables. Two displayed rates cannot be directly ranked when any of those components differ unless an explicit reduction translates them into a common accounting model with quantified overhead.
assumptions_latex: Each result declares its quantified problem instances and initialization conditions.
Each result declares what one charged oracle operation contains.
Each result declares the exact criticality or accuracy termination predicate.
Constants and asymptotic variables are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_1\asymp_{\mathrm{cmp}}\mathcal C_2\Rightarrow(\mathfrak P_1,\mathfrak O_1,\mathfrak T_1,\mathbf z_1)\text{ and }(\mathfrak P_2,\mathfrak O_2,\mathfrak T_2,\mathbf z_2)\text{ are aligned or reduced with stated overhead}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Absent alignment, \(N_1(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^{-a})\) and \(N_2(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^{-b})\) do not by themselves imply that the first method is cheaper when \(a<b\).
special_cases_latex: An evaluation bound and an arithmetic-operation bound are comparable only after evaluation costs and inner work are quantified.
First-order and second-order criticality bounds require a mapping between their termination predicates before rate comparison.
immediate_consequences_latex: The complexity tuple should accompany any rate quoted outside its original theorem.
Dimension dependence hidden in oracle calls or constants can invalidate an epsilon-only comparison.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns logical comparability, not empirical runtime prediction.
No inspected source supports this exact tuple as a standard named object.

notation.meaning: Direct comparability after alignment or quantified reduction.

review_flags: Requires an authoritative source on oracle complexity and the comparability of optimization complexity results.
The tuple formalization is a candidate synthesis rather than established notation.

children.title: Evaluation-versus-Operation Complexity Gap
children.top_down_role: Divergence between oracle counts and arithmetic effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-versus-Operation Complexity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle evaluations do not control implementation-level arithmetic work without an explicit per-evaluation and subproblem-solution cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be an oracle algorithm that makes \(q(x)\) evaluations on input \(x\), and let \(A_M\) issue exactly the same queries and return the same output, but perform \(M(x)\) outcome-independent arithmetic operations between queries. Then \(N_{\mathrm{eval}}(A_M,x)=N_{\mathrm{eval}}(A,x)=q(x)\), whereas \(N_{\mathrm{op}}(A_M,x)\geq N_{\mathrm{op}}(A,x)+M(x)\). Because \(M(x)\) may be chosen arbitrarily, no finite function \(\Phi\) can ensure \(N_{\mathrm{op}}(A,x)\leq\Phi(N_{\mathrm{eval}}(A,x))\) for all implementations solely from an evaluation-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two implementations can make identical oracle queries yet perform arbitrarily different arithmetic work; evaluation complexity therefore cannot determine operation complexity without an explicit cost model.
assumptions_latex: \(A_M\) preserves every oracle query and the final output of \(A\).
The inserted arithmetic does not itself invoke the counted oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{eval}}\) alone yields no implementation-independent upper bound on \(N_{\mathrm{op}}\).

notation.meaning: inserted arithmetic workload on input x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oracle complexity counts queries and excludes unrestricted internal arithmetic unless a cost model is specified

children.title: Derivative-Order Cost Gap
children.top_down_role: Incomparability of evaluations carrying substantially different information.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Order Cost Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts of derivative evaluations of unequal order are incomparable until their information and computational costs are weighted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,p\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\geq 1\) and \(p\geq 2\), let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(p\)-times differentiable at every queried point, and let \(A\) be an oracle algorithm. For \(j\in\{0,\ldots,p\}\), let \(N_j(A,f)\) count calls to an oracle returning \(\nabla^j f\), with the convention \(\nabla^0 f=f\), and assign each order-\(j\) call a cost \(c_j>0\). Define \(C(A,f)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}c_jN_j(A,f)\). If \(A_1\) makes exactly one order-one call and \(A_p\) makes exactly one order-\(p\) call, then \(\sum_{j=0}^{p}N_j(A_1,f)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}N_j(A_p,f)=1\), while \(C(A_1,f)=c_1\) and \(C(A_p,f)=c_p\). Across positive cost assignments, the ratio \(c_p/c_1\) is unrestricted; hence the unweighted total evaluation count cannot compare methods using different derivative orders without a derivative-cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient call and a pth-derivative call each contribute one to an unweighted evaluation count, although their assigned costs can have any positive ratio. Counts across derivative orders therefore require an explicit cost model to be comparable.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(p\)-times differentiable at every queried point.
Each order-\(j\) oracle call has a specified positive cost \(c_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j=0}^{p}N_j\) is not a cost-comparable complexity measure across derivative orders without the weights \(c_j\).

notation.meaning: number of order-j derivative-oracle calls made by algorithm A on f
positive cost assigned to one order-j oracle call
comparison algorithms making one order-one or one order-p oracle call, respectively

children.title: Worst-Case-versus-Typical-Case Gap
children.top_down_role: Separation between adversarial guarantees and observed behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case-versus-Typical-Case Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected or median evaluation counts under a chosen instance distribution need not control the classwise worst-case count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm have evaluation counts \(T(f_{\mathrm e})=1\) and \(T(f_{\mathrm h})=B\) on two admissible instances, where \(B>1\). Under the distribution \(\mathbb{P}(f=f_{\mathrm h})=1/B\) and \(\mathbb{P}(f=f_{\mathrm e})=1-1/B\), one has \(\sup_fT(f)=B\) but \(\mathbb{E}[T]=2-1/B<2\). If \(B>2\), the median is also \(1\). Thus uniformly bounded typical complexity under instance distributions can coexist with arbitrarily large worst-case complexity, so empirical or distributional behavior cannot replace a worst-case guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rare hard instances can make worst-case complexity arbitrarily large while expected and median evaluation counts remain uniformly small.
assumptions_latex: The problem class contains admissible instances \(f_{\mathrm e}\) and \(f_{\mathrm h}\) with the stated evaluation counts.
Typical-case complexity is measured under the displayed instance distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[T]<2\) and \(\operatorname{median}(T)=1\) do not imply any uniform upper bound on \(\sup_fT(f)=B\).

notation.meaning: algorithmic evaluation count on instance f
evaluation count on the hard instance

No inspectable source is supplied, however, so the record requires a dedicated worst-case-versus-average/typical-case complexity citation. Because \(T\) counts evaluations, the sourced version should also declare \(B\) to be an integer greater than one.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For every size \(n\), let \(\mathcal I_n\) be a measurable instance class, let \(\mu_n\) be a probability distribution on \(\mathcal I_n\), and let \(T_A(I,\omega)\in[0,\infty]\) be the resource consumption of algorithm \(A\) on instance \(I\), with \(\omega\) denoting internal randomness. For a deterministic method, the variable \(\omega\) is omitted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-dependent average or quantile behavior is compared with an adversarial worst-case bound. The definition applies to evaluation counts, arithmetic work, or runtime, provided the same resource is used on both sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the worst-case complexity and the distributional mean complexity by \[W_A(n)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_n}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\omega}T_A(I,\omega),\qquad M_A(n)=\mathbb E_{I\sim\mu_n,\,\omega}[T_A(I,\omega)].\] For \(\tau\in(0,1)\), define the typical \(\tau\)-quantile by \[Q_{A,\tau}(n)=\inf\{t\ge0:\Pr_{I\sim\mu_n,\,\omega}(T_A(I,\omega)\le t)\ge\tau\}.\] A worst-case-versus-typical-case gap exists relative to the mean if \[\sup_{n\ge1}\frac{W_A(n)}{1+M_A(n)}=\infty,\] and relative to quantile level \(\tau\) if \[\sup_{n\ge1}\frac{W_A(n)}{1+Q_{A,\tau}(n)}=\infty.\] The definition makes the quantifiers explicit: worst case is a supremum over all admissible instances, whereas typical case is meaningful only after fixing \(\mu_n\) and either an expectation or a probability level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case complexity is the largest resource consumption over every admissible instance of a given size, including the essential worst case over any algorithmic randomness. Typical complexity is defined only after selecting a distribution: it may be the expected resource use or a fixed-probability quantile. A worst-versus-typical gap exists when the worst-case quantity divided by one plus the selected typical quantity is unbounded as problem size grows.
assumptions_latex: Each \((\mathcal I_n,\mu_n)\) is a probability space and \(T_A\) is a measurable nonnegative extended-real random variable.
Worst-case and typical quantities count the same resource and use the same success and termination conventions.
For a mean-based comparison, \(M_A(n)<\infty\) on the dimensions being compared; quantiles remain defined without this moment condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Gap}^{\mathrm{mean}}_{\mathrm{wc/typ}}(A,\mu)\iff \sup_n\frac{W_A(n)}{1+M_A(n)}=\infty,\qquad \operatorname{Gap}^{\tau}_{\mathrm{wc/typ}}(A,\mu)\iff \sup_n\frac{W_A(n)}{1+Q_{A,\tau}(n)}=\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The mean gap is absent exactly when some dimension-independent \(K<\infty\) satisfies \(W_A(n)\le K(1+M_A(n))\) for all \(n\); the analogous statement holds with \(Q_{A,\tau}\).
special_cases_latex: A method may have exponential worst-case behavior in \(n\) but polynomial mean behavior under a specified distribution, producing an exponential-versus-polynomial separation.
For deterministic \(A\), \(T_A(I,\omega)\) reduces to \(T_A(I)\), while the distributional distinction remains unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: An observed empirical median is not an average-case theorem unless the sampling distribution and success event are specified.
A worst-case upper bound can be valid yet highly nonpredictive of typical resource use; conversely, a small mean does not exclude rare costly instances.
boundary_notes: There is no distribution-free mathematical notion of a typical instance.
Finite benchmark averages estimate behavior under the benchmark sampling mechanism, not automatically under an application population.
Smoothed analysis and high-probability complexity are neighboring regimes but require their own perturbation or tail parameters.

notation.meaning: Adversarial worst-case resource consumption at size n.
Mean resource consumption under the declared instance distribution.
Smallest resource threshold attained with probability at least tau.

children.title: Local-Rate-versus-Global-Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinguishes local convergence order from global evaluation complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Rate-versus-Global-Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fast asymptotic recurrence does not bound the iterations required to enter the neighborhood where that recurrence holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any integer \(K\geq1\), define an error sequence by \(e_k=1\) for \(0\leq k<K\) and \(e_{K+m}=2^{-2^m}\) for \(m\geq0\). Then \(e_{k+1}=e_k^2\) for every \(k\geq K\), so every sequence in the family has the same quadratic local rate. Nevertheless, for every \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), the first index satisfying \(e_k\leq\varepsilon\) is \(K+\lceil\log_2\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rceil\), up to the equality convention. Since \(K\) is arbitrary, the local rate alone gives no global iteration or evaluation-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic convergence after entering a local region does not bound how long an algorithm may take to reach that region.
assumptions_latex: Accuracy is defined by the first index \(k\) for which \(e_k\leq\varepsilon\), with \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence \(e_{k+1}=e_k^2\) for all sufficiently large \(k\) does not bound the global hitting time uniformly in \(K\).

notation.meaning: entry index of the quadratic local regime
